haystack_sessions.content: The night delivery team meeting point is the south arcade.
I will record the south arcade for the night team meeting.
The daytime team has its own supervisor and route.
I will not merge those team arrangements.
The parcels contain demonstration supplies, not medical items.
I will preserve that limited description.

Dispatch desk opening workbook. The fictional delivery exercise is tracking parcel labels, a driver briefing, and the vehicle loading plan as separate work streams. The parcels contain demonstration supplies. The desk will use a parcel identifier to connect a contents list to a recipient-code label without putting a recipient's descriptive details on the outside of the carton. The identifier scheme is proposed here; no labels have been printed and no packing count is established by this entry.

The contents-list draft separates items supplied for a demonstration from items that should be returned afterward. A sample list has spaces for a kit component, quantity checked, and a note about missing pieces. The packing volunteers have not completed it. The desk proposes reviewing the list with the demonstration organizer before filling cartons, since a neat list would still be wrong if it omitted something the activity requires. This review is a next task rather than a completed inventory.

The driver briefing will distinguish route planning, vehicle allocation, and actual departure. Its first page is a blank template with spaces for the responsible team and the latest contact role. The daytime team's supervisor and route belong in a separate section. The desk does not have a night driver assignment yet. It should not copy a daytime name into the night briefing simply to avoid a blank. The meeting arrangement and vehicle readiness are also different pieces of information.

For loading, a volunteer has proposed grouping cartons by their order on a route, while another proposed grouping them by demonstration kit type. Neither plan has been chosen because the desk has not reviewed the contents list or confirmed the vehicle. The next session should establish label requirements, approve the parcel identifier format, and identify who can review the kit list. The workbook has a separate actual-events log so later printing, loading, departure, and delivery can each be recorded when they occur. A prepared document or folded carton will support that workflow but should not stand in for an event that the team has not reported. This opening entry therefore records the work plan and leaves the operational states open.

The desk has assigned the kit-list review to organizer Petra and label reconciliation to volunteer Dev. The transport coordinator will maintain the driver briefing. This division keeps a packing decision traceable to the organizer while allowing Dev to resolve print mismatches without inventing a change to what the demonstration kit should contain.
I will keep inventory, transport planning, and actual events in separate records.
Every parcel must carry a printed recipient-code label before dispatch.
The dispatch checklist requires a printed recipient-code label on each parcel.
A volunteer suggested color-coded tape as an extra aid.
Tape is optional and not a substitute for the required label.
We folded the empty cartons yesterday.
Carton folding is complete, not dispatch.

Identifier decision and carton-preparation record. The organizer approved a simple parcel identifier consisting of a kit-letter prefix and a sequence entry. The identifier is a local inventory aid, not a recipient address. The desk has added it to the contents-list form and the label-printing worksheet. A printed recipient-code label is required on every parcel before dispatch; the proposed colored tape would be an extra sorting aid only. The tape idea has no approved color mapping yet.

The empty cartons are folded. The packing log records that preparation separately from filling, sealing, and dispatch. The organizer reviewed the contents-list draft and requested a returnable-items column so borrowed demonstration pieces can be checked back in later. The revised form is contents-r2. No completed kit count has been entered. The next packing volunteer should use r2 rather than the earlier sample so the returnable pieces are not lost in a general supplies total.

The driver briefing template now has a page for unresolved questions: who will drive, which vehicle will be assigned, and whether the chosen loading arrangement fits that vehicle. The night driver remains unassigned. The desk has asked the organizer to review which demonstration kits must stay together during loading. That answer will help choose between route-order grouping and kit-type grouping. It is not yet available in this session.

The daytime section of the workbook remains separate. Its route can be updated by its supervisor without closing a night-team task. The desk proposes a reconciliation at each shift change: compare printed label identifiers with the packing list, record any unmatched identifier, and leave the affected carton unready until the mismatch is resolved. This is a proposed checking procedure, not an already completed reconciliation. The next session should bring the kit-grouping recommendation and the state of driver recruitment. A clean form and a stack of folded cartons are useful preparation, but the desk still needs contents checks, labels, transport arrangements, and actual event entries before it can describe parcels as dispatched.

Petra has returned the form review with the added returnable-items column marked clearly. Dev will prepare a paper reconciliation exercise before the first print run. The exercise should include an unmatched identifier so volunteers practice holding a row open rather than forcing every printed label into a parcel entry that merely looks similar.
The approved identifier format does not establish printing or dispatch.
The daytime team finished its route.
That completed route does not establish a night-team departure.
The night vehicle is still awaiting a driver.
Driver assignment is pending.
Please draft a driver briefing.
A draft briefing will not imply that a driver accepted it.

Kit-grouping review and draft briefing. The organizer has asked that each demonstration kit stay together in loading. The desk therefore chose kit-type grouping as the working loading plan, with a route-order note attached to each group. This decision will need a fit check once a night vehicle is allocated. It does not establish that cartons have been loaded. The alternative route-order-only plan is retained in the planning notes with the reason it was not chosen.

The packing team used contents-r2 to make a trial inventory of an example kit. The trial revealed that the form's returnable-items column lacked a place to note condition. The desk added a short condition note to create contents-r3. The example exercise is filed as a form test, not a full inventory of all night parcels. The next packing task is to use r3 for the actual kits and resolve any missing components with the organizer.

The daytime team has completed its route. The night vehicle still awaits a driver assignment. The draft night briefing now includes the kit-grouping decision and the open driver question, but its acknowledgment space is empty. A prepared briefing does not show that a driver accepted the task. The desk proposes asking any volunteer driver to review the kit handling notes as well as the route, because grouping decisions affect how cartons should be handled.

The label worksheet is ready to receive print results by parcel identifier. The desk has not entered a completed printing run. The colored-tape idea remains a proposal and should not displace the recipient-code labels already required. The next shift should review that optional idea, continue driver recruitment, and begin the actual contents checks using r3. A packing volunteer can advance the contents work while transport remains unresolved. The workbook will keep those streams visible so a completed daytime route or a successful sample-form exercise cannot be mistaken for the night team being ready to leave. This entry narrows the loading method and improves the form while leaving real loading and dispatch unrecorded.

Dev completed the reconciliation exercise. One sample identifier was deliberately left unmatched, and the volunteers correctly placed it in the exception list. The desk has retained that training sheet separately from the real printing worksheet. Its successful review supports the procedure, but none of its sample rows counts as a printed night-parcel label.
The form trial improves the next real inventory without counting sample labels.
Prepare a team reminder using the recorded night meeting point.
The draft reminder sends the night team to the south arcade.
The reminder has not been sent.
I will keep it marked unsent.
We rejected the color-tape idea because labels already distinguish parcels.
The optional tape proposal is rejected.

Reminder draft and packing-form decision. The team reminder is an unsent draft. It belongs in the internal coordination packet, not in the actual departure log. The desk has removed the colored-tape proposal from the active work list after the team rejected it as redundant with the parcel labels. The label worksheet will therefore use the recipient-code labels and local parcel identifiers without adding a second color scheme that volunteers would have to reconcile.

The packing volunteers completed the first pass through the actual kit contents using contents-r3. They found that one demonstration kit lacks a small display stand. The organizer has agreed to supply that stand but has not delivered it yet. The affected kit stays marked incomplete on the packing list. The other entries are recorded as checked contents, not dispatched parcels. The condition-note addition from the earlier form trial was useful for distinguishing a worn returnable clip from a missing item; the clip is present and marked for later organizer review.

The driver briefing has been revised to describe the incomplete kit and the working kit-grouping plan. It still has no accepted night driver. The desk proposes adding a brief acknowledgment checklist for a future driver: review the kit groups, note any handling concerns, and confirm which vehicle is actually allocated before loading. The checklist remains a proposed briefing procedure. It does not assign a person or a vehicle.

The next desk tasks are to follow up on the missing display stand, obtain the organizer's decision on the worn clip, and continue driver recruitment. Label printing can begin for entries whose identifiers and recipient codes have been checked, but a printed label alone will not close the contents issue. The unsent reminder should be retained for revision when transport arrangements are clearer. The workbook now contains genuine progress in packing and a rejected optional aid, while preserving a specific open component request and transport uncertainty. The next shift can act on those requests rather than repeating a broad instruction to finish packing without knowing what is missing.

Petra owns the display-stand request and the worn-clip decision; Dev owns the label worksheet. The desk added links between the affected contents rows and their open questions. That arrangement lets printing proceed for checked identifiers without hiding a kit-content problem or making the print volunteer decide whether an incomplete kit is acceptable.
The missing stand and worn clip have named owners for resolution.
A driver volunteered for the night route, but no vehicle is allocated.
Driver availability and vehicle allocation are different requirements.
The printer jammed after six labels.
Six printed labels are not six dispatched parcels.
The unprinted labels remain on the task list.
I will preserve the remaining labeling work.

Driver availability and print exception. A volunteer is available to drive the night route, but no vehicle is allocated. The desk has given the volunteer the draft handling questions for review, leaving the vehicle fit check unresolved. The volunteer's availability closes the recruitment question; it does not fill the vehicle row or establish a departure. The briefing acknowledgment will need to identify the actual plan reviewed once transport is known.

The printer jammed after six labels. The printing worksheet lists those successful outputs by parcel identifier and leaves the remaining rows open. The desk asks volunteers not to restart the whole queue blindly, because duplicate labels could create confusion during attachment. The proposed recovery is to compare the printed stack against the worksheet, clear the printer, and resume only the unprinted rows. Clearing the jam has not yet occurred in this entry.

The organizer delivered the missing display stand, and the packing volunteer added it to the affected kit's contents entry. The organizer also decided that the worn clip can remain in the demonstration kit, with its condition noted for return checking. Those two contents questions are now resolved. The desk has marked the corresponding first-pass inventory items complete while keeping sealing, label attachment, and dispatch as separate states. A resolved contents question does not show that a parcel has been handed to a driver.

The driver reviewed the kit-grouping rationale and asked for the heaviest group to be identified in the loading plan before the vehicle fit check. The desk proposes weighing the groups during the next packing session and adding a relative loading note. No weight is supplied here. The next shift should therefore recover the printing queue, obtain a vehicle allocation, and collect the information needed for the fit check. The earlier display-stand request and clip decision should remain closed unless new evidence changes them. Carrying forward their resolutions prevents the next handoff from wasting time chasing parts that have already arrived while more immediate printing and transport questions remain open.

Dev has marked the six successful prints on the real worksheet and left the training exercise untouched. Petra's component decisions now close the linked contents questions. The dispatcher can therefore separate an active printer exception from resolved kit issues when handing work to the next volunteer, instead of treating every open-looking paper as equally current.
The contents questions are closed while printing and vehicle work remain open.
The printer was cleared and the remaining labels were printed.
Label printing is complete; attachment still requires a check.
The daytime supervisor returned an empty tote.
A returned tote does not concern the night meeting point.
We have not loaded the night parcels.
Loading remains pending.

Recovered print queue and loading-plan measurements. The printer is cleared and the remaining labels are printed. The desk reconciled the output stack with the printing worksheet, so the printing task is complete. Attachment still requires checking against the parcels. The local identifier on a label will help that check, but it does not guarantee a volunteer attached the label to the right carton. The desk has prepared a separate attachment column rather than copying the print-complete status into it.

The packing team measured the grouped cartons and recorded their relative weight order in the loading worksheet. The group containing the display bases is the heaviest. The driver has requested that its position be considered first in the fit check, with lighter groups arranged around it only after the vehicle is known. The worksheet now supplies the information requested in the previous session, but it remains a plan. The night parcels have not been loaded.

The daytime supervisor returned an empty tote. The desk recorded it in the daytime return log, leaving the night loading list unchanged. The returnable-items column in contents-r3 will be useful for later night-kit reconciliation, but there are no night recipient acknowledgments to enter yet. The resolved display-stand and worn-clip entries remain visible in the contents record so a later return check can compare what actually went out with what came back.

The current transport gap is vehicle allocation. Driver availability and the weight-order worksheet are ready to support the fit check once a vehicle is assigned. The next dispatcher should then review the grouping against the actual vehicle, check label attachment, and address any damaged or unclear label found in that check. No such defect has been reported in this entry. The earlier reminder is still retained as an unsent draft for controlled revision. The next shift can now focus on a smaller set of physical checks instead of reprinting completed labels or reopening resolved component requests. Printing recovery is complete, while loading and departure remain genuinely pending.

Dev reconciled the resumed print output by identifier and signed only the printing column. The attachment column is reserved for whoever checks labels on actual parcels. The desk chose this separation after the training exercise showed why a stack of correct labels does not establish that each one has reached the right carton.
Printing is complete; attachment and actual loading still need evidence.
A vehicle is now allocated, but the night team has not left.
Allocation does not establish departure or delivery.
Keep the earlier reminder for controlled revision.
Reusing its location detail requires current access.
One parcel has an unreadable label.
That parcel needs a replacement label before dispatch.

Vehicle allocation and attachment exception. A vehicle is now allocated. The driver has compared the kit-grouping plan with its available loading area and accepted the grouping for a later load. The fit check closes the vehicle-planning question but does not record physical loading. The team has not left. The dispatcher has kept the loading, departure, and delivery spaces empty so the completed plan does not become a fictional route event.

The label attachment check found one unreadable label. The affected parcel identifier is marked on the attachment worksheet, and the desk has held that parcel out of the ready group pending a reprint. The other checked labels can remain marked checked. The proposed recovery is to print a replacement for the affected identifier, remove the unreadable copy, and have a second volunteer confirm the replacement matches the contents-list entry. That recovery has not been completed yet. Reprinting the entire label batch would create unnecessary duplicates.

The driver briefing has a second open item. The volunteer has reviewed handling and fit, but the contact-role line still names the recruitment desk rather than the dispatcher who will supervise the actual shift. The coordinator proposes changing that line to the duty dispatcher role and having the volunteer acknowledge the revised briefing. No personal contact details are invented in this record. The content can be corrected by role while the team waits to load.

The earlier reminder is retained for controlled revision. Its meeting detail should not be copied into every unrelated packing document. The contents and label checks can proceed from parcel identifiers and the kit list. The next practical tasks are the targeted label reprint and the briefing contact-role correction, followed by a final attachment review before loading. The vehicle allocation and accepted grouping remain completed planning facts. There are still no confirmed night deliveries or recipient acknowledgments. This entry makes the remaining defects concrete enough for the next dispatcher to resolve without undoing successful print recovery or assuming that an allocated vehicle has already traveled.

The attachment exception is assigned to Dev for a targeted reprint, with a second volunteer to check the result. The duty-dispatcher wording is assigned to the transport coordinator. These tasks can proceed in parallel, but neither closes the later loading entry. The handoff should name both outstanding actions instead of a vague request to finalize paperwork.
The targeted reprint and briefing-role correction are separate remaining tasks.
Prepare a handoff for the next dispatcher.
The handoff can separate meeting details, vehicle status and label checks.
No night deliveries have been confirmed.
I will not invent recipient acknowledgments.
Suggest one permitted next task.
Reprint the unreadable label and verify attachment before loading.

Dispatcher handoff. The night operation has an available driver, an allocated vehicle, a reviewed kit-grouping plan, and a completed contents check. The missing display stand was supplied, and the organizer accepted the worn clip with its condition recorded for later return checking. The relative weight worksheet identifies the display-base group as the heaviest, and the driver accepted the grouping after reviewing vehicle fit. Those planning results can be reused without claiming that loading or departure happened.

The immediate parcel defect is one unreadable label identified in the attachment worksheet. The next dispatcher should reprint only that parcel's label, remove the unreadable copy, and obtain a matching check against the contents record. The prior printer jam was resolved and the full print queue was reconciled, so restarting all labels would lose the benefit of that work. The attachment check is a separate step from printing and must confirm that every parcel carries the required printed recipient-code label before dispatch.

The briefing also needs its contact-role line changed from the recruitment desk to the duty dispatcher role. After that correction, the volunteer should acknowledge the current briefing. The earlier unsent reminder remains a retained coordination draft, with its meeting detail subject to current access when reused. The dispatcher can complete label and briefing tasks using their own records without broadcasting meeting information into the packing workflow.

No night delivery has been confirmed, and no recipient acknowledgment exists. The actual-events log should stay empty for departure and delivery until those events are reported. The returned daytime tote belongs to a separate completed route and does not close any night entry. The next useful sequence is to repair the identified label, correct and acknowledge the briefing, verify attachment, and then record loading when it actually occurs. This sequence uses the latest exception notes rather than treating all paperwork as unfinished or all preparation as delivery. It also preserves the returnable-item condition notes for a later check when demonstration kits come back, a task that has not yet begun in the night operation.

Dev's targeted reprint and the coordinator's briefing correction are still open at transfer. The new dispatcher should collect their completion notes before loading proceeds. Petra's contents decisions remain closed and available for the later return check. This preserves responsibility across shifts without requiring volunteers to reconstruct the entire packing history from loose documents.
The new dispatcher can resolve those exceptions before recording any actual loading.

haystack_sessions.content: The miniature tram set is stored in the violet equipment cupboard.
I will record the violet equipment cupboard as the tram set storage place.
The seaside set belongs to a different film exercise.
I will keep the two sets separate.
We painted the tram wheels yesterday.
Wheel painting is complete, not filming.

Animation office opening file. The tram exercise will use a storyboard register, a media index, and a prop-condition card alongside the equipment collection record. These documents have different purposes. The storyboard describes intended action, the media index identifies actual files, and the condition card records the physical state of a prop. The office does not yet have tram footage to index. It can prepare the index structure without filling it with clips borrowed from another exercise.

The director has proposed a simple storyboard sequence: establish the empty stop, bring the tram into view, and end with a waiting figure noticing it. That is a proposed narrative, not an approved shot list. The storyboard pages use rough drawings with no movement increments or frame counts. The director wants the next team meeting to discuss whether the waiting figure is necessary to understand the scene. The discussion can change the plan without implying that any puppet has already been posed or photographed.

The media-index draft has columns for project, file role, source device, and current use. A reference clip would be identified as a reference rather than placed in the footage column. The coordinator proposes keeping production stills, continuity images, and animation frames in separate roles so a useful photograph cannot accidentally be counted as finished film. The team has not agreed the folder naming convention yet. That convention is a next administrative decision, not a record that the corresponding files exist.

The prop-condition card currently records the completed wheel painting. It has a separate open space for later checks before use. The seaside set belongs to another exercise and has its own condition record. The next session should agree how to name files, review the proposed narrative, and establish any preparation requirements before movement. The collection note will remain separate from those creative decisions. An equipment location can help a crew plan collection, but the storytelling and media-control work can proceed on paper. This opening record therefore sets up the production documents while leaving the storyboard, frame-rate choice, photography, and actual collection to later decisions and observations.

The office assigned the storyboard register to artist Mina and the media index to coordinator Jules. The prop volunteer will supply condition updates separately. The handoff should retain these roles so a creative approval, a file classification, and a physical repair report remain traceable even when one person later assembles the packet.
The storyboard, media index, and condition card will retain different roles.
Before changing a puppet pose for a filmed frame, save a continuity reference photograph.
Changing a puppet pose for a filmed frame requires a saved continuity reference photograph first.
We may shoot through a colored filter.
The filter remains a proposal.
The director has not approved a frame rate.
Frame-rate selection is unresolved.

Storyboard review and media-role convention. The team has adopted a media naming convention with a project prefix, a role label, and a revision entry. The role labels distinguish reference material, continuity records, and captured animation frames. The index will keep a separate project column even when a filename is copied into a shared folder. This should make it harder for a clip from the seaside exercise to become apparent tram footage simply because someone can see it in the same browser.

The director reviewed the rough narrative and asked for a clearer reason that the waiting figure notices the tram. The storyboard artist proposes adding a sign that the figure can look toward. The sign is a paper design idea, not a built prop. The artist will compare a plain shape with a lettered sign at the next meeting. No frame rate is approved yet, so the storyboard still describes action in words and drawings rather than assuming a number of frames per movement.

The continuity-reference requirement is recorded with the preparation tasks. The camera operator proposes a checklist that asks where a reference image will be saved and how the crew will identify it before moving a puppet for a shot. The draft checklist has no completed image entry. The proposed colored filter belongs in a separate visual-test note because its effect can be studied using a chart without posing the tram scene. The team has not performed that chart test yet.

The prop-condition card still carries the wheel-painting entry and an open pre-use review. The coordinator asks the next session to check the puppet condition, compare the sign designs, and confirm that the media index can distinguish a reference clip from a captured frame. These tasks do not require the crew to claim that a scene is set. The office will leave actual-file rows empty until files are created or received. This convention gives the later crew a way to record concrete evidence without allowing a prepared folder name or blank checklist to stand in for a completed photograph, a selected frame rate, or an animation sequence that has not been shot.

Mina has dated the sign alternatives in the storyboard register, while Jules has prepared empty rows for future files. The prop volunteer has not yet supplied a new condition check. The office will request that update rather than infer readiness from the painted wheels, which describe only one completed preparation task.
Empty index rows will remain empty until actual files exist.
The seaside exercise finished its test shot.
That test does not establish a tram sequence.
One tram puppet has a loose arm.
The arm issue should be recorded before movement.
Could we use removable adhesive?
Adhesive is a suggested repair, not completed work.

Prop exception and storyboard alternatives. The loose arm on one tram puppet has been entered on the prop-condition card. Removable adhesive is a suggested repair, not an approved or completed action. The prop volunteer has asked to compare repair options before anyone poses the puppet for the tram sequence. The condition card should record the chosen action and its result when known, rather than letting a suggestion in a conversation become the repair history.

The storyboard artist has compared the plain and lettered sign drawings. The director prefers the plain shape because the scene should not depend on a viewer reading small text. The sign drawing is now part of the storyboard working revision, but no physical sign is built. The artist also proposed a wider opening view to make the stop visible before the tram enters. The director has asked for a revised sketch before deciding that change. These are creative decisions at the planning stage, separate from the puppet repair.

The seaside exercise has finished its test shot. The media coordinator entered that clip as another project's reference material, preserving its project label and role. It is not a tram capture. A small index check found that the draft form did not say who supplied a reference file, so the coordinator has added a supplied-by role column. That form correction is complete; the team still has no captured tram frames to list.

The next work packet should contain the wider storyboard sketch, the result of the prop repair decision when made, and the planned filter-chart test. The camera operator has drafted a save-location question for the continuity checklist, but no continuity image is available. The office should not fill that row from the seaside test merely because it is a convenient image. Each project needs evidence appropriate to its own setup. This session advances the sign design and improves file provenance while leaving a specific prop defect and a framing decision open. The next crew can act on those items without treating preparation in another exercise as progress in this film's actual photography.

Jules entered the other-project test under its supplied-by role and asked Mina to mark the accepted sign drawing. The loose-arm issue stays with the prop volunteer. These linked requests make the next review specific: file provenance, storyboard choice, and repair decision each need a different kind of evidence and cannot close one another.
The accepted sign and known prop defect have separate next actions.
Draft an equipment collection note for the tram set.
The note directs the crew to the violet equipment cupboard for the miniature tram set.
Keep it as a draft until the crew leader reviews it.
The draft does not establish that equipment was collected.
We rejected the colored filter after a separate color chart test.
The filter proposal is rejected, without implying a film shot.

Collection draft and visual-test decision. The equipment collection note remains a draft pending crew-leader review. It can be retained with the production packet, but it does not establish a completed collection. The office has added a separate receipt line to the packet so any later physical handover can be recorded as its own event. That blank line should not be filled merely because the crew leader reads or approves the note.

The colored filter has been rejected after a separate color-chart test. The camera operator has filed the chart images as visual-test references, with the purpose and project role visible in the media index. They are not animation frames from the tram sequence. The unfiltered approach is now the working visual plan. The team does not need to keep listing the rejected filter as an open choice unless new evidence leads to a documented reconsideration.

The revised wider opening sketch has been reviewed and accepted for the storyboard. The director wants the stop visible before the tram's entrance, retaining the plain sign shape chosen earlier. The artist has combined those decisions in storyboard-r3 and left the movement timing unspecified pending the frame-rate choice. The next shot-list draft should use r3 rather than the narrow opening sketch. No physical sign or set pose is created by this storyboard approval.

The loose-arm repair remains unresolved in this entry. The prop volunteer is comparing the suggested adhesive with a mechanical joint option and has not reported completed work. The office asks the next session to record the repair choice with its actual outcome, settle the frame-rate question, and establish how the storyboard decisions will be turned into a shot list. The media index now has enough role labels to preserve the filter-chart evidence without calling it film footage. The practical value of the packet is that the next crew can identify which choices are settled, which documents are drafts, and which physical work has not happened, rather than recreating the creative discussion from memory.

Mina has signed the storyboard-r3 decision note. Jules has filed the chart-test references with the rejected-filter decision. The prop decision is still awaited. The crew leader can now review settled creative inputs while requesting the missing physical-work update, instead of delaying all paperwork until every production stream reaches the same state.
The wider storyboard and rejected filter are settled planning inputs.
The director selected a frame rate after reviewing test clips from another project.
That choice is approved, but those clips are not this film.
We repaired the loose arm with a replacement joint.
The joint repair is complete.
No puppet has been posed for the tram sequence.
I will not invent a continuity image.

Repair entry and production-specification review. The loose arm has been repaired with a replacement joint. The prop-condition card records that completed repair and leaves the pre-shot setup check open. The earlier adhesive suggestion remains in the decision history as an option that was not used. The crew should not describe adhesive as the fitted repair merely because it appeared first in the conversation. The repaired prop has not been posed for the tram sequence.

The director selected a frame rate after reviewing clips from another project. The media index retains those clips as references with their own project labels. The selected rate is a production choice, not a measurement extracted from tram footage. The office has created a specification note for that choice without inventing a numerical rate that the source discussion did not record. The next crew should consult the director's approved specification rather than infer the number from a reference clip's appearance.

The storyboard remains r3, with the wider opening and plain sign shape. The artist has drafted a shot-list layout containing shot purpose, required props, and the reference record needed before movement. The layout is a form, not an approved list of captured shots. The crew leader asks for a dependency column so a shot that needs a repaired prop or an approved design can be distinguished from one ready for setup. That column is now added as a draft improvement.

The next production work is to turn the storyboard into a shot list and to verify that the repaired prop is ready for the intended setup. The continuity record remains unfilled; no image should be invented to make the new form look complete. The filter decision and wider framing choice can be carried forward as settled planning inputs. The media index should keep the color-chart test, outside-project clips, and eventual tram frames in distinct roles. This entry supplies a completed repair and a selected production setting while preserving the absence of a posed scene. It gives the next team enough structure to plan the sequence without counting another film's work or a blank form as this film's actual capture.

The prop volunteer supplied the replacement-joint entry, and Mina linked it as a preparation input in the draft shot list. Jules left the actual-image rows empty. A repaired prop can support a setup plan, but the file coordinator still needs a real saved image before recording a continuity artifact or a captured frame.
The repaired joint does not create a posed scene or a captured image.
The seaside set was packed for storage.
That packing record does not move the tram set.
We charged the camera batteries.
Charging is preparation, not filming.
The crew wants a shot list.
A shot list can be drafted from the available production notes.

Shot-list drafting and battery preparation. The crew has requested a shot list, and the artist is using approved storyboard-r3 as its basis. The draft separates the wider establishing view, the tram entrance, and the waiting figure's response. Each row has a purpose, a required-prop note, and a dependency space. The list does not contain frame counts, captured-image filenames, or claims that a shot has been completed. The director still needs to review it before it becomes the working list.

The camera batteries are charged. The equipment worksheet records charging as preparation and leaves the later camera setup check open. A charged battery can support the next task without proving that the camera produced a file. The seaside set has been packed for storage under its own project entry. That action does not relocate the tram set or establish a tram collection. The media coordinator will keep the two projects separate in the index even when their equipment worksheets are stored together.

The shot-list review has found one dependency that needs clearer wording: the repaired puppet's row says ready without identifying the continuity record required before shot movement. The artist has changed the draft row to say repaired, with setup checks pending. This preserves the completed joint work while making the next stage explicit. The continuity checklist now has a space for both the saved image and a check that the file can be reopened. That is a proposed verification step, not a completed photograph.

The crew leader also asked for a naming example for future frames. The coordinator supplied a fictional filename pattern showing project, shot, and sequence position, clearly labeled as a pattern rather than an existing file. The index still has no tram frame entries. The next session should approve the shot list, inspect the planned save location, and prepare the continuity image before posing. The charged batteries and repaired prop are useful inputs, but the next crew must not convert them into an invented filming milestone. The handoff should identify the latest draft and its remaining approval rather than sending the team back to the earlier narrow storyboard or rejected filter option.

Mina owns the pending shot-list approval, and Jules owns the save-location review. The crew leader asked them to return separate notes. That request will let the next team use an approved list while still seeing a file-routing problem, rather than collapsing both streams into a single production-ready label that conceals the remaining task.
The shot-list draft and save-location review have separate owners.
The shot list is approved, but no tram frames have been captured.
Approval and capture remain separate.
Retain the collection note for the next crew.
Its stored-location content may need access review.
The continuity-photo folder is empty.
The required photograph still needs to be saved before movement.

Shot-list approval and empty-folder finding. The director has approved the shot list. The office has labeled it shot-list-r2 and linked it to storyboard-r3. The list preserves the wider opening and the chosen plain sign, and it distinguishes the repaired puppet from the still-pending shot setup. No tram frames have been captured. Approval authorizes planning from the list; it does not populate its capture or file-reference columns.

The continuity-photo folder is empty. The camera operator checked the proposed save location and found that the workstation shortcut opens a reference folder for the other project rather than the intended tram continuity folder. The shortcut needs correction before the first image is saved. The folder finding therefore creates a concrete file-routing task in addition to the requirement to take the photograph. The operator should correct the link, open the intended destination to verify it, and only then create and reopen the required image. None of those new actions is completed in this entry.

The crew leader retains the collection note for the next team. Its stored-location content should be reviewed when used, while the storyboard and shot-list work can proceed from their own records. The equipment worksheet still records charged batteries and no capture result. The prop card retains the completed replacement-joint repair. The seaside packing entry and its test clip remain separate from the tram exercise.

The next handoff should emphasize the current approved shot list and the stale save-location shortcut. Reopening the rejected filter choice or rebuilding the narrow storyboard would discard settled decisions without addressing the real next obstacle. A crew can make meaningful progress by fixing the shortcut and preparing the continuity image before posing. The office has left the actual image row empty so a reader will not mistake the naming pattern supplied last session for a real photograph. Once an image exists, the crew should record its actual file and check it reopens. At present, the project has ready plans and repaired props, but still no posed tram sequence or captured frames.

Jules recorded the wrong-folder shortcut as a file-routing exception and linked it to the empty continuity row. Mina's shot-list approval remains valid. The next crew can correct the route and create the needed image without asking the artist to reopen the story or treating approval as proof that the file system is ready.
The approved list can stand while the stale file route is corrected.
Prepare a transfer sheet for the next animation team.
It can separate storage, repaired props and unstarted filming.
Do not call test clips from another film our footage.
I will preserve their distinct provenance.
Suggest a next permitted task.
Capture and save the continuity photograph before posing a puppet.

Animation-team transfer note. The current creative plan is storyboard-r3 and approved shot-list-r2. They include the wider opening and the plain sign shape. The colored filter was rejected after a chart test, and the loose arm was repaired with a replacement joint rather than adhesive. Those decisions should be carried forward with their evidence notes, not reintroduced as open questions merely because the crew has changed. The selected frame rate is an approved specification whose numerical value is not repeated in these notes.

The next practical task concerns the continuity-image workflow. The designated folder is empty, and the workstation shortcut currently opens another project's reference folder. The new crew should correct and verify that destination before saving the first continuity photograph. It should then save the actual image, reopen it, and record its filename before posing the puppet for the sequence. The naming pattern in the earlier packet is only an example; it is not an existing image and cannot satisfy the requirement.

The media index keeps other-project test clips, the filter chart, planned documents, and future tram captures in separate roles. The new crew must not count the seaside test or another project's frame-rate references as tram footage. The charged batteries and repaired joint are completed preparation, while no tram frames have been captured and the shot remains unposed. The collection note remains a draft to check when equipment is collected, not a receipt that collection already happened.

The transfer sheet can therefore identify three useful actions in order: repair the save-location link, create and verify the continuity record, and proceed with the approved shot setup only when the prerequisite is met. A later capture log should name the actual shot and file produced. This sequence advances the work using the latest documents while respecting the empty-folder finding. It avoids wasting effort on superseded creative alternatives and avoids making up files to fill blank cells. The next team has enough planning context to begin, but it still needs to create the physical and digital evidence that separates a prepared animation exercise from completed footage.

The transfer index passes the shortcut exception to the incoming file coordinator and the approved shot list to the crew leader. The first completed continuity record should cite the verified destination and actual image. Until then, Jules's empty row remains an honest missing artifact, not a place to paste a convenient reference from another project.
The next crew can correct the destination and create the actual continuity record.

revision_note: Correct unsupported storyboard-approval assertion; original v1 source preserved in input_sources_read.json.
expansion_note: Eight newly authored task documents, with independent decisions and cross-session revisions. Original turn indices are retained; appended user document is turn 006 and response is turn 007. Not a real-user history.

creation_note: Original fictional scripted conversation for evaluation, not a real user log; all dates and roles are authored. No public-source citation or third-party data license is claimed.

haystack_sessions.content: The first test sheet was reported at twenty-eight percent ink coverage.
I will record twenty-eight percent for that first test sheet.
The screen print and the risograph run are separate jobs.
I will not transfer measurements between their sheets.
We cut the risograph paper this morning.
Paper cutting is complete, not a print run.

Production desk note, issue A. We are preparing two outreach products alongside the test-sheet review: a folding activity leaflet for the neighborhood workshop and a packet of blank practice sheets for the mobile library. The leaflet is meant to be opened with one hand. Its trial text has three panels: arrival instructions, a materials list, and a return address. Readers must encounter those panels in that order when the sheet is unfolded. Our current mock-up places the return address on the outside flap, where it is visible before the instructions; that is an unresolved layout problem, not a print defect. The mobile-library sheets require no text at all and must stay separate from the leaflet pile.

I recorded the stock ledger at opening. We have twelve reusable paper bands, two rigid carrying folders, one cracked transparent sleeve, and a carton of unprinted practice paper. The cracked sleeve has been removed from the packing table because its edge catches folded corners. A volunteer suggested trimming the damaged edge, but we have not decided whether that would leave enough material to hold a packet securely. Both carrying folders still close properly. One belongs to the library collection and the other to the workshop; pencil labels currently distinguish them. We should replace those temporary labels before handing either folder to a driver.

The workshop coordinator wants the leaflet draft by the fourth session so an accessibility volunteer can examine the unfolding sequence. They are reviewing sequence and legibility, not signing off colors. The library coordinator instead needs a count of usable blank sheets. These are separate requests with different evidence. I assigned the count to the afternoon helper, who has accepted the task but has not opened the carton. We have not promised a delivery quantity to the library.

The next planning meeting should decide how to mark the two product piles without adding marks to the blank practice sheets. Possible solutions are removable tray labels or divider cards placed beside each stack. Writing directly on every sheet would defeat the library request. Please keep both options open in the desk log until the coordinators agree on a handling method. The count, leaflet sequence review and folder labeling can advance independently of the first test-sheet report.
I will keep the leaflet sequence review, blank-sheet count and folder labels as separate open tasks. No library quantity or delivery has been confirmed.
Each approved print bundle must have its matching color-reference strip attached.
The matching color-reference strip is required for every approved bundle.
We might add a foil title later.
Foil remains an unapproved proposal.
The folding guide has been proofread.
Text proofreading does not approve printed colors.

Desk log, issue B. The afternoon helper counted sixty usable blank practice sheets and found four sheets with torn corners. The torn sheets were moved into the scrap tray for testing pencil marks; they are not part of the library allocation. A second helper checked the sixty-sheet count by dividing the pile into six groups of ten. The library coordinator has now requested forty sheets for one introductory class, leaving twenty available for later requests. No sheets have been packed or collected. The requested forty should be reserved in the ledger so another workshop does not promise the same stock.

We selected divider cards beside the stacks rather than writing directly on the paper. The cards read Library Practice and Workshop Leaflet. These labels identify product piles and must travel with the pile when a volunteer moves it. I found that the large workshop table is shared with a sewing group on alternate afternoons. Our current storage plan therefore uses the two rigid folders between sessions. The plan still needs a check that the divider cards fit inside without bending the sheets. A pencil sketch of the folder arrangement is attached to the internal log as a draft, not as proof of packing.

The leaflet editor revised the order of the three panels. The arrival instructions now appear on the outside flap, while the return address moves to the last panel. The materials list still crosses a fold line, which may obscure the small text when the paper is held partly closed. The editor has proposed shortening the list by removing the optional apron, but the workshop coordinator has not agreed. The apron is optional safety clothing for a messy activity, not equipment every visitor must bring. That distinction should remain clear in any shortened wording.

We also received a request to translate the arrival instructions. The coordinator has not named a language or a translator, so there is no translation task ready to assign. I asked them to identify the audience before anyone copies text into an automatic translation service. This new request must not delay the independent library-sheet reservation. At the next session, the useful checks are the folder fit, the partly folded materials panel and confirmation of whether a translation is actually needed. None has yet been completed.
The reserve is forty usable sheets, with twenty unreserved. The proposed collection and translation questions remain open; the revised panel layout still needs its specified checks.
The screen-print job used a larger stencil.
That equipment difference does not determine this coverage measurement.
The risograph master is ready but unused.
I will not claim copies were printed.
Please draft a quality sheet.
It can separate measured claims from pending checks.

Workshop mock-up review, issue C. We tested the divider cards inside both rigid folders using scrap paper with the same dimensions as the reserved stock. Both cards fit without bending the sheet corners. This establishes the proposed arrangement fits the folders; it does not show that the forty reserved practice sheets have been packed. The helpers can now use that arrangement once the library coordinator confirms collection. I have moved the pencil sketch from proposed arrangement to approved handling diagram and dated that change within this fictional work log. The cracked sleeve remains in the discard box and will not be repaired for this job.

The accessibility volunteer examined the three-panel leaflet using a blank folding mock-up alongside a separate text-layout printout. They could open it with one hand when the starting tab was wider, but the narrow tab on the earlier mock-up repeatedly slipped. The volunteer recommends the wider tab for the next draft. Their test concerns this handling trial and does not certify universal accessibility. They also asked for a written description of the unfolding sequence, because the workshop assistant may need to demonstrate it verbally. That description has not been written. The materials-list text is readable when fully opened but becomes hidden across the middle-panel fold.

The workshop coordinator declined to remove the optional apron from the materials list. Instead, the editor will separate required materials from optional clothing and move the optional line to the final panel. This is an approved content arrangement, while the actual revised file is still pending. Please do not use the rejected shortened list as the current text. Its draft remains in the editing folder so the team can see why the change was rejected. It must carry a superseded-draft label before another helper uses it for proofreading.

The translation request has been clarified as a request for a plain-language English version, not another language. A community reader has agreed to review sentence length next session. They will need the revised required-versus-optional list first. The library coordinator has separately asked whether collection can occur in the morning rather than the afternoon. We have not confirmed a time because the sewing group controls access to the shared table that morning. The reserve remains forty sheets; the proposed time change does not increase or reduce that quantity.
The folder arrangement and content arrangement are approved, while text revision and collection timing remain pending. The rejected shortened list must retain its version warning.
Prepare a printer note using the first test-sheet result.
The note records twenty-eight percent ink coverage for the first test sheet.
Do not describe it as a production average.
One sheet does not establish a run average.
The foil proposal was rejected for budget reasons.
The rejected finish should not appear as completed work.

Coordination record, issue D. The editor completed the revised leaflet file with the wider opening tab, the required materials grouped together, and optional clothing on the last panel. The community reader reviewed that exact file and marked two long sentences for revision. One sentence combines the arrival door and the return address; the reader could not tell which instruction applied before the workshop. The other uses a passive construction for returning borrowed scissors. Neither comment is a color or ink-coverage judgment. The editor has accepted the comments and will split the arrival sentence and name the person responsible for collecting scissors.

We discovered a version mix-up at the proof table. A helper printed the rejected shortened list from issue B because its filename sorted before the newer draft. That printout has been crossed through and marked withdrawn. It is retained with the error note so a future reader can explain the discrepancy rather than silently treating the missing apron line as a new decision. The current working filename is leaflet-layout-D. The planned plain-language changes will create leaflet-layout-E. File letters record document versions, not approval grades. Issue D incorporates the earlier handling recommendation; its new wording still needs review.

The sewing group confirmed that the shared table is available after noon on the proposed library collection day. The library driver cannot collect then, so we have not booked that day. The coordinator offered a later afternoon collection slot and is waiting for the driver's response. The reserved practice sheets remain in their unsealed stack under the divider card. Both folders are still empty. An accepted packing diagram and a requested collection day must not be combined into a fictional completed handover.

I assigned the next helper to check that withdrawn paper proofs cannot be mistaken for live packing instructions. They should leave the withdrawn-proof envelope in the audit drawer, away from the supply folders. The helper also needs to check whether the new plain-language draft preserves the required-versus-optional distinction. There is no reason to recount the reserved pile unless it is moved or a discrepancy is reported. The working priorities are document version clarity, the two accepted wording edits, and confirmation of the collection appointment; these do not require deciding whether the first test-sheet figure is valid.
Issue D is the current layout draft; issue E is planned. The withdrawn print stays in the audit drawer, and the driver has no accepted collection date yet.
The measurement tool may have cropped a margin.
We should record that uncertainty without guessing a new percentage.
We have not repeated the measurement.
No replacement value is available.
The matching reference strips are printed.
Strip printing is complete; bundle attachment is separate.

Desk log, issue E. The editor produced leaflet-layout-E and split the confusing arrival sentence into two short instructions. It now names the workshop greeter as the person who collects borrowed scissors at the end. The community reader checked both requested edits and accepted the revised wording. This approval is for the text only. We still need a physical folded proof to confirm that the wording changes did not push the return address over the last fold. The wider tab remains in the file. No one has authorized a final leaflet print run on the basis of the reader's message.

The withdrawn paper proof has been put in a closed envelope labeled Superseded Text, with a note explaining the missing optional-clothing line. A helper initially suggested shredding it immediately, but the coordinator requested that we retain it until the next shift can compare the versions. We therefore preserved the record rather than quietly losing the reason for the correction. The active proof tray now contains only the issue-E text and the handling diagram. There is no measured color approval sheet in that tray; any future printer must obtain the appropriate approval separately.

The library driver confirmed a later afternoon collection appointment. I copied the confirmation into the transport log and noted that the driver will accept one closed rigid folder, not a loose carton. The forty reserved sheets can fit that folder according to the earlier scrap-paper trial. We have not yet performed the actual packing. The driver also requires the coordinator's contact extension on the external folder label. That extension is still being confirmed because the coordinator is moving offices. We must not substitute the workshop greeter's contact details merely because those are already available.

The workshop coordinator asked for ten extra blank sheets for a later demonstration. Those ten can come from the unreserved twenty, leaving ten unallocated if the request is approved. The request is currently pending because the library has priority over its reserved forty. The helper should record the prospective allocation separately, rather than subtracting it from physical inventory before approval. At the next session, an independent useful task is checking the external label information against the transport log while another person checks the folded text layout. These are distinct checks with separate owners and evidence.
Issue E has text approval but still needs a folded check. Forty sheets are reserved, the label extension is unresolved, and the extra workshop allocation is only requested.
The folding guide was used in a paper-only rehearsal.
That rehearsal does not establish color quality.
We kept the rehearsal sheets unprinted.
I will not count them as approved print bundles.
A volunteer proposed changing the paper weight.
The paper change is pending approval.

Packing and layout record, issue F. The workshop coordinator approved ten extra practice sheets for the later demonstration. A helper counted those ten from the unreserved pile and placed them under the Workshop Leaflet divider, leaving ten blank sheets unallocated. The library reserve is still forty. The four torn-corner sheets remain scrap. These categories now account for the original counted stock without treating the torn sheets as usable supply. We should preserve the allocation ledger when the two folders move, because a simple total count would not identify which organization has been promised which sheets.

Separately from the unprinted paper rehearsal, we folded one text-layout proof of leaflet-layout-E using scrap paper. The revised return address sits completely within the final panel, and the wider tab remains usable in this trial. The helper found a new problem: the folded edge covers part of the optional-clothing heading when the leaflet is partly opened. The coordinator asked the editor to move that heading upward without changing the accepted wording. The next file will be leaflet-layout-F. The current physical proof is annotated rather than silently corrected by hand, so another printer can distinguish the observed layout defect from the proposed fix.

The library coordinator confirmed their contact extension, and we wrote it on the removable folder label. The driver has seen a photograph of that label and accepted it. We packed the forty sheets into the library folder, using the approved arrangement and keeping the divider card beside the paper. The folder is closed but remains on the studio packing table. A photograph of a label and a closed folder do not prove collection. The transport log still shows collection pending for the confirmed appointment. The second rigid folder contains only the workshop's ten practice sheets, not finished leaflets.

A volunteer proposed attaching a decorative sticker over the library folder latch. We rejected that proposal because it could hide whether the latch was closed. The label belongs on the flat outer panel, where it does not obstruct the latch. Please keep this rejection in the handling note; otherwise a later helper might interpret an undecorated folder as unfinished. The next shift can verify the latch, label and forty-sheet allocation together, while the editor separately completes the heading-position adjustment. Neither workstream establishes a production average or verifies any disputed test-sheet measurement.
The library folder is packed but uncollected. The workshop allocation is approved, while the new heading-position problem requires issue F rather than a silent alteration.
The paper change was rejected to preserve folding behavior.
The original paper specification remains selected.
Keep the earlier printer note in the audit folder.
Archiving does not verify its measurement.
There are no approved production bundles yet.
I will not invent completed bundle inspections.

Collection exception report, issue G. The library driver arrived at the confirmed appointment, but their vehicle had a water leak in the cargo compartment. The coordinator declined the handover because the folder is rigid but not waterproof. The closed forty-sheet folder remains at the studio. Record this as an attempted collection with no transfer, rather than a completed delivery followed by a return. The driver has offered a replacement vehicle on another afternoon. We have not confirmed that proposal; the coordinator first wants assurance that the replacement compartment is dry.

After the driver left, a helper inspected the outside of the library folder and found no water marks. They did not reopen it or recount the sheets because it never left the dry packing table. This inspection supports only the observed external condition. The next collection check should include the cargo compartment as well as our folder latch. We have asked the driver to report the replacement vehicle condition before leaving their depot, but an advance report will not substitute for looking at the compartment when it arrives. The transport note now lists these two checkpoints separately.

The editor completed leaflet-layout-F by moving the optional-clothing heading upward. A new folded scrap proof shows that the heading remains visible during opening. The accepted wording from issue E is unchanged. The coordinator approved the leaflet layout, subject to the separate production and bundle checks already in the job log. This is the first layout version combining the accepted text, wider tab and corrected heading position. The withdrawn shortened list and annotated issue-E physical proof remain in the audit drawer, with their reasons for replacement attached.

The workshop's ten blank practice sheets were used in a supervised folding rehearsal. Eight remain usable, while two were creased beyond the planned practice exercise and moved to scrap. That usage affects the workshop practice allocation only; it does not consume any library sheets or create approved printed bundles. The unallocated stock remains ten. We should carry these counts forward instead of copying the earlier ten-sheet workshop allocation as a statement of current usable stock. A useful next task is to update the supply ledger and check the proposed replacement collection conditions, without inventing a completed delivery or a new coverage result.
The failed collection was not a transfer. Issue F has layout approval, eight workshop sheets remain usable, and a replacement vehicle arrangement is still pending.
Prepare the quality-sheet handoff.
The handoff can distinguish measurement uncertainty and required bundle attachments.
No new ink-coverage result exists.
I will not infer one from blank rehearsal sheets.
Suggest a next task independent of the disputed number.
Organize the color-reference strips so each future bundle receives the matching one.

Transfer note, issue H. The next coordinator should continue from leaflet-layout-F, the approved layout with the widened opening tab, separated required and optional information, and the raised optional-clothing heading. Its approval does not cover a production run or bundle release. The printer note about the first test sheet remains in the audit folder with the later uncertainty note attached. No later record establishes a new ink-coverage result. The separate bundle attachment requirement remains a live preparation task and should appear in the next handoff even while the disputed measurement needs review.

The library folder still contains the forty reserved blank practice sheets and has not been transferred. The replacement-vehicle collection proposal is pending. The transport log asks for an advance dry-compartment report and an arrival inspection; the latter has not occurred. Do not close the delivery line merely because an earlier appointment was confirmed or a driver arrived. The unsuccessful collection attempt is retained with the reason for refusal. If a different driver comes, the coordinator should explain the dry-compartment requirement before carrying the folder outside.

Our current usable loose stock is eight workshop practice sheets and ten unallocated blank sheets. The original four torn-corner sheets and the two sheets damaged in folding rehearsal are scrap. The two rigid folders remain distinct: the library folder holds its reservation; the workshop folder can hold the usable workshop practice sheets. The cracked sleeve is discarded and the decorative-latch sticker proposal is rejected. None of these supply records should be merged into a total of approved printed products. The material states describe preparation stock, not completed outreach deliveries.

For the incoming helper, I suggest two independently actionable checks. First, compare the live layout filename with the issue-H transfer note before producing another folding proof. Second, contact the library coordinator about the replacement vehicle and record the response as either confirmation or a pending offer. These steps use the document and transport evidence already available. They do not depend on accepting the disputed measurement. Preserve earlier reports with their dates rather than overwriting them with assumptions from later transport activity. The next coordinator should preserve the distinction between a proposed transport arrangement, an observed condition and a completed transfer when updating the log.
I can continue with issue F and the pending replacement collection. The forty-sheet library folder remains here; production approval and physical transfer must be recorded separately.
