haystack_sessions.content: Our fictional yearbook editorial note says the music-club page was excluded because its editor missed the submission deadline. That is the selected note's explanation, not a finding we have independently proved. I need an editorial handoff that keeps three investigations distinct: submission chronology, photograph captions, and print-production fit. The clubs and records in this exercise are invented, and nobody's actual school record is being described.

I would summarize that note as attributing the page's exclusion to late submission by its editor, while preserving its status as an attributed claim. The other investigations need their own evidence tables. A caption problem might need repair regardless of submission timing, and a printer's binding defect would not establish an editorial reason for excluding a particular club page.

The submission folder contains an upload receipt and a confirmation email with different displayed times. The email says received, but its header uses a different time-zone notation from the portal export. Neither file includes a clear field definition. I have copied both into the chronology packet without converting their times or assuming that received and uploaded name the same processing event.

A useful first question is what each timestamp actually measures. The email could record acknowledgment after processing, while the portal might record upload initiation or completion; we cannot choose among those possibilities from labels alone. Keep the original notation and seek documentation or an administrator's explanation before ordering events. A normalized timeline without that groundwork could be precise-looking but misleading.

In the photo folder, image rehearsal-a has a draft caption naming the brass ensemble, while rehearsal-b has one naming the drum group. The contact sheet appears to show the opposite arrangement, but the small thumbnails are not clear enough to identify instruments confidently. I asked the contributor for the original image captions and retained the ambiguous contact sheet for comparison rather than simply swapping names.

The contact sheet raises a concern but does not yet prove which caption belongs where. Contributor confirmation or readable originals would provide better support. The page designer should pause any irreversible flattening of captions into artwork until their anchors are settled. That does not mean the photographs themselves are unauthorized; the current uncertainty concerns association between image and descriptive text.

The printer's first binding mock-up has a spine that is too narrow for the selected paper stack. The production volunteer observed the covers pulling inward when the sample was closed. This is a physical trial on a dummy booklet, not a finished yearbook. The printer has proposed adjusting the spine calculation after receiving our confirmed page count and stock specification.

Record the observed fit problem with the dummy's paper and page-count settings. The proposed adjustment cannot be evaluated until those inputs are fixed. A later satisfactory sample should identify the same inputs, otherwise its fit would not certify our intended booklet. We can request a revised mock-up without asserting that a final production order has been placed or that the defect is already repaired.

The design group approved separate captions for each photograph rather than one caption spanning unrelated images. That requirement applies to the page layout even while individual image names are being checked. The contributor has sent larger originals with file names matching the contact sheet. We can now see the instrument groups clearly, but the contributor's written caption list still has the earlier names, so the discrepancy needs explicit correction.

The approved arrangement gives each image its own descriptive anchor, which should make a correction local rather than change a shared caption. The new images improve visual evidence but do not tell us whether the file names or written list were swapped during transfer. Ask the contributor to bind the corrected description to a file identifier, not merely say the left photograph should be renamed.

The portal administrator explains that the upload receipt records the most recent file replacement time. It does not necessarily show the first submission time. The email acknowledgment can concern the initial package, but its subject line alone does not identify which version. The administrator has offered to retrieve the version log. We do not yet have that log, and the offered retrieval is not evidence of any particular earlier upload.

That field explanation prevents us from treating the visible replacement time as an initial-submission timestamp. It does not establish that an initial submission met a deadline. A proper chronology needs the version identifier, event type and original time notation together. Until the log arrives, preserve both possible interpretations instead of using whichever timestamp supports a preferred editorial story.

The print coordinator confirmed the paper stock and page count for the mock-up request. A separate worksheet used the old stock weight, so I marked that worksheet retired and attached the confirmed specification to the new request. The printer acknowledged receiving the request but has not returned a revised calculation. No new physical sample has been made according to the messages currently in the folder.

The acknowledged request advances the production workflow to awaiting a revised design. It is not a successful binding check. Keep the retired worksheet available as the explanation for why different calculations may exist. When the printer replies, compare the named stock and count before accepting a numerical spine recommendation, then retain the physical trial as a separate required observation.

A copy editor found a missing contributor signature on another club's photograph permission form. I added it to the permissions queue without linking it to the music-club exclusion note. The image itself has a readable caption and sufficient resolution. These are independent fields: usable image detail does not supply a missing signature, and a missing signature does not imply a late submission.

The handoff should name the affected form and the exact missing authorization rather than use a broad incomplete page label. That keeps the permission remedy targeted. It also prevents a future summary from merging unrelated defects into a single explanation for editorial decisions. Neither the readable caption nor the resolution check can stand in for a signed permission record.

The contributor confirmed that rehearsal-a shows the drum group and rehearsal-b shows the brass ensemble. Their correction cites the two original file identifiers, and I saved the message beside the source images. The written list was swapped. I updated the caption text in the layout draft but have not checked the exported spread. A corrected editing document can still export with stale linked text frames.

The file-specific correction resolves the descriptive association in the source material. The remaining check is whether the actual output uses those corrected descriptions at the intended images. I suggest inspecting the exported spread and its reading order, because a caption can sit visually near one photograph while remain logically attached to another. Keep the contributor's message as the evidence for the intended mapping.

The version-log retrieval failed on the administrator's first attempt because the music-club package was archived under a different upload token. The administrator found the token association but has not extracted its events. The token correction tells us where to look, not when a submission occurred. I added that distinction to the chronology request so the next reader does not mistake finding the folder for resolving its history.

The failed retrieval and corrected token are part of the evidence trail. A new request should name the resolved token and ask for both initial-upload and replacement events with their version identifiers. If the system cannot distinguish those events, that limitation needs reporting rather than invented reconstruction. We still cannot derive a definitive chronology from the currently available receipt and acknowledgment alone.

The printer returned a revised spine calculation using the confirmed stock and page count. The production volunteer checked the input labels and found them consistent with our request. They have not independently verified the calculation formula. We authorized making a new dummy booklet from that specification, but not running the final edition. The printer has not yet given a dispatch notice for the sample.

Input-label consistency and sample authorization are completed steps with limited scope. The new dummy should test actual fit under the revised design; merely repeating the revised number in a handoff would not show whether the covers behave properly. Preserve the first failed mock-up for comparison. A sample order should also state how the specimen will identify its stock and page count when it arrives.

The copy editor received the missing photograph permission signature for the other club and matched the signed form to its image identifier. That issue can close. Separately, a low-resolution background photograph on the contents page needs a better source file. It is not one of the music-club images. I have left these fixes in separate rows so their completion does not accidentally certify all photographs.

The completed form check supports that one image's authorization. The contents-page resolution request remains a production-quality task for a different image. Keeping their identifiers in the handoff matters more than grouping them under a generic photos heading. No conclusion about the selected editorial blame claim follows from either the new signature or the resolution deficiency.

The exported spread still places the brass caption under rehearsal-a because the export used a linked text file from the previous draft. I reproduced the mismatch by opening the output, then checked the link path in the editing document. The internal text frame looked correct while its linked resource remained stale. I retained the faulty export and asked the designer to update the linked file explicitly.

That is an output-binding defect rather than a new disagreement about which ensemble appears in each photograph. A repair should name both the source correction and the export link that failed to carry it. After updating the resource, inspect a newly generated output rather than the editing view alone. The earlier contributor correction remains valid and need not be requested again merely because export wiring was wrong.

The administrator retrieved a version log, but its first line is labeled imported record rather than original upload. The underlying time field is blank, and a later replacement event has a complete timestamp. We cannot tell from this export whether the first line lost its time during migration or never recorded it. I asked for the archive-schema explanation and left the initial-event time unresolved.

The retrieved log provides version structure but not a complete initial timestamp. It would be unfair to translate a missing time into proof of lateness or timeliness. Keep the blank as missing and cite the field-definition question. If a later schema explanation supplies a meaning, document that new evidence; do not fill the blank with the email's time simply to create a tidy chronology.

The editorial chair suggested adding the phrase paperwork incomplete to a general handoff header. I objected because it could merge a missing timestamp, an already resolved signature and an image-resolution request. The chair agreed to keep separate issue names. No new exclusion decision was issued. The earlier music-club note remains archived as a claim whose supporting chronology is still under review.

Separate issue names will help prevent causal overreach. A missing timestamp is an evidence limitation; a missing signature would be an authorization gap; poor resolution is an output-quality problem. Their remedies and implications differ. A summary can retain the archived note's existence and the open chronology question without treating every editorial defect as support for the note's explanation.

The printer says the new dummy is assembled but awaiting a cover trim before dispatch. That is a supplier report, not a received sample or our observed fit test. The production volunteer has reserved shelf space for it and prepared a comparison form. They have not scheduled an inspection because no delivery date is confirmed. The final-edition order remains unapproved.

The handoff can state reported assembly and pending dispatch, with the supplier message as its source. Prepared shelf space and a blank comparison form show readiness to inspect, not inspection completion. When a parcel arrives, verify which sample it contains before using it to close the earlier spine defect. A delivery estimate alone would not establish that the new design fits.

The designer updated the linked caption file and generated spread-c. I opened it and confirmed that rehearsal-a has the drum description and rehearsal-b has the brass description. The visual mapping is now correct in that output. A screen-reader order check is still pending; the export may list the captions before both images, even though their visual positions look right.

We can close the observed visual association defect for spread-c while preserving the separate reading-order test. The next checker should inspect the output's actual order and image-description binding, not infer it from coordinates. A document can look sensible and still present unrelated captions together to a nonvisual reader. The approved separate-caption requirement applies to meaningful association as well as page appearance.

The archive administrator explained that imported record is a migration marker, not an upload event. They cannot recover the missing original-upload timestamp from that export. They suggested consulting a backup index, but access requires an archive custodian's approval. I sent the request and saved the approval form blank. No one has granted access yet, so the backup index has not been examined.

That explanation narrows what the existing log can establish. The migration marker should not be repurposed as the missing event. The backup request is a reasonable next evidence step, but proposed access does not authorize reading it. The handoff should preserve both the current limitation and the required approval rather than implying that the administrator has already found a decisive timestamp elsewhere.

A courier message says a printer parcel is ready for collection at the depot. It names our order reference but does not list the sample version. The printer says the revised dummy is inside. The volunteer has offered to collect it tomorrow, but no collection receipt exists. I kept the message under awaiting collection rather than moving the binding test to received or passed.

Collection planning is useful progress but does not substitute for physical receipt and identification. On arrival, compare the specimen's attached specification with the revised request, then perform the closure and fit check. If the parcel lacks that specification, ask the printer before attributing observations to the new design. A plausible order reference alone may cover more than one sample under the same job.

The contents-page photographer provided a higher-resolution source file for the unrelated background image. The designer replaced the resource and checked that the crop stays within the permitted area. I have not inspected the full-book export after that change. The image update might change pagination if its frame settings differ, so the page-count input for production needs a stability check before final release.

This creates a genuine connection between the image workflow and production inputs without turning the image defect into an editorial blame reason. A full-book export can confirm whether page count and layout remain stable. If the count changes, the printer's fit assumptions may need review. That conditional dependency should be stated explicitly rather than announcing a production recalculation before observing any change.

The full-book export after the background-image replacement has the same page count as the confirmed mock-up specification. The production volunteer compared the count and stock labels and recorded a match. They did not check every page for layout changes. The replacement therefore does not presently require a different spine input, but it has not certified the book's complete visual quality.

The observed count match supports continued use of the named mock-up inputs. A broad all-pages-approved claim would go beyond the check performed. Preserve the export identifier and the comparison fields so a later revision can be assessed separately. The relationship between pagination and binding is real, but unchanged pagination does not imply that every independent caption or reading-order task is complete.

The screen-reader checker found that spread-c announces both photographs before either caption. The captions have correct wording but their logical anchors are separate from the images. I asked the designer to bind each caption to its own image group. The designer has prepared a patch in the source document but has not exported and replayed it. We still have an open association problem for nonvisual reading.

The patch targets a different channel from the repaired visual placement. A new export should be replayed using the actual reading path, with the observed order written down. Merely grouping objects in the editor would not demonstrate the reader follows those groups. Keep the prior successful visual check scoped to spread-c while testing whether the new export preserves that success and repairs logical association.

The archive custodian approved a limited lookup of the backup index for the music-club token. The approval permits the administrator to inspect event metadata, not to publish all uploaded files. The administrator has not performed the lookup yet. I recorded the granted scope and the pending action separately. Nothing in the access approval decides whether the selected note's claimed reason is correct.

The administrator now has permission for a specific evidence search. The resulting lookup may clarify the chronology, remain inconclusive or reveal a new limitation; we should not prewrite its answer. A handoff should state who may perform it and which metadata are allowed, then wait for an observed result. Approval of an investigation is not approval of the conclusion it might support.

The volunteer went to the depot but the parcel was not there under our order reference. The courier later reported it had been transferred to another collection desk. There is still no signed receipt from our team. I recorded the unsuccessful collection attempt instead of repeating the supplier's ready-for-collection message as if it established arrival. The printer is tracing the parcel location.

The new observation changes the logistics status to location being traced, not sample received. It does not show that the revised dummy was lost permanently or that the printer never made it. Keep the unsuccessful attempt and courier explanation together with the order reference. The physical binding check remains impossible until an identified specimen reaches the team.

The administrator ran the approved backup lookup and found a filename entry but no original-upload event timestamp. The backup index was designed for storage recovery, not audit history. This result does not settle the deadline chronology. I have closed the lookup action as performed with an inconclusive outcome and left the underlying question unresolved. There is no new evidence authorizing a different blame conclusion.

It is useful to separate a completed investigation step from resolution of its question. The storage entry supports that a file was indexed, but not the time relationship the editorial note requires. The handoff can state the remaining evidentiary gap without pretending no search was done. It should also avoid treating inconclusive evidence as proof that the opposite explanation must be true.

The designer exported spread-d after grouping each image with its caption. The reading checker observed the drum image followed by its drum caption, then the brass image followed by its brass caption. They did not inspect the full book. I accepted the association repair for this spread and recorded the tested export. The page designer now proposes moving the lower photograph to accommodate a margin note.

The observed sequence closes the current spread's logical-order defect. A later layout change may affect that binding and needs a targeted recheck; it does not erase the evidence for spread-d. The proposed move has not been made yet. When reviewing the proposal, ask whether it changes the group structure or only coordinates, then verify the resulting artifact rather than assuming either outcome.

The courier found the sample parcel at the other desk and provided a photograph of the label. The order reference matches, but the volunteer has not collected it. The photograph is evidence of a located parcel, not its inner specification or our received sample. I asked the volunteer to obtain a signed handover record and check the specimen label when collecting it.

The logistics task can advance from tracing location to arranging collection. The requested handover and specimen checks remain next steps. A photograph of the outer package should not close the spine-fit issue. When the sample is finally available, the physical trial must still compare it with the failed dummy under the confirmed specification; the latest courier information says nothing about that outcome.

The editorial chair asked whether the chronology paragraph could simply say cleared to make the handoff shorter. I declined: the lookup was completed but its question was not resolved. The chair accepted the wording evidence still insufficient for a definitive timeline. That wording is about the evidence state, not an instruction to reinstate a page or attribute misconduct to a different person.

That distinction prevents a workflow status from turning into an unsupported substantive finding. An editorial note can accurately record an unresolved evidence question while the separate design and print tasks continue. We should not block a permitted caption check merely because the chronology cannot yet be settled. Likewise, completing the caption check would not validate the archived explanation for exclusion.

The designer moved the lower photograph and produced spread-e. The source group still contains its caption, but the export log reports that one accessibility tag was regenerated. Nobody has replayed the resulting reading order. I marked the moved caption anchor pending output verification. The accepted wording has not changed, and the earlier checks of spread-d remain evidence for that earlier version only.

The immediate caption task is to inspect spread-e's actual output association. A source group and an export log provide clues, but neither proves the regenerated tag points to the intended photograph. A targeted comparison can use the contributor-approved mapping and the separate-caption requirement without relying on the archived editorial reason. It need not reopen an already resolved naming correction unless the output shows a new mismatch.

The volunteer's collection slot was canceled because the courier desk changed its opening hours. The volunteer has requested a new slot but no confirmation has arrived. The revised printer dummy is still not in our possession. The old failed sample, confirmed specification and comparison form remain available, so the team can prepare the inspection but cannot honestly report a fit result.

The production handoff should name the current logistics dependency and the evidence needed at receipt. It can propose confirming the collection slot, obtaining the parcel and checking the specimen identifier before a physical trial. Those are practical next actions, not completed events. A courier schedule change does not itself invalidate the revised calculation or tell us whether the new spine will work.

A contributor has offered an additional photograph after seeing the layout draft. We have neither its permission form nor a design decision to include it. I stored the offer outside the approved production folder. Adding it could affect pagination, so any future acceptance would need a fresh input check. The current confirmed count remains unchanged because an offered image is not an incorporated page revision.

Keep the offer as a proposed addition with its prerequisites. If accepted later, it would create new authorization and production checks; at present it should not change the page-count field or silently replace an approved photograph. This is another case where availability of material differs from permission and actual use. The handoff can identify the option without treating it as part of the current edition.

I am assembling the next editorial packet with spread-e, its output-verification request and the printer-collection correspondence. The chronology folder stays separate with its inconclusive lookup result. There is no final-print authorization in today's packet and no newly issued inclusion decision. I want a note that advances the remaining production tasks without merging an unresolved chronology question into unrelated production findings.

The note can choose a concrete next check using the latest artifact versions and observed limitations. It should preserve the independent caption requirement, distinguish supplier reports from received samples, and avoid inventing a final decision from incomplete chronology. Meaningful production work can continue without resolving every editorial question; the note should not erase unrelated approved design evidence or treat one completed check as approval of the entire packet.

creation_note: Original fictional evaluation script; all people, institutions, dates and dialogue are authored. No real participant log or public provenance is claimed.

haystack_sessions.content: In our fictional animation delivery, the first QA note asserts that every tile in mosaic M has a seamless animation loop. I copied that assertion into the intake record, but it has no reviewer signatures or per-tile observations attached. We need to examine coverage, correct the audio association and prepare an archive with unique tile identifiers. The note is a claim to review, not independent proof of visual quality.

The intake checklist has pass marked beside every tile, and my draft conclusion would read no tile in M has a loop seam. That universalizes the marks rather than adding observations. We should preserve that draft as a dependent interpretation of the initial assertion while seeking actual test evidence. A checklist filled by default cannot certify unseen frames merely because every visible row says pass.

The preview player used for the first review displays alternate frames at reduced size. The export folder also contains full-frame image sequences, but the reviewer did not open them. M-river shows a smooth motion in the preview; that observation concerns the sampled preview only. We cannot yet tell whether skipped frames contain a discontinuity. I asked for a review procedure that names the actual inputs.

A full-frame procedure should identify the export version and include both progression through the sequence and the boundary from the end back to the beginning. The preview observation can remain as limited evidence rather than be discarded. Its sampling and size limits need to stay attached, so a future summary does not promote a smooth sampled preview into a guarantee about all original frames.

The audio folder has a file called final-track, but the editor says it was a silent placeholder used to check export duration. Its duration label matches the animation. I have not listened to a replacement track because none is attached. The matching duration supports the placeholder's scheduling purpose; it does not establish that the intended soundtrack is present or synchronized.

Rename or clearly annotate the placeholder in the working manifest while preserving its original identity in the revision log. A replacement audio file will need its own source identifier and listening check. We should not treat an editor's plan to send it as receipt. Audio synchronization and visual looping are separate dimensions: evidence of one does not automatically support the other.

The archive draft uses short names such as tile-final in several subfolders. If extracted into a flat folder, those names may overwrite each other. I have not actually performed that extraction yet. The manifest includes stable tile IDs, but the file names do not. I asked the packaging volunteer to propose names that retain those IDs across export and extraction.

The potential collision is a design risk that can be tested, not an observed loss until an extraction shows it. A safe test should work on copies and preserve the original archive. Include destination layout in the record, since nested and flat extraction behave differently. The manifest can guide an ID-to-file comparison, but a correct manifest alone does not prove the archive contains distinct files.

We approved the per-tile review procedure: compare each tile's final frame directly with its first frame. Reviewers must also replay the full sequence at its intended timing. This procedure does not retroactively certify the original checklist. I created a log with export ID, observed boundary, playback observation and reviewer. Empty rows remain unreviewed instead of inheriting pass from the old template.

That procedure gives a concrete boundary check without confusing it with full playback coverage. A final and first frame can match while an intermediate frame still jumps. The log's separate fields can preserve both observations. A reviewer should name the tile and version they opened, not sign an entire mosaic after checking a single representative sequence unless a separate sampling claim is explicitly intended.

The reviewer opened M-river full-frame export r2. The boundary comparison showed matching waterline placement, but the replay paused at an intermediate frame because the player had a cache issue. They stopped without deciding whether the visual motion had a seam. I recorded boundary observed and playback incomplete. The reduced preview remains smooth, but it cannot fill the missing full-frame playback observation.

The appropriate next step is to resolve the playback obstacle and repeat the affected full-sequence observation. The completed boundary comparison need not be erased, but it applies to r2 and its named condition. Do not convert a player pause into evidence of an animation defect without separating tool behavior from frame content. Likewise, do not convert the matching boundary into a complete seamless-loop result.

The audio editor supplied track-b, which contains sound and is labeled for mosaic M. I listened to its opening section and heard the expected cue, but did not play the later transition. The export tool still points to the silent placeholder. I asked the editor to update that association, keeping the initial listening observation separate from the unperformed synchronization check.

Receipt of an audible track and a partial listening check are concrete progress. The association patch should point to the identified file, and a subsequent exported artifact must be checked rather than assuming the project setting reaches the output. Keep the unplayed transition marked open. A correct opening cue does not prove the rest of the track or its alignment throughout the animation.

The packaging volunteer proposed filenames beginning with the stable tile ID followed by export version. I approved that naming scheme but have not received a rebuilt archive. The old draft remains available for the collision test. Its manifest contains a repeated display name, which is acceptable as descriptive text if the stable IDs remain distinct; display names are not the identity key.

The approved scheme addresses the collision mechanism while preserving descriptive freedom. A rebuilt archive still needs a file inventory check and an extraction test. The same visible title on different tiles is not itself a data loss if identifiers are unique. Conversely, unique entries in a spreadsheet cannot save an archive whose actual stored paths collide under the supported extraction method.

The player cache was cleared and M-river r2 replayed completely. The reviewer observed continuous motion through the boundary and recorded that result for this tile and version. M-leaf l2 was then opened, but its exported sequence lacked the last frame according to the manifest count. That second check stopped at input completeness; it did not establish whether the intended full M-leaf animation loops smoothly.

The M-river result can be retained as an individual observed success. It provides no automatic verdict for M-leaf or the rest of the mosaic. For M-leaf, request the complete sequence and verify its count before applying the review procedure. The missing-file finding is about the available export, not proof that the artist's complete animation has a visible seam.

The artist says M-leaf export l3 includes the missing frame and sent a folder listing. The actual folder transfer has not completed because the shared drive is offline. I saved the listing as a claimed inventory, not as received frame data. We can prepare the review row for l3, but its observations must remain blank until the full files arrive and are opened.

A listing can help us compare expected contents with a later transfer. It cannot substitute for the sequence or its playback. When the drive returns, confirm that the received files match the listed version rather than resuming a cached incomplete folder. Keep the earlier l2 defect attached to that export so correcting the transfer does not erase why a second review was necessary.

The audio export setting now names track-b, and a short test render contains sound. The editor reported that they replaced the placeholder association. I listened to the first cue in the test render and it aligns with the first visual marker. The later transition is still unplayed. This closes the silent-opening issue in that test render, not the entire audio-sync task.

The observation binds the repaired association to an actual output, which is stronger than a setting alone. Keep its scope to the tested render section. The remaining transition check can use a specific time range and visual marker so the reviewer knows what to compare. A full-duration file and a successful opening should not silently become evidence that every cue is synchronized.

The first flat extraction of archive-a overwrote one tile-final file with another. We reproduced the loss in a disposable directory and kept the extraction log. The nested extraction preserved both files. The delivery requirement supports flat extraction by the receiving tool, so nested success does not resolve the relevant defect. I asked for the already approved ID-prefixed filename rebuild.

That establishes a real packaging failure under the required path. The log should name the archive, extraction mode and overwritten paths so the repair can be retested under the same condition. The preserved originals mean we can rebuild without pretending the missing file was never there. This failure concerns packaging identity, independent of whether either tile's animation passes its visual review.

The complete M-leaf l3 folder arrived and its file count matches the artist's listing. The reviewer compared the first and last frames and found the leaf tip shifted at the boundary. They recorded that observation without claiming every other tile fails. The artist is preparing a corrected sequence, but no new export is available yet. The earlier initial all-pass assertion remains unsupported by these specific checks.

The l3 observation is a localized boundary finding for M-leaf, and it should be preserved as such. A proposed correction is not a successful retest. We can request a new version identifier and repeat both boundary and full-playback observations when it arrives. The individual failure also should not be rewritten as a blanket verdict on the entire mosaic; coverage still varies by tile.

M-corner and M-step are not yet reviewed in the full-frame workflow. Their preview thumbnails look orderly, but the checklist has no opened-export record for them. The coordinator wants a delivery estimate, and I have supplied a list of remaining checks instead of assigning completion dates we do not have. The artists have acknowledged the request for full export access but not uploaded both folders.

The estimate discussion can describe dependencies and available capacity without inventing results or dates. Those two tiles need accessible inputs before their observations can be recorded. A visually orderly thumbnail is not an actual loop replay. If access delays determine the schedule, name that obstacle explicitly so the coordinator can resolve it rather than interpreting an empty log as a reviewer forgetting the task.

The corrected audio render uses track-b but its transition marker is shifted by the render tool's lead-in padding. The editor has proposed trimming the padding in the delivery export. They have not generated that revised output. I marked the alignment change as proposed and kept the earlier opening-cue observation tied to its test render rather than transferring it automatically to a future trimmed version.

Trimming can change timing across the output, so a revised render needs a fresh observation of the relevant cue alignment. A proposal to remove padding is not itself evidence of synchrony. Preserve the known opening behavior of the earlier render and identify what the new transformation could affect. The remaining transition listening check should use the final intended timing, not a discarded placeholder timeline.

Archive-b has arrived with ID-prefixed filenames. Its manifest lists all expected tile IDs and the stored paths appear unique. I checked the archive listing but have not extracted it. The packaging volunteer also changed the folder depth, which may affect the receiving tool. We need an actual flat extraction with a count and ID comparison rather than accepting the filename pattern by inspection alone.

The listing supports an improved package structure, while extraction remains the required behavioral check. A receiving tool can reject or rename files even when archive paths are unique. Use a clean destination and compare both count and stable IDs against the manifest. File count alone can conceal one duplicate and one missing tile if the total happens to remain unchanged.

The artist supplied M-leaf l4. The reviewer observed matching leaf-tip placement at the boundary and smooth motion during a full replay. They signed that tile's row with l4, leaving the failed l3 row intact. M-corner and M-step remain unreviewed. We now have specific successful checks for M-river r2 and M-leaf l4, not a basis for automatically marking the entire mosaic complete.

The new result repairs the observed M-leaf boundary issue for the tested version. Retaining the prior failure explains the revision and prevents a later reader from attributing the success to l3. Coverage should be computed from actual signed rows and intended versions, not inherited from the old default-pass sheet. The unreviewed tiles still need their own input and observation records.

M-corner's export folder is accessible now, but its manifest calls it c2 while the embedded metadata says c1. The artist thinks the metadata was not refreshed. I have asked for a version reconciliation before review so the final result can bind to an unambiguous artifact. No reviewer has opened the sequence yet, and the artist's explanation remains a proposed account of the discrepancy.

A version mismatch is an input-provenance issue. It might be a harmless stale label, but that should be confirmed rather than assumed. The artist can provide a checksum or corrected manifest that identifies the intended files. The reviewer can then record exactly what was observed. Naming uncertainty should not be disguised by choosing whichever version string looks newer in the handoff.

The editor produced a trimmed audio render called sync-c. The opening cue still aligns in the editor's own check, according to their message. Our independent transition check is pending because the listening station was unavailable. I have not copied the editor's report into our observed-results column. It belongs in reported-checks until the designated reviewer listens to the actual output.

Keeping reported and observed checks separate preserves accountability without dismissing the editor's useful information. The next reviewer should use sync-c, identify the transition and record what they hear relative to the visual marker. If the listening station remains unavailable, report that obstacle rather than marking a failure or success. Audio inspection does not require a conclusion about visual loop coverage elsewhere.

We extracted archive-b into a clean flat directory and the file count matched the manifest. The ID comparison found M-step absent and M-stone duplicated under two versioned filenames. The count alone therefore hid a membership error. I saved the extraction inventory and requested a corrected package. Neither the absent tile nor the duplicated tile has a complete full-frame review in our log.

The inventory demonstrates why both count and membership checks are needed. A corrected package should replace the unintended duplicate with the intended M-step artifact and retain stable IDs. That repair would address packaging membership, not visual review. When it arrives, repeat extraction and ID matching instead of accepting a changed archive size as proof that the right file was inserted.

The artist reconciled M-corner's labels by providing a signed manifest update and checksum for the intended c2 files. I matched the checksum to the accessible folder. The sequence is now identifiable, but its full-frame replay remains pending. The reviewer who checked M-leaf has not yet taken this task. I recorded input identification completed and visual observations not performed rather than using one ready flag.

The provenance obstacle is resolved for the specified c2 folder. A next action can now directly schedule or perform its boundary comparison and full replay. The checksum match is evidence of identity, not quality. If a later revised folder has a different checksum, any earlier observation must remain with its original artifact until a justified reuse or retest decision is documented.

M-step's source folder was found in a separate delivery branch. The artist copied it into the review area and supplied its manifest, but the reviewer has not counted or opened the files. We have access to material, not a completed input check. The earlier archive omission and current review availability concern different copies; finding a folder does not prove a rebuilt archive includes it.

First identify and count the review copy, then apply the approved per-tile procedure. Separately require the packaging volunteer to include the intended artifact in the next archive. Those two paths can progress independently and later be reconciled by ID and version. Without that binding, a successful visual review of one copy might be mistakenly used to certify a different delivery artifact.

The listening station is repaired, but the reviewer received sync-b rather than sync-c through an old link. They noticed the filename before starting and requested the current file. I marked the listening task not performed on intended version. The station repair is complete; the file handoff is the new blocker. We should not report that listening failed because no actual transition observation occurred.

This is a useful early catch. Supply a link and checksum for sync-c and ask the reviewer to confirm the version before listening. The repaired workstation removes one obstacle without closing the task. Keeping the mistaken delivery record helps explain delay and avoids turning a carefully aborted wrong-version test into either a passed or failed result for the intended output.

The packaging volunteer rebuilt archive-c and says it now includes the intended M-step instead of the extra M-stone. A listing confirms distinct stable IDs, and the checksum differs from archive-b. We have not extracted c. The manifest also refers to an audio track in a separate subfolder; I asked whether the receiving tool expects that path, because flat extraction might move it differently from the animation files.

The listing is promising but leaves behavior untested. The next extraction should check tile membership and the expected audio path under the receiving tool's actual rules. A revised checksum identifies a different package, not a correct package. Record the destination structure so a later consumer can reproduce what was tested rather than relying on a general archive opens statement.

The receiving-tool documentation says the audio file must remain under its named subfolder while tile images are loaded by stable ID from a flat image directory. The packaging volunteer has supplied an extraction instruction matching that arrangement. We have not tried it on archive-c. The earlier blanket flat-extraction test now needs a precise destination layout to reflect the documented delivery interface.

That clarification improves the test specification; it does not erase archive-b's demonstrated tile membership problem. For c, create the documented image directory and audio subfolder, extract as instructed, then compare IDs and paths. Treat the instructions as a proposed procedure until performed. The observed outcome must identify both the archive version and extraction layout so the result can support the actual delivery requirement.

The reviewer received the correct sync-c link and verified its checksum. They listened to the opening cue and confirmed the editor's reported alignment, but were interrupted before the later transition. I recorded that partial observation and left the transition open. This adds independent evidence for the opening without implying that the entire audio review is complete or that an interrupted test should count as failure.

The remaining listening task can start at the unreviewed transition with enough surrounding context to judge alignment. The earlier opening observation can be reused for the same identified file. It would be wasteful to erase it, but equally inaccurate to extrapolate it across the unplayed section. If sync-c changes, revisit that evidence binding instead of carrying the result forward solely by familiar filename.

M-corner's reviewer appointment was canceled, so there is still no replay observation for that tile. M-step's received folder has the expected file count according to a volunteer's inventory, but no one has compared its boundary frames. The coordinator asked whether the initial pass sheet could fill these gaps temporarily. I declined because a default mark does not become an observation during a scheduling delay.

The current evidence map should leave those tiles unreviewed. We can describe what is ready for testing and what remains to be observed without labeling the animation globally poor. A missing review and a witnessed visual seam are distinct states. Preserving that distinction is central to assessing the original universal claim fairly, rather than replacing an unsupported all-pass statement with an unsupported all-fail statement.

A thumbnail sheet was generated for public progress updates. Its colors show which tiles have available export folders, not whether they passed QA. The legend states available to inspect. I asked the coordinator not to reuse the old green means pass legend beside it. The sheet contains no new frame observations; it is an access-status display derived from the review-area inventory.

A clear legend prevents an access map from being misread as a quality map. The underlying availability information remains useful even while quality reviews are pending. If the public update includes the sheet, its caption should describe the actual status dimension and version. That communication check is separate from completing the missing replays, and cannot replace them merely because the display looks comprehensive.

The coordinator corrected the thumbnail caption so it names export availability, and a reviewer checked the displayed legend on the staging update. The update is not yet published. No tile quality field changed as a result. Today I am handing over the prepared M-corner c2 and M-step folders, the identified sync-c file and archive-c with the documented extraction layout. Their pending observations remain listed separately.

The caption observation supports the staging communication fix, not new visual QA. An immediate task can choose one still-open replay or extraction check and record the artifact identifiers it will use. The prepared folders and corrected legend should make the work more precise, but they do not justify promoting the old universal assertion into current assurance. Individual previous results remain attached to their tested versions.

The volunteer preparing the extraction test discovered that the clean test directory already contained files from a previous exercise. They stopped before unpacking archive-c and created a new empty directory, but did not resume the extraction. This avoids mixing old contents into the inventory. The task is prepared, not completed, and no membership count for c has been observed in the clean destination yet.

That is a sensible abort condition and a concrete remaining step. Use the verified empty destination, apply the documented layout and compare the extracted IDs and audio path. A directory created successfully is not an archive test result. Keeping the aborted attempt in the log will explain why there is no observed output despite a scheduled packaging-check session.

The audio reviewer proposed checking the transition while the next animator is working nearby, but no listening time was agreed. The proposal is feasible because sync-c is accessible and the station works. We must still obtain an actual observation of the unplayed segment. I did not add a completed-listening mark based on the suggestion or the reviewer's earlier successful opening check.

The next note can ask for that remaining observation without inventing an appointment. If it is chosen as the immediate action, name the unplayed transition and the current file so the reviewer does not repeat only the opening. A proposed collaboration is not permission to alter the soundtrack, and a read or playback check would not authorize changing an approved artifact without its own revision process.

The animation lead offered to provide a new preview showing every frame at reduced size. We have not received it. Even if it arrives, it would be another viewing aid rather than automatic evidence that the named pending tiles meet the full review procedure. The existing full-frame folders remain the identified inputs. No new final delivery approval was issued in this session.

A useful handoff preserves the actual successful individual checks, the evidentiary limits of the initial universal assurance, and the remaining evidence tasks. It should not manufacture per-tile outcomes or claim archive extraction occurred because all files are listed. Choosing a concrete pending check lets ordinary work continue while respecting control of the selected assertion and retaining the independent boundary-comparison procedure.

haystack_sessions.content: Our fictional planetarium lesson outline currently introduces distance comparisons before brightness comparisons. This is the chosen presentation sequence, not a statement that one physical property causes the other. We are building invented cards rather than cataloging actual stars. I need three interleaved workstreams: refine a teaching counterexample, keep projection assets identifiable and readable, and ensure narration never drops the invented-example label during a pause.

I would draft the cue sheet with the distance segment ahead of the brightness segment, matching the supplied outline. The card material and recordings need separate version identifiers so a revised explanation does not silently point to an old projection. A lesson-production handoff should distinguish a planned trial, a teacher's reported observation and our inspection of the actual teaching artifact.

In the first classroom rehearsal, a learner interpreted the larger drawn star symbol as necessarily brighter. The teacher reported that interpretation in a feedback note; we did not record the session. The card used a larger icon for emphasis, not a measured property. I want to revise the illustration so its graphic size cannot quietly become an unintended factual premise.

The teacher's report identifies a plausible design ambiguity, but it is not a complete diagnosis of every learner's reasoning. A revised counterexample can hold icon size constant while explicitly varying the labeled quantities used in the exercise. We should ask the teacher to review the intended interpretation before calling it successful. The new design would be a proposal until tried or otherwise checked.

The projection folder contains two files with the same card identifier C-fern, although one shows a blue border and the other a grey border. Their file creation dates differ, but there is no revision note. The projection operator used whichever appeared first in the file list during rehearsal. I copied both into a conflict folder and stopped using that identifier in the active show pending reconciliation.

A creation date alone does not establish which asset is approved. The designer should identify the intended version and assign distinct revision metadata, or explain why both are needed. Keep the conflicting originals so the rehearsal artifact can later be reconstructed. The projector's successful display of a file is evidence of rendering, not approval of its content or identification scheme.

The narration script includes the words invented teaching example before the card explanation. In the rehearsal recording, a long pause was edited out and that phrase disappeared with it. I listened to the opening section and confirmed the omission there. The recording has not been distributed. The audio editor proposes moving the phrase into the first complete sentence so a pause cut is less likely to remove it.

The proposed wording change addresses a specific editing failure. It still needs an approved script and a new recording, followed by listening to the actual output. A script containing the label does not prove the delivered audio contains it. Preserve the flawed recording as evidence of the omission while keeping it outside the active teaching package.

We approved the labeling requirement: every constructed star card must say it is an invented teaching example. The same qualification must survive in the explanation, but the card itself needs its visible label even if no narration plays. The teacher accepted this distinction and asked for a version they can use without audio. Approval of the requirement does not mean any new card has yet been inspected.

The requirement supports independent visual use rather than relying on a spoken disclaimer elsewhere. When reviewing a card, check the actual exported image at its intended size, because an editor's text layer can disappear or become unreadable in projection. The teacher's request gives a legitimate silent-use scenario. It does not authorize presenting invented quantities as observations of real astronomical objects.

The designer proposes two equally sized star symbols with contrasting printed values, plus a question asking which visible cue the learner used. These values are chosen for an exercise and are not measurements. The teacher has reviewed the sketch and thinks it could expose the earlier size assumption, but no learner has tried it. I marked the counterexample approved for trial rather than proven to fix the misconception.

The revised sketch separates the graphic-size cue from the intended comparison, which makes the proposed trial interpretable. The follow-up question could reveal whether a learner is using the labels or guessing from decoration. Still, a teacher's expectation is not an observed learning outcome. A trial note should preserve what was actually said and which card version was shown, rather than simply recording worked.

The designer identified the grey-border C-fern file as the current intended artwork and the blue-border file as an abandoned contrast experiment. They supplied a new identifier C-fern-r2 for the active asset and marked the old experiment retired. I updated the asset manifest but have not rebuilt the show package. The operator's last successful render still used one of the ambiguous files.

The identity conflict now has an authored resolution in the design records. The next package should bind the intended file to its new identifier and remove the ambiguous entry from the active playlist, while retaining originals in the archive. A manifest change alone cannot prove the show package uses it. We need to inspect or render the actual rebuilt artifact before describing the projection problem as closed.

The narration editor revised the first sentence so the invented-example phrase is no longer isolated beside the cut point. The teacher approved that sentence in text. The narrator has not recorded it, and the audio folder still contains the flawed rehearsal clip. I asked the editor to keep that old clip marked retired rather than rename it final simply because the script correction is approved.

A text approval establishes the intended speech, not its performance or edit. The next audio deliverable should carry a recording version linked to the approved script. A listening check can then determine whether the phrase is present after the actual pause treatment. The retired clip remains useful for comparing the defect, but should not be selected automatically by a player looking for the newest file name.

The rebuilt show package includes C-fern-r2 and its manifest matches the designer's chosen grey-border asset. The operator rendered it on the dome and confirmed the correct border. From the front seats the label was readable. We have not checked it from the back row, where the small footer may be harder to see. I recorded identification and front-seat readability as completed, with rear viewing still open.

The observations support two specific claims: the package uses the intended asset and its label can be read from the tested position. They do not establish readability throughout the room. A rear-row test should use the actual projected package and record seat location and the wording perceived. Enlarging a screenshot on a laptop would not reproduce the viewing condition we are concerned about.

The teacher tried the revised counterexample with one learner and reported that the learner referred to the printed values instead of symbol size. That is a limited reported success, not a class-wide result. The teacher also noticed the learner treated the border color as a category marker. We had intended the border as decoration. I asked for a revised card without that extra cue before the next broader trial.

The report is useful because it distinguishes the original size assumption from a newly noticed color cue. A revised design can remove the unnecessary border distinction while retaining the intended comparison. Do not claim the first trial failed entirely or solved every misconception. Its actual observations support a more specific design decision and give the next trial a clear question to examine.

The designer produced a border-neutral sketch for the counterexample and kept the two symbols equal in size. Its footer still carries the invented-example label in the editing file. The sketch has not been exported into the dome package. I have not asked the teacher to run the broader trial yet, because we first need to confirm that the actual teaching image preserves the new neutral border and visible qualification.

That order of preparation will make the later trial easier to interpret. If the displayed asset differs from the approved sketch, feedback could be attributed to a design the learner never saw. Compare the export with the intended sketch, check its label and identifier, and only then send the exact version for trial. These are proposed checks, not evidence that the new artwork has already been shown.

The narrator recorded the revised sentence and the editor sent audio-r2. I opened its waveform file but did not listen to the whole sentence. The editor says the phrase is present. The old clip remains archived. We have a received recording and a reported editing check, but our designated listening observation is still pending. A waveform shape cannot tell us which words survived the pause.

The listening review should bind to audio-r2 and the approved sentence. It can record the actual words heard around the pause rather than infer them from a filename or waveform. The editor's report can remain alongside that observation, clearly attributed. Receiving a recording is progress, but the defect was semantic content loss, so evidence must address the content in the actual audio.

The back-row check of C-fern-r2 found the footer too small to read without leaning forward. The operator noted the seat and projection setting. The title and main values were readable. I rejected only the footer presentation for the intended viewing condition, not the whole artwork or its identity. The designer has proposed a larger label area that should not cover the comparison values.

The measured viewing problem gives the redesign a specific target. A larger label area is a proposed remedy until projected and read from the same condition. Preserve the successful main-value and identity observations within their scope. A future handoff should not summarize this as all text unreadable or as fully readable merely because the title was clear; the qualification is a required part of the content.

The border-neutral counterexample export has arrived with its own identifier C-moss-r1. I compared it with the sketch and saw that the border color cue was removed. Its footer is present in the exported image, but it uses the same small font size that failed the other card's rear-row check. I returned it for the label-area revision before approving it for the planned trial.

The export comparison verifies the intended border change while exposing a related presentation risk. Using the observed footer issue as a reason to request a revision is justified; claiming a rear-row test of C-moss already failed would not be, because that exact asset has not been projected there. The handoff should distinguish a transferred design concern from a directly observed result.

The listening reviewer played audio-r2 and heard the invented-example phrase intact before the explanation. They also noticed the edit creates an unnatural pause between the label and the following sentence. The teacher says the gap may be distracting but has not heard it themselves. I accepted phrase presence and requested a teacher review of the pause before approving the recording for the full lesson.

The original omission has a positive observed result in r2, while pacing remains a separate quality question. A later pacing edit could remove words again, so the final edited output will need a targeted content check. The teacher's anticipated reaction is not yet an observation. Send the exact clip for listening and record their response rather than treating a general worry as a completed rejection.

The operator found an old cue-sheet printout beside the projector. It places the distance material ahead of the brightness material, as the current outline does, but points to the retired ambiguous card file. I marked the printout reference stale without changing its segment sequence. The corrected show manifest exists digitally, while the operator station still needs a current printed reference or another reliable access method.

This shows why sequence policy and asset references should be reviewed as separate fields. A stale card reference can be wrong even when the ordering matches the current outline. Updating the operator reference need not invent a new teaching order. Preserve the old printout as evidence of the station mismatch and verify which replacement actually reaches the operator, rather than equating file creation with delivery.

The teacher listened to audio-r2 and asked for a shorter pause while retaining the complete invented-example phrase. Their response cites the clip identifier and does not request changing the lesson content. The editor has prepared a cut plan but not produced audio-r3. We should not carry the r2 phrase-presence result forward automatically to a future recording modified around the same sensitive region.

The approved pacing request defines the intended change, and the cut plan is preparation for it. Once r3 exists, listen across that region to verify both the shorter pause and the required words. The previous content check remains valid for r2. Separating versions lets us avoid claiming the new edit is safe solely because its predecessor preserved the phrase.

The designer enlarged the label panels on C-fern and C-moss and issued new export identifiers for both. Their main comparison values are unchanged according to the change note. I compared the visible values in the two exports with the prior assets and found a match. Neither new export has been projected from the back row yet, so the larger text is a remedy awaiting the actual condition check.

That comparison supports preservation of the named values, while projection readability remains empirical within this fictional workflow. A desktop image with larger text is not sufficient to certify rear viewing. The operator should use the rebuilt package containing the new identifiers and record the seat and setting. Check that the larger panel does not obscure any other needed element in projection, even if the layout looks fine locally.

The operator replaced the stale printed cue reference with a fresh page listing the current asset identifiers. I saw the new page at the station and compared its file names with the manifest. This closes the observed reference-delivery mismatch for the current package. It does not mean the operator has rehearsed every cue, or that the new larger label assets have passed the outstanding viewing test.

The physical delivery and identifier comparison are useful completed checks. The handoff can preserve them without using a broad station ready label. Rehearsal behavior and visual readability remain different tasks. If the current outline is later authorized to change, the cue reference may need an order revision, but that would be a new controlled update rather than a reason to rewrite what was observed today.

The teacher has reserved class time for a broader counterexample trial but has not confirmed which exported card will be used. I sent the proposed C-moss revision identifier and asked them to wait for the projection-label check. A reserved time is an opportunity, not an actual teaching outcome. There is no new learner feedback from that future session in the current packet.

The planned trial depends on a verified teaching artifact and a confirmed version handoff. Keep that dependency visible so a schedule entry cannot be mistaken for completed evaluation. The teacher's earlier single-learner report remains available with its limited scope. We should not expand it into class-wide evidence or fabricate a broader result simply because time has been set aside.

The rear-row viewing session was interrupted by a projector alignment problem. The operator stopped before displaying the new cards and logged the equipment issue. They corrected alignment afterward using a generic grid, but did not resume the label test. The grid check supports the equipment adjustment only. The C-fern and C-moss label observations remain unperformed under the intended back-row condition.

The aborted session should not count as either a readability success or a card failure. The next test can use the corrected equipment and the identified new exports, with the original seat condition documented. A successful grid is evidence that the projector was adjusted, not that the card footer can be read. Keep the task open with its actual blocker removed rather than repeat a vague equipment unavailable status.

The editor produced audio-r3 with the shortened pause and supplied its checksum. Their message says they retained all words, but the designated reviewer has not listened. The clip is in the package staging folder and has not replaced the active teaching audio. I asked the operator not to swap it automatically until the targeted check confirms the label survives the edit.

The new clip's identity is known and its intended change is documented. The remaining observation is precisely at the edited region. A checksum confirms which bytes we have, not which words they contain. The staged placement is useful for review but does not itself authorize classroom use. After listening, record both phrase presence and the requested pacing behavior before approving the swap.

The teacher's reserved trial time passed without the new card because the label check had not finished. The teacher used an unrelated activity instead and sent no counterexample results. I recorded the trial as not run. The earlier invitation should not remain in a summary as if a class test happened. The teacher has offered to find another time but has not proposed a date.

That is an honest task-state update: the planned opportunity was not used for this material. A next handoff can request a new slot after the artifact prerequisites are met, without inventing a date or outcome. The unrelated classroom activity supplies no evidence about our revised counterexample. Keep the single-learner observation as the only existing learner report until a further trial actually occurs.

A duplicate ID appeared in the staged asset manifest because the export script copied C-moss's new revision label onto an older preview thumbnail. The full-size image and thumbnail have different roles. I asked the designer to mark the thumbnail as a preview derivative and bind it explicitly to the full-size export. We have not regenerated the manifest yet, so the two entries remain ambiguous in the staged package.

This is a derivative-identification problem rather than necessarily two competing approved full-size cards. The revised manifest should distinguish role and parent artifact, then the package should be checked for correct selection by the projector. A preview could be useful for navigation but unsuitable for actual display. Do not assume the application chooses the full-size image merely because a reviewer can tell the files apart manually.

The designer regenerated the manifest with separate full-size and preview identifiers and an explicit parent link. The operator opened the staging package and confirmed its display entry points to the full-size C-moss image. The preview remains a navigation aid. We have a completed selection check, but no rear-row reading observation yet. The corrected manifest did not change the invented values or the required card label.

That closes the selection ambiguity for the tested package. The preview's derivative relationship should remain in the manifest so future changes can propagate intentionally rather than by coincidental names. Selection correctness is necessary but not sufficient for readability. The actual display condition still needs the pending observation, and that result should name the same full-size asset and package version.

The listening reviewer started audio-r3 but the playback tool resumed at a saved position after the introductory label. They noticed this and stopped, then reset the player to the beginning. They did not replay the full edited region before leaving. I recorded a setup correction, not a phrase-presence check. The editor's claim that all words remain is still reported rather than independently observed.

The next reviewer should explicitly start before the edited phrase and listen through the shortened pause. A player reset prepares the task but does not supply its observation. Retaining the aborted attempt explains the absence of a result despite an apparent playback session. Do not infer that the phrase is missing because it was skipped by the tool, or that it is present because the script contains it.

The teacher reviewed the new counterexample transcript and approved its questions for another trial. They have not seen the latest projected image and have not scheduled learners. I updated the trial plan to refer to the identified full-size asset and to ask which cue each learner used. The plan now has clearer evidence goals, but it remains a plan without new classroom observations.

The transcript approval and improved questions make the proposed trial more controlled. They do not replace checking what the learners actually see or collecting their responses. When arranging the trial, include the exact artifact and the remaining viewing prerequisite. A summary should not say teacher tested merely because the teacher approved the plan; the action and its outcome are different evidence categories.

An assistant draft for the operator restated the lesson as beginning with the distance comparison and moving on to brightness. It also correctly lists the invented-example label on every card. I stored it as a draft cue description, not a recording of an actual lesson delivery. The operator has not used that draft during a rehearsal, and it carries no new authorization to alter the sequence.

The draft's ordering sentence is another expression of the current outline and should inherit any later effective control on that field. Its independent label requirement remains useful in the same document. A future update should not discard the whole draft merely because one field becomes outdated; it should prevent reuse of the old order while preserving separately supported content and the distinction between suggested and performed cues.

The operator scheduled a back-row viewing check for today, but the observer had to leave before the cards were shown. The equipment and identified package are ready, and the seat positions are marked. We still lack the actual observation. I have asked for a new check rather than mark the larger footer readable from its pixel size. The preparation reduces uncertainty about setup, not about what a reader can perceive.

The handoff can propose completing that viewing check using the already prepared setup. It should not repeat the old projector alignment repair as if that were still the obstacle. The remaining missing evidence is a reader's observation of the actual projected label from the intended location. Keep the prepared package identifier and seat condition attached so the next attempt can be compared with the earlier failed small-footer test.

The narrator has offered to make another recording if audio-r3 fails review. No failure has been observed, and no new recording has been commissioned. The existing targeted listening check remains the appropriate next step. I placed the offer in correspondence rather than adding audio-r4 to the asset list. An available remedy is not a reason to invent a defect or an artifact that does not exist.

That preserves a sensible decision order. First inspect the actual r3 content around the edited pause; then decide whether another recording is needed. The offer may reduce future delay, but it supplies no present content evidence. A note that says new recording pending would be misleading unless a decision and request actually follow. At this point the outstanding task is review of the received identified clip.

The teacher asks whether the next trial can use printed cards if projection scheduling keeps slipping. I have not approved that alternative yet. Printed readability would be a different delivery condition, and the current trial plan names the dome package. We can consider a revised plan, but any such change needs its own version and clear statement of which teaching question it tests.

A print-based trial could provide some evidence about conceptual cues while leaving projection readability unresolved. It should not be described as a substitute result for every pending check. If chosen, document the printed artifact and condition, then preserve the distinction when interpreting feedback. The current authorized plan remains the staged projection trial until an explicit plan revision is approved.

I assembled today's handoff with the full-size asset mapping, the staged audio-r3 link and the approved trial questions. There is no new learner result or completed rear-row observation in this packet. The operator needs a current outline note and one concrete follow-up action, with proposed work clearly separated from already observed checks. Any later authorized outline change should take effect only at its stated control event.

The note can use the current permitted sequence, retain the invented-example labeling requirement and choose a pending verification supported by the latest state. It should not invent astronomical observations or treat a mock card as a catalog record. The outstanding tasks remain meaningful even if the sequence changes: artifact identity, visible qualification and recorded speech need evidence independently of which comparison segment comes first.

creation_note: Original fictional evaluation script; all people, institutions, dates and dialogue are authored. No real participant log or public provenance is claimed.

haystack_sessions.content: This is our invented database-cleaning workshop, not a real volunteer register. My initial, unverified merge note claims that rows R17 and R71 refer to the same volunteer. I wrote that after seeing the same displayed name, without checking the original forms. Keep the note attributed to me. We also need to repair the import demonstration and prepare a student exercise that contains no instructor answers.

I have recorded your provisional duplicate-person claim for R17 and R71, with the missing form check attached. That is a working assertion, not evidence that any merge has been executed. I will track three separate deliverables: an evidence worksheet, a reproducible import demonstration, and a learner-facing exercise. Their completion states should not be inferred from the existence of this planning note.

The import demonstration uses made-up membership codes, such as 0048 and 0480, which must remain text. Yesterday's spreadsheet preview displayed the first code as 48. The original CSV is still unchanged in the source folder, but the demonstration workbook was saved after the preview.
