The photo reviewer found a learner name at the edge of image W3 and cropped that edge in a new export W3b. The fold arrows and all face labels remain visible in W3b. The revised picture has been checked for that label. Approval to release the photograph set is still pending, so a completed crop is not a publication event.

Record the W3-to-W3b correction and the completed label check while retaining the original version in its working context. The checked image can be submitted for the still-pending release decision. There is no need to redo the same crop merely because approval has not arrived, and no basis to equate a successful edit with permission to publish.

The seated projection test was run with one learner, who correctly identified the first upward hinge movement on M1. We have that observation, but no comparison across other seats or visual conditions. The projection crop itself remains fixed. I want the facilitator's next note to state these limits rather than calling the display universally clear.

Describe the completed single-seat observation and leave broader readability as untested. That preserves useful evidence without turning a limited check into a universal finding. A further test can target another seat if needed, while the next lesson can also use the checked paper master as an available alternative for a participant who cannot read the projection.

A supply count found one unused checked M1 sheet and two blank sheets. I therefore need one additional printed copy for the two catch-up learners if both accept. They have not confirmed a date. This count supersedes our old availability estimate, but it does not change the original distribution record or either learner's assessment status.

Use the current one-sheet stock for planning and request one more checked print before committing to two paper copies. Keep scheduling and printing as separate open tasks. The absence of a date confirmation is not a cancellation, and the historical ten-sheet preparation should remain a completed event rather than being rewritten as a mistaken count.

The extension worksheet still has no recorded T/U trace. The assistant proposed recording the folding steps on the reverse side so a reviewer can distinguish a derived opposite pair from an answer copied from another sheet. I agreed to try that format, but no new trace has been submitted, and the extension table remains partial.

The next extension step is to obtain the missing trace in the agreed format and compare its steps with N's supplied arrows. Preserve the completed Q/S and P/R rows and the older flat-neighbor note with its context. Do not present the format agreement itself as completion of the geometry exercise or fill the final pair without evidence.

The organizer has not replied about releasing the reviewed photograph set. There is no fixed release date to infer from elapsed time. W3b remains the checked image, and the old W3 stays in the restricted working archive with its original context. Our next communication should request a release decision without claiming that the set has already been published or rejected.

Ask for the missing release decision and refer to the reviewed version by its actual identifier. Keep publication status unresolved until a response arrives. The photograph task can progress independently of the unfinished extension trace and catch-up arrangements; completing one line of work should not silently mark the other lines complete.

The first log says that all frames in the first review export follow capture order. This is an unverified statement by the compiler; I do not have that export's frame manifest. We are making a stop-motion puzzle, and I want to distinguish what the log claims from what the surviving frame evidence actually shows.

The compiler's claim is that no frame in the first review export is out of capture order. Without its manifest we cannot inspect that universal statement frame by frame. We can still organize the surviving material and record local observations without presenting them as proof about the complete export that has not been supplied.

The story has a clay fox move a blue cup from a shelf to a table, then turn a paper flag. Three contact-sheet pictures show the cup on the shelf, on the table, and in the fox's hand. Their printed filenames are 04, 06, and 05 respectively. There is no take label visible on that sheet.

For the depicted action, holding the cup can plausibly connect shelf and table, but filenames alone do not establish capture times. Record the visible prop states and the missing take information separately. A proposed story sequence should not be mislabeled as a recovered shooting chronology, especially if a frame may come from a different take.

A second folder also contains files named 04, 05, and 06. Its slate photograph shows scene B, take 2, while the first folder's slate has scene B, take 1. The camera reset its counter when we changed cards. I have not yet checked whether the contact sheet mixed frames from the two folders.

The counter reset makes a bare filename ambiguous across folders. Keep the source folder and slate identity with each item before comparing pictures. A file numbered 04 in one take is not automatically an earlier capture than 06 in another take. The contact sheet needs a membership check before it can support a take-specific sequence.

The sound notebook contains a short bell recording intended for the table landing. Its filename also ends in 06, but it is an audio file with its own recording session. We have no synchronizing slate for it. I want to compare the sound and picture by their intended action, not assume matching suffixes prove simultaneous recording.

Separate the audio asset's identity from the picture filenames. A shared suffix may be a convenient local naming choice, but it is not a cross-recording timestamp. The intended table-landing cue can be recorded as an editing requirement and checked against a playback once a particular version has been assembled.

For our independent identification method, use the slate scene and take identifiers to distinguish reshoots. We have separate B1 and B2 slate photographs, and I want both identifiers attached to extracted frames. A matching filename or similar prop pose does not establish that two pictures came from the same shooting attempt.

Use a compound scene/take/frame reference when discussing the material, with the original folder recorded as supporting provenance. That allows a later correction without renaming the raw photographs. If a slate is missing, keep the take identity unknown instead of assigning it from a nearby picture merely because the pose looks continuous.

I checked the first contact sheet against its export list. All three pictures came from B1, so the sheet itself does not mix those two takes. The list does not contain capture timestamps. The pictures establish the shown states, but they do not tell us whether the animator photographed a later story pose before returning to an earlier pose.

The membership concern for that three-picture sheet is resolved, while capture ordering remains a separate question. Keep those conclusions apart. The story exercise can ask learners to explain a plausible action chain from the cup states, but it should not require them to invent shooting timestamps that the available list does not provide.

The B2 reshoot changes the cup to red and removes the flag from the background. The script still names a blue cup and a flag, so the director must decide whether to accept those differences or request another reshoot. I have sent comparison stills, but no decision has arrived and no third take has been scheduled.

Prepare a concise comparison of the two visible changes and request the missing decision. Treat the red cup and absent flag as observations, not evidence that the director has approved a new story. A proposal for another take is different from scheduling or completing it, and the current record supports neither of those later stages.

The first sound placement uses the bell at the beginning of the hand-held cup pose. The director wanted it at the table landing instead. I have sent the timecode of the misplaced cue to the editor, but I have not heard a corrected mix. A cue-placement request should remain separate from the still-image membership check.

Keep the misplaced cue observation and the requested landing position with the version that was heard. A later reply should identify its corrected mix before the issue is marked resolved. The visual source membership result does not demonstrate that the sound cue has moved; those checks concern different material and require different evidence.

The director accepted the red cup for the next version but asked that the flag remain visible. This does not retroactively change what B1 or B2 depicts. We planned a B3 reshoot using a red cup and the flag, but the set has not been rebuilt yet and there are no B3 frames to inspect.

Record the new production choice alongside the unchanged visual evidence for earlier takes. The next preparation step is to rebuild the required set and label the new slate B3. Do not describe the requested combination as already captured, and do not recolor or relabel the earlier source stills to make them appear consistent with the new instruction.

A helper found two B1 files with different filenames but identical image bytes. The file list shows one was copied into a second subfolder for a contact sheet. That establishes a duplicate file, not a second photograph of the same pose. I have linked the two paths but have not removed either original working file.

Count the linked files as two file occurrences of one image when discussing the archive. If the editing task needs unique pictures, use the documented duplicate relationship rather than inferring two captures from the two names. Keep the original paths available so a later sheet can be traced back without silently losing its provenance.

The story continuity test has another problem: the flag changes orientation between the hand-held cup picture and the table picture. We do not know whether it was intentionally turned in the action or moved between shots. I can identify the visual discontinuity, but the stills alone do not explain the cause.

Ask for the intended flag action or a supporting intermediate picture before adding a causal explanation. A visible change is enough to raise a continuity question, not to decide whether the animator made a mistake. The teaching exercise can preserve the unresolved alternatives and ask what evidence would distinguish them rather than forcing one explanation.

The editor returned a sound test with the bell at the table landing. I listened to that isolated test and the placement matches the request. The sound has not yet been combined with the planned B3 reshoot, which has no frames at this point. We should keep the successful isolated timing test without claiming the final sequence is mixed.

The isolated sound test supports the requested placement in that test only. Preserve its result and wait for an actual B3 sequence before calling the new combined output checked. It is possible to reuse the recording while still needing to verify the cue's position in the later edit, whose timing has not yet been established.

B3 has now been captured with the red cup and visible flag. Its slate reads scene B, take 3, and the three selected stills show shelf, hand, and table states. I checked those visual features. The files have not yet been placed into a new review export, so completing the reshoot has not completed the edit.

The requested prop combination is now observed in B3. A next editing step can use those identified stills while keeping B1 and B2 as historical alternatives. Make the new selection explicit, and avoid claiming that a completed capture proves either the ordering or the existence of an export that has not yet been assembled.

The animator replied about B1's flag: the script called for the fox to turn it after placing the cup, but we lack a picture of the turning action. That explains the intended action, not which omitted frame was captured. I have added an explicit gap between the placement and the changed flag state on our story diagram.

Use the reply as evidence of intention and keep the missing visual transition marked as a gap. The diagram can represent a proposed bridge without pretending a surviving frame supplies it. This also keeps story chronology distinct from shooting order: a scripted action can have a defined place even when the related capture evidence is incomplete.

The compiler's shorthand index defines E as the first review export and C as capture order. The old note reads every E frame follows C. It records the same whole-export assertion from the first log, and it adds no manifest, timestamps, or independent observation that would let us verify that assertion.

The indexed assertion every E frame follows C refers to the first export and capture order through that legend. Its support remains the compiler's note, rather than a separate inspection. Do not treat the change to shorthand as new evidence or confuse it with the local B1 contact-sheet membership check that addressed a narrower question.

The new B3 stills now give us a concrete sequence for the sound test, but the editor has not attached the bell to a B3 draft. The previous isolated test remains a reference, not a completed B3 mix. I asked for the cue to be checked again once the chosen edit has a stable table-landing position.

That dependency is sensible: an available audio file and a successful isolated test are not a completed mix for a newly captured take. Bind the next sound check to an identified picture edit. If its frame slots move, record the resulting cue adjustment rather than treating an earlier absolute timecode as permanently correct.

An editor built a new draft D2 from the identified B3 stills. The draft displays the hand pose before the shelf pose, which contradicts our intended shelf-to-hand-to-table action. I checked the playback and requested a reorder. D2 is a new draft, not the unlocated first review export mentioned in the compiler's old log.

Record the observed story-order problem in D2 and request the specific correction. It does not establish the contents of a different missing export. When checking the revision, compare the displayed action sequence with the agreed story, and keep that judgment separate from any claim about the times when the source frames were photographed.

The editor proposed duplicating the hand frame to make the action hold longer. We have only three selected B3 source images, so a four-slot sequence could still use three distinct images. I asked them to label repeated edit slots explicitly. A repeated display slot should not be counted as another captured source photograph.

Use separate counts for source images and timeline slots. If the hand frame is repeated, record both slot references to the same identified source. That makes the longer hold inspectable without inventing another photograph. The duration change remains a proposal until a revised timeline is supplied and compared with the requested sequence.

A separate working folder contains a file marked scene C, take 1, showing a green door and no cup. Someone suggested using it to fill the missing flag action because its filename fits the gap. I have left it separate. Its visible content and slate identity do not support treating it as the missing B-scene transition.

The matching number is not a valid scene match. Keep the C1 frame available for its own purpose, but reject the unsupported substitution into B's flag transition. The missing bridge can remain explicitly unresolved or be designed as a new shot; neither choice requires pretending that an unrelated door image depicts the absent action.

The D2 picture order is still under correction, so I have postponed the final bell placement. That is a dependency on the landing position in the edit, not a cancellation of the bell recording. The audio file is available. I want the timeline note to explain why placing the cue now could create work that the reordered sequence immediately invalidates.

Keep the bell as an available asset and the final placement as pending on the corrected picture sequence. The dependency does not require discarding the sound or declaring its isolated test invalid. It means the placement in this particular edit cannot be finalized until the landing event has a defined position in that edit.

The revised D3 playback now shows shelf, hand, hand, and table in that order. The two hand slots point to the same B3 image, and each slot lasts half a second. I checked those references and timing entries. The resulting two-second edit holds the hand pose for one second; it still has only three distinct source images.

That resolves the specific requested reorder and repeated-slot labeling. Keep four timeline slots, three distinct images, and two seconds of display as separate measures. The checked story sequence does not settle the chronology of B3's captures, and it should not be used to fill missing evidence about the first review export from the old compiler note.

The flag action remains absent from D3. The director agreed that a visible pause card could explain the missing transition in the workshop exercise, but the wording has not been drafted. We are not treating a pause card as a newly discovered source frame. It would be an explanatory addition created for the exercise.

Draft the proposed card as an editorial aid and distinguish its text from the surviving visual evidence. Ask the director to check whether it accurately names the gap without inventing a photographed action. Its creation would support teaching the continuity problem while preserving uncertainty about the unavailable transition material.

One exported thumbnail sheet labels every B3 picture as take 2, although the linked source slate says take 3. The images themselves match B3. I traced the error to a reused caption template and asked for the sheet labels to be corrected; no evidence suggests the raw photos or their slate were changed.

Correct the derivative sheet's captions while preserving the raw image and slate identities. A label-template error is not evidence that the shooting attempt changed. After correction, verify the links as well as the visible captions so that a clean-looking sheet does not hide a pointer to a different source file.

D3's corrected picture sequence is stable enough for the editor to place the bell at the table landing. I asked for that new mix and specified D3 by version. No mix has been returned. The old isolated sound test and the new request are both in the notebook, and they must not be counted as two completed checks of the same output.

Record the D3 mix request as pending. Once it arrives, compare the audible cue with the table slot in that named version, not merely with the old isolated test. Version binding prevents a truthful report of an earlier successful sound check from being mistaken for evidence about a different output that has not yet been heard.

The thumbnail sheet has been relabeled take 3, and its links were checked against the B3 slate and source folder. That repair is complete. The pause card draft says the fox definitely turned the flag between these two captures. I rejected that wording because the director confirmed intended story action, not an observed sequence of captures.

Request wording that describes the missing story transition without asserting an unseen shooting event. Keep the completed sheet-label correction off the pending list. The two issues have different evidence: one was a documented derivative label error, while the other risks turning an intended action into an unsupported historical claim about production.

A camera-clock test used three new calibration images whose timestamps increased in the same order as we pressed the shutter. That test was performed after the original shoots. It checks this present camera setting, not whether a prior card reset or copied file preserved old timestamps. I do not have a calibration record from the earlier shoot.

Keep the new calibration result with its test date and scope. It can inform future recording practice without proving what happened in an earlier session. If someone asks for capture chronology of old material, request contemporaneous evidence instead of treating a later successful clock test as a retroactive guarantee.

For the workshop handout, I want a comparison table with columns intended action, visible state, source scene/take, edit slot, and capture time evidence. Some cells in the last column must remain unknown. The editor has made the headings but has not filled the rows, so there is not yet a completed comparison table to inspect.

Fill a small supported portion first, using the checked B3 identifiers and D3 slot references, and leave unsupported capture-time cells explicitly unknown. The table should make differences between the columns easier to see. Do not copy a story-position number into the capture-time column simply to avoid an empty or uncertain entry.

The D3 mix was returned and checked: the bell begins when the table slot begins. That resolves placement for D3. Adding a pause card later could shift the absolute timeline position, so any new edit version would need its own cue check. The sound recording itself does not need to be recreated merely because an edit offset changes.

Retain the completed D3 result and require a fresh placement comparison only if the edit changes. A shift caused by inserting a card is an offset issue, not a reason to infer a new recording session.
