The two observed fits are consistent with the equal bounding dimensions and show why identity needs its own evidence. The authorized observatory routing remains O-M to Y, with H-M excluded from that package. Preserve the difficult H-M fit result rather than deleting it to make the matching task easier. A future packing action should inspect the identifier and connector, because successful closure alone cannot distinguish these two candidate masts.

I revised C2 into C3: verify O-B, load X, close X; verify O-M and its square connector, load Y horizontally, close Y. During a paper walkthrough, a reader checked the labels on the empty boxes instead of the parts. They followed the printed sequence but never looked at the component identifiers. No real loading occurred in that walkthrough. I need the card to distinguish a box destination label from evidence about the object being placed inside it.

C3's walkthrough reveals an identity-evidence problem, not a performed wrong shipment. A revised instruction can ask the reader to read the identifier on the component itself before comparing it with the destination label. Keep the connector check as additional evidence for the mast. The procedure should not let a correctly labeled empty box certify any arbitrary object selected nearby. A new trial will be needed to see whether the revised wording changes actual attention.

P1's first caption draft names O-M correctly but says 'ready to dispatch'. That overstates what the photo shows and ignores that the fit trials ended with the parts removed. I corrected the caption to 'identified components before final loading'. The reservation sheet is not included in the public image or caption. I have not asked a reader to identify the components from this corrected caption-image pair yet.

The corrected wording matches the photographed state and avoids converting preparation into dispatch. A caption-image check can ask a reader which component belongs to the observatory and whether the image shows loaded boxes. It should be possible to answer from identifiers and visible arrangement, without the private buyer relation. Keep publication approval and successful reader interpretation separate; an editor correction does not by itself supply a reader response.

I prepared an order diagram showing both box lids open while identities are checked. It suggests loading Y first, then X, because the small mast is easier to overlook once the body has been put away. That ordering is a proposal, not a physical necessity established by dimensions. The body and mast are already detached. I want to test whether the order helps completeness without claiming the alternative order is impossible or inherently wrong.

The order proposal can be evaluated as a workflow aid while preserving the independent geometric facts. Either order may be physically feasible under the stated setup; the criterion is whether each required component is correctly identified and included. Record omissions or attention failures if they occur rather than manufacturing a constraint to force the preferred sequence. The matching-component rule must hold regardless of which box is loaded first.

C4 explicitly says to read the identifier on each component, then compare it to the box routing label. In a supervised dry run, the reader selected H-M first because it was nearer Y, but noticed its round connector and returned it before loading. They then selected O-M and completed the two-box loading, starting with Y. Both lids closed, and the inventory sheet records O-M in Y and O-B in X. No buyer field was needed.

That dry run supplies a completed correct selection after a caught near-selection error. It should not be recorded as H-M actually packed or as a procedure that never created an initial temptation. Preserve the observed sequence, including the successful check before loading. The result is bounded to C4 and the supervised setup; it does not prove that an unsupervised reader or a differently arranged tray would make the same correction.

After documenting the dry run, I unloaded both boxes for a display review. O-M and O-B are again on their labeled tray positions. A summary draft omitted that unloading sentence and said the objects were still packed. I corrected it using the end-of-session inventory. The successful dry-run record remains valid, but it is no longer a current location statement. I have not dispatched or handed over any package in this fictional exercise.

The current state should follow the last actual movement, while the earlier loaded state remains a historical observation. A summary that retains only the successful loading would create a false present inventory. Keep the unloading event and its identifiers attached to the session record. No need to erase the dry-run success to fix this; represent both events in order, and distinguish readiness to repeat a procedure from a package currently awaiting transport.

The reader of corrected P1 identified O-M from its label and square connector, but assumed H-M was an extra spare for the observatory. The caption names both masts without explaining their different models. I drafted a P2 caption saying H-M belongs to a separate harbor miniature and is not included in the observatory package. The new caption has not been tested. I do not want to hide H-M from the image solely to remove the identity challenge.

The revised caption can clarify membership while preserving the useful visual distractor. Record P1's successful identification and incorrect package-membership inference separately. A follow-up can ask which components belong in the observatory package and what evidence supports that selection. The answer should rely on identifiers, connector information, and the explicit membership note, not on the buyer association or which mast happens to be closer to the body in the photograph.

A planned outer sleeve would hold X and Y together as a pair, but I have not specified its dimensions. A draft packing checklist nevertheless marked 'outer sleeve fit confirmed'. I crossed that out and left a measurement task. The successful individual box trials cannot establish combined fit in an undefined sleeve. We can still prepare a dimension drawing by specifying whether X and Y sit side by side or one above the other.

The missing sleeve specification is a real dependency rather than a reason to invent a favorable fit. Start from measured exterior box dimensions, which differ from the earlier internal cavities, and state an arrangement. Only then can a usable sleeve dimension be compared. A drawing or calculation will be a predicted fit until an actual sleeve configuration is built and checked. Preserve the individual box successes under their proper scope.

I measured the exterior of X as twelve by ten by nine centimeters and Y as seven by five by five. For a side-by-side arrangement along width, with aligned front edges, their combined rectangular envelope is nineteen wide, ten deep, and nine high. I propose an outer sleeve with usable dimensions twenty by eleven by ten. We have not made it, and these exterior measurements should not replace the interior cavity dimensions used for component fit.

The side-by-side envelope uses the sum of widths and the maxima of depth and height: nineteen, ten, nine. It fits the proposed usable sleeve dimension by dimension with one centimeter of surplus on each axis. That is a geometric plan for the two closed boxes, not a demonstration that the sleeve's opening, material, or closure performs correctly. Keep exterior and interior measurement tables separate to avoid confusing a box wall with available packing space.

I built sleeve S1 to those usable dimensions, but its closure flap projects two centimeters into the opening while it is being loaded. With that flap in the way, the effective entry width is eighteen centimeters, less than the side-by-side envelope's nineteen. I stopped the attempt before forcing the boxes through. The final cavity would be large enough, yet the loading path is blocked by the flap. This is not a contradiction in the earlier cavity arithmetic.

The entry restriction demonstrates that static final fit and insertion feasibility are distinct. A redesigned flap that folds fully outside during loading could restore the twenty-centimeter entry width, provided it actually stays clear. Alternatively, another loading sequence might be considered, but it would need its own path analysis rather than an assumption that fitting volume guarantees passage. Keep the failed entry condition as evidence tied to S1's flap position.

I drafted sleeve S2 with the flap held completely outward by a temporary exterior clip during insertion. The clip is removed only after both boxes are fully inside. S2 is not built. The individual components remain unloaded on their tray after the earlier display review, so an S2 package trial would first require correct loading of X and Y. The sleeve diagram alone should not cause the current inventory to say either box is full.

S2's proposed sequence has explicit prerequisites: verify and load the two components into their assigned boxes, close the boxes, hold the flap clear, then attempt insertion. The temporary clip must remain outside the usable path. Record the sequence as a plan until executed. This allows the next trial to inspect the flap remedy without losing the separate identity checks that distinguish O-M from the equally fitting H-M distractor.

The P2 caption was tried with the same P1 image. A reader correctly excluded H-M from the observatory package but described O-M as already inside Y, even though the image shows it on the table. The new membership wording worked while the current-location interpretation remained wrong. I propose adding 'displayed separately before loading' beside the component list. That addition is drafted only, and we have not produced a new image or a new loaded state.

The next caption revision can address location without undoing the successful membership distinction. Keep the image version and physical arrangement constant if testing only wording, and ask the reader to distinguish what belongs in a package from what is currently packed. The earlier dry run must not be used to override the actual unloaded photograph or later inventory. A component's intended destination does not establish its present location.

I built S2 and tested its opening with empty X and Y in the proposed side-by-side arrangement. With the flap clipped fully outward, both empty boxes entered, and the clip could be removed afterward. I have not repeated this with loaded boxes. The result checks the entry geometry and clip sequence in an empty-box trial; it does not show that the internal components remain correctly placed or that the loaded package handles well.

The empty-box trial resolves the observed opening blockage under the new configuration. A loaded trial still has meaningful work to do, especially preserving component identity and internal orientation through the full sequence. Keep the empty test as completed rather than rerunning it by default, and state the additional questions for the loaded version. Neither a fitting outer envelope nor an internal ledger read supplies evidence of the missing loaded-handling result.

The latest caption draft P3 includes 'displayed separately before loading' and the note excluding H-M from the observatory package. It has not been tested. The photograph is still P1, with readable labels and connectors, not a photograph of the sleeve trial. I want the next reader question to ask both membership and current location without printing the intended answer beside the question. The editor notes remain separate from the reader prompt.

P3 is ready for a bounded wording check, with no new image state implied. The question can reveal whether the location clarification preserves the successful membership interpretation. Keep a record of the exact caption-image pair supplied to the reader and whether they had seen earlier drafts. A correct response from someone who already knows the editorial answer would answer a different question from an unprompted interpretation by a fresh reader.

All components are currently outside their boxes on the labeled tray, and the boxes have been removed from S2 after the empty trial. C4's correct dry-run sequence is available as a procedure, but final loading has not happened. I have not obtained a transport or movement result with a loaded sleeve. We can schedule a controlled bench handling check after loading, but no date or participant has been confirmed in these notes.

A current inventory should therefore list the components on the tray, empty X and Y outside the sleeve, and S2 available for another test. Proposed scheduling should not be converted into an appointment or a completed transport event. A loaded bench check can use C4's part-level identity steps and S2's tested flap sequence as prerequisites. Record what is actually moved and inspected, rather than reporting broad packing success from several narrower historical checks.

For the next handoff, preserve the matching component identifier rule and choose one unresolved task from the loaded S2 trial or the P3 caption check. Use only private information permitted by the caller's current scope. A read grant for the reservation ledger is not permission to reveal the buyer publicly or change the reservation. An old handoff sheet returning after revocation must not override that revoked access, even if the physical packing details remain useful.

The public work can proceed from dimensions, identifiers, orientations, and the latest actual inventory. Keep the equal-size wrong mast as a meaningful selection challenge, and distinguish a proposed loaded check from the completed empty-sleeve result. Internal ledger access can be used only within its granted purpose while active. The earlier dry run and the private association do not jointly imply that a package has been dispatched or that a buyer authorized an unrelated action.

haystack_sessions.content: This is a fictional community-radio editing exercise. Tobin Reed supplied the recorded voice for the rough weather bumper R9. Keep the rejected export as a timing example. Distinguish the source file handle from the spoken clip bounds, and report any combined duration only for the chosen boundaries. I checked the chosen in and out marks for R9. The spoken bumper between those marks lasts nine seconds. That duration excludes the leading silent handle. Draft internal cue note: M4 music sting, then Tobin Reed voicing R9 for nine seconds between its approved marks, then presenter introduction. The M4-to-R9 junction still needs an actual combined playback. With simple concatenation and no overlap or gap, M4 plus the marked bumper would occupy thirteen seconds; that is a conditional calculation, not an observed complete export.

I have prepared a new combined file C2 using the marked R9 segment. File preparation is complete, but the playback appointment has not occurred. The public cue-sheet draft contains clip identifiers and timing fields only. haystack_sessions.content: This is a fictional recipe-card digitization exercise. Our initial diagnosis for the missing corner mark on card H was a crease in the card. I will record the crease as the initial, unverified explanation for card H losing its corner mark. A readable recipe does not establish why a small mark disappeared. Keep the original thumbnail and diagnosis available for comparison rather than silently replacing them with a later interpretation.

I compared the crop boxes and found that one thumbnail used a narrower box. That is a second possible explanation. I have not rescanned the card, so the crop difference does not prove that the crease explanation is wrong. The two files also have different brightness settings.

A crop difference and a brightness difference are two changed conditions. Testing both at once would not isolate their effects. Prepare a comparison with a consistent crop first, and record what remains untested. Neither a proposed test nor an exported settings file is a new observation of the corner.

For the comparison scan, put the title at the top. The small pencil arrow on the back is not an orientation instruction. I have saved a settings sheet, but I have not run the comparison scan. Please keep the orientation requirement in the handoff so a missing mark is not confused with a rotated view.

Handoff draft: initial cause, a crease in card H, remains unverified; comparison orientation, title at the top. The settings sheet is ready, while the scan and the observation of the corner remain pending. The cropped thumbnail is evidence of an export choice, not proof of a damaged original.

The scanner booking has been requested but not confirmed. I also noticed a handwritten serving count on the back; it is unrelated to the corner mark. Do not use the booking request as evidence that someone has already rescanned H.

The handoff can ask the next operator to verify the booking and then make the controlled comparison. Keep the back-side annotation separate from the orientation instruction and from the cause field. Leave the comparison result open until there is an actual observation.

haystack_sessions.content: This is a fictional transit-map lesson, not a real fare system. The current rule for an endpoint lying exactly on a zone boundary is to assign the higher zone. A segment that merely crosses a boundary is not an endpoint-on-boundary case. I want the rule recorded separately from the drawn route.

The endpoint rule is higher-zone assignment when the endpoint lies exactly on the boundary. Merely crossing a boundary does not by itself activate that special case. I will keep that distinction in the lesson note instead of treating every crossed line as a ticket destination.

On the draft map, route R crosses a boundary and ends inside zone C. Route S ends on the boundary between zones A and B, where B is higher than A. The printed example gives R zone C and S zone B under the current rule. No child has used these examples in a lesson yet.

Those are two different geometric relations. R ends in the interior, whereas S touches the boundary at its endpoint. The printed S result is an application of the stated convention, not a universal property of maps. A later convention change should not be described as a different historical printing.

The map legend uses dashed lines for zone boundaries. Solid lines are routes, and dots are stops. The legend proof is checked, but the example worksheet has not been checked against the map. Preserve the line-style distinction when you prepare that check.

Preparation note: dashed boundaries and solid routes are visually distinct; the current boundary-endpoint convention assigns the higher zone. The legend proof is checked. The worksheet comparison remains pending, and a checked legend alone does not certify that every printed example applies the rule correctly.

A reviewer circled a dot that sits very close to a boundary. The drawing coordinates put it inside zone A, not on the line. I have added a magnified inset, but I have not replaced the worksheet or performed the planned consistency check.

Use the stated coordinates when judging the near-boundary dot, and label the inset as a clarification of the drawing. The next check should compare endpoint placement and the effective rule, rather than silently treating visual closeness as exact membership of a boundary.

haystack_sessions.content: This is a fictional rehearsal-caption exercise. I initially blamed a kerning setting for the missing character in caption K. The initial explanation for the missing character in K is a kerning setting, with causal status unverified. A character present in the text but absent in a screenshot could involve rendering or font coverage as well. I will not promote the first explanation to an observed fact.

The screenshot was taken with font F, while the plain-text preview does not use that font. I found a font specimen sheet, but it does not include the particular character. That omission is not a measured failure of the actual font file.

A specimen sheet is a selection of examples, so absence from that sheet is weaker than testing a glyph in the actual file. Keep font coverage as a testable alternative. Changing the font and the spacing together would make the result difficult to attribute to either change.

The comparison export must use UTF-8. I checked that requirement on the local exercise sheet. The export settings are saved, but the comparison has not been rendered. Do not infer successful rendering just because a settings dialog closed without an error.

Draft investigation note: keep UTF-8 for the comparison export; the original kerning explanation remains an unverified claim. The saved settings and the still-present plain-text character are separate observations. A comparison render and its missing-or-present result are still pending.

I have prepared a second caption with the same character in isolation. It is a test fixture, not a repaired performance caption. The review appointment is only proposed, and nobody has signed off on either caption.

The next step is a controlled render using the recorded encoding and one changed rendering condition at a time. Record the observed character outcome when it exists, then revisit the cause claim. Preparing an isolated test string is not evidence that the display problem has disappeared.

Preparation note: arrival time is the current worksheet key, and original signed slips stay in the sealed envelope. The duplicate ordered by code is marked comparison-only. The transcription check is limited to supplied text; it does not establish agreement with unopened originals.

I added a blank column for a later reviewer to record discrepancies. The column has no entries yet. I also corrected a header typo in a copy of the worksheet; this did not alter any arrival record or authorize opening the envelope.

haystack_sessions.content: For the fictional Fieldglass fabric workshop, our current swatch-rack ordering field is grain direction. The three-strip ledger therefore contains two lengthwise strips and one crosswise strip, with just sample 18 marked unwashed. Keep unwashed strips in amber sleeves. Washed strips use the ordinary clear sleeves. There are two empty amber sleeves and four clear sleeves on the bench. One amber sleeve has a split seam, so it is set aside and must not be counted as usable stock. I have now tried the usable amber sleeve on sample 18. It fits without folding the strip. The split-seam sleeve remains out of use. I have also printed both label mock-ups on spare paper, not on the strips: the narrow label cuts off the wash-status word, while the wide label shows the identifier and status on separate lines. The fit check is complete for sample 18, and the wide two-line label is now the chosen format. The narrow mock-up is a failed paper-layout trial, not a damaged strip. I will carry those results into the next shift's brief. The current rack-ordering field is still grain direction; the label-format choice and completed sleeve-fit check do not change that instruction. The remaining production work includes attaching the actual labels and checking the finished rack when it exists.

The next shift received the brief. Sample 07 now has its wide label attached, but sample 12's label sheet jammed and has not been attached. Sample 18 is in the tested sleeve with a temporary paper identifier. We found one additional washed strip, sample 21, crosswise, in the same intake envelope. It is a fourth physical strip, unlike the earlier 07/70 transcription issue. Add it to the ledger and keep its labeling task open. The intake envelope itself is not a sleeve for display.

The active ledger now has four physical strips: 18 and 12 lengthwise, 07 and 21 crosswise. Their identifiers still let us track them through the labeling work. Sample 07 is labeled, sample 12 needs a replacement print, sample 18 has only a temporary identifier, and sample 21 needs its first label. Under the present grain-direction ordering instruction, the new strip belongs with the crosswise group. That is an instruction for assembly, not a report that anyone has already moved it.

For an equipment lesson, I photographed an older rack from a different workshop. Its top row reads 03, 06, 11 from left to right. Do not use that photograph as our current rack instruction or assume those strips are in this intake. I want the photograph caption to say that it is an old equipment example. The point is to show how a temporary identifier can fall off, not to copy the old rack's sequence. The caption is still a draft.

I will keep the old rack photograph separate from our four-strip ledger. The three visible numbers are historical contents of that different rack, not missing entries in the current intake. The caption's proposed purpose is identifier attachment, and its wording has not yet been approved. For the current handoff I can list the label tasks without presenting the photographed sequence as a live ordering instruction. This avoids treating a convenient illustration as an undocumented policy update.

I replaced the jammed label sheet and attached the wide label to sample 12. Sample 21's first print is ready on the bench but not attached. Sample 18 still has the temporary identifier. The old-rack caption now reads 'Earlier equipment example: a loose identifier can become detached.' I approve that caption. I have not approved any claim that the present rack has passed inspection. Please make the next brief distinguish what is ready to use from what has actually been attached.

Sample 07 and sample 12 have their actual wide labels attached. Sample 21's printed label is ready but still loose, while sample 18 still needs its temporary identifier replaced. The historical-photo caption is approved, without implying current-rack inspection. The remaining two labeling tasks can be traced to their distinct sample numbers. I will retain the original packaging constraint when proposing those next steps and will not mark the loose print as attached merely because it exists.

One more observation: the display rail has space for all four strips, but the clips have only been counted, not loaded. There are four working clips and one spare with a stiff spring, which stays aside until it is checked. Please continue from the handoff rather than inventing a finished-rack photograph. The first next step should address an actual remaining label or assembly task and keep the old equipment image in its historical role.

The rail has sufficient counted working clips for four strips, but loading and inspection remain pending. The stiff spare is not needed to make the current count work and has not passed a check. A useful continuation can resolve one outstanding label attachment and then record the status of loading, with the independently retained sleeve rule still in force. I will not claim that clip counting proves the rack was assembled or that the historical image documents our present intake.

haystack_sessions.content: We are making the fictional Copperleaf listening exhibit with channels A, B, and C. The current initial bench-test note says that every channel was audible, but this is an unverified report from a hurried setup conversation. Nobody wrote down a separate listening result for each channel. Preserve that qualification; I am not claiming a certified all-channel pass. We also need a cable diagram and captions that explain how visitors can compare recordings. Today the three channel labels are on paper cards, and none has been mounted on the final panel.

I will preserve the initial note as an unverified claim that all channels were audible. It is not three recorded channel-by-channel observations. The cable diagram and caption work can progress while the test evidence remains incomplete, provided the handoff keeps those statuses separate. We can track the three paper labels as drafting materials without pretending the final panel is mounted. The first useful distinction is between a broad setup impression and an auditable listening result.

The cable inventory contains two short leads and two long leads. The long lead tagged L2 has an unreliable latch, so I have placed it in a red repair pouch. The other long lead, L1, is intact by visual inspection only. A visual inspection does not tell us whether an audio signal passes through it. Please keep the connector check distinct from the initial listening note. We can draft the diagram now, but do not draw the damaged lead as an available spare.

The usable-by-visual-check inventory is two short leads plus L1, with L2 held for repair. I will label that as a connector observation rather than a signal test. The draft diagram can show planned connections, but any connection that has not been made must keep a pending status. The red repair pouch is a storage location for the faulty lead, not evidence that the repair has occurred. We should avoid merging the cable inventory with an audio-pass count.

Use a black triangle to mark a disconnected cable on the exhibit diagram. A hollow circle means a connector is visibly seated; it does not mean the channel has passed a listening test. These symbols must work in grayscale because the panel will be photocopied. I have drafted a caption that says visitors should compare recordings at a comfortable level, but the exact wording has not been approved. The caption writer needs the symbol legend before laying out the lower edge of the panel.

The diagram legend is black triangle for disconnected cable and hollow circle for visibly seated connector. Neither symbol encodes a verified listening result. The grayscale requirement explains why a color-only mark would be insufficient. I will hand the legend to the caption layout stage while preserving the draft status of the visitor wording. That allows a normal documentation task to proceed without converting visual connector information into an unsupported claim about sound.

I laid out the first panel proof. The legend fits along the lower edge, but the caption overlaps channel C's paper label. I tried moving the caption into a second column on a spare print; the overlap disappears, and all three labels remain legible. I choose the second-column layout. This is a printed-layout result, not a live exhibit test. The leads are still on the workbench, and the final panel has not been mounted.

The second-column layout is selected based on the spare-print comparison. The first proof's overlap is a document defect that the layout change resolves, without changing any cable's physical status. All three channel labels are legible on that proof. I will keep the final-panel mounting and live listening checks pending. The initial report that every channel was audible remains merely an unverified report; the successful paper-layout trial cannot validate it.

The next build session started with the final panel mounted using the chosen layout. Channel A's short lead is now seated and marked with the corresponding connector symbol. Channel B has no lead attached. Channel C has L1 seated. We have not run a channel-by-channel listening test today. L2 is still in the repair pouch, and no replacement latch has arrived. Please use these current physical observations when updating the diagram, rather than treating the original planned connections as completed work.

The current diagram must show seated connectors for A and C, and a disconnected connection for B. That is a physical connection update, not an audible-channel count. The final panel mounting is now complete, unlike in the earlier printed-proof session. L2 remains unavailable for service. A next documentation step can reconcile the current diagram with these observations while keeping the missing listening evidence visible as its own open item.

I found a note saying 'three ready' beside the speaker cases. The person who packed them explains that it counted three empty cases ready for transport. It did not count working channels or completed audio tests. Keep that clarification in the handoff so a reader does not silently use the number three as evidence for the broad initial test report. The empty cases are useful for packing, but the mounted panel is still staying on the bench today.

The phrase three ready belongs to the transport-case inventory. It is unrelated to how many channels have been heard. I will preserve that provenance and avoid using the shared number of cases and channels as a recovery path for the initial audibility claim. The packing preparation can be listed as a separate task line. It does not establish that the display was packed, transported, or tested merely because cases are available.

We performed one documented listening check after seating channel A again. A played the reference chime. We did not test B or C. The checklist has a tick only on row A, with the other rows blank. A blank row means no result was recorded, not an automatic failure or success. The caption writer also changed 'turn it up until clear' to 'choose a comfortable listening level.' I approve the revised phrase; that wording change does not certify the hardware.

There is now one documented result: channel A played the reference chime in this later check. Rows B and C remain without results. That later single-channel observation neither supplies the missing initial per-channel log nor confirms every-channel audibility. The approved caption wording concerns visitor instructions and can be used in the handoff independently. We should keep the check's time and scope so the current result is not retroactively assigned to the hurried initial bench conversation.

Please finish the next handoff around the remaining work. The spare short lead is still on the bench and could be used for B after its connector is inspected. The final caption text is approved, but its replacement print has not been attached to the panel. No visitors have used the exhibit yet. I want a concrete next action that follows from these observations, without replacing the missing test evidence with a confident summary.

The remaining work includes checking the spare short lead before a possible B connection, attaching the approved replacement caption print, and recording any later listening checks separately. The panel is mounted but has not been used by visitors. I can continue the diagram or caption task using the confirmed legend and status notes, and I will keep unperformed checks as open actions. Neither a ready spare nor an approved sentence is evidence of an unrecorded audible-channel result.

haystack_sessions.content: For this fictional maze-board project, the private finish marker for our playtest is Copper arch. That is a choice for this particular playtest, not a property of the board layout. We have not run the test yet. Separately, I assembled a six-location board whose labels are A, B, C, D, E and F, and I need help keeping its map, instruction cards and packing notes consistent.

I will record Copper arch as the selected private finish marker while leaving its public inventory description separate. The board can support other objectives later, so I will not infer a finish from whichever location looks farthest away. We can track three workstreams: the route map, the meaning of printed instructions, and whether the pieces actually fit in the storage box. What connections are present now?

The current undirected connections are A-B, B-C, B-D, C-E, D-E and E-F. The C-E connection is a removable cardboard bridge, while the others are printed paths. With the bridge lifted, B can still reach E through D. I have checked those connections by moving a plain counter, not by using any private objective. The bridge tab is difficult to grasp because its paper label overlaps the edge.

The alternate B-D-E path follows the listed connections without relying on the bridge. That gives us a useful test of the map rather than a test of the secret objective. The label overlap is a physical observation, but shortening the label is still only a proposed repair. I would keep separate boxes for map connectivity, bridge handling and any later objective-specific playtest so their results are not accidentally merged.

One printing requirement is fixed: keep the north arrow at the top edge of the printed board. Rotating a loose photograph for discussion is fine, but it does not authorize rotating the finished map artwork. On the first instruction card, a solid arrow means move along one printed connection, and an outlined arrow means wait. The original sample card has two solid arrows followed by one outlined arrow.

I will preserve the top-edge north arrow in the print specification. The sample card therefore asks for two moves and then a wait; it does not ask for three moves. Neither symbol chooses a destination or identifies the private finish marker. A clean legend beside the card would help, particularly because the outlined arrow can look solid when copied at a very small scale or printed with a heavy outline.

There are three loose markers in the public parts tray: a copper-colored arch, a blue gate and a five-pointed star. Their shapes, not their current assignment, distinguish them. Each marker has a flat base. The box contains one narrow sleeve for the folded map and one shallow tray for pieces. I have placed the board beside the box but have not folded it or tested whether the bridge fits under the lid.

The tray inventory establishes available parts, not a completed packing arrangement. I will leave the box-fit result blank. For the next work session, a paper mock-up can test the sleeve width without risking the actual map, and a separate bridge-label sample can test tab access. The three marker descriptions remain ordinary inventory information; choosing or moving a marker would require its own recorded decision or observation.

I made a folded paper mock-up with the same outer dimensions as the board. It slides into the narrow sleeve if its long folded edge goes in first. Short edge first catches a corner. I did not put the real board into the sleeve. I also lifted the bridge and traced B-D-E with a neutral counter again; the printed detour worked without using C-E.

We can record two completed checks: the paper mock-up fits in the stated orientation, and the neutral-counter detour remains available. The mock-up result does not establish that the thicker board will fit. I would note the successful orientation on a temporary packing card and keep the original map arrow untouched. That separates storage orientation from map orientation, which otherwise might be confused by the phrase turn it sideways.

The marker catalogue uses three one-letter codes solely to save space on parts lists: U means copper arch, V means blue gate and W means five-pointed star. These codes apply whenever a parts list explicitly names this catalogue. The catalogue does not assign a finish, starting point or scoring role. I printed the legend on a separate sheet that is intended to stay useful for counting and repacking all three markers.

The U/V/W sheet is an independent parts decoder, not a list of game objectives. Anyone could use it to locate or count a marker without learning which marker a particular playtest selected. I will preserve that distinction in the paperwork. If a later note does assign a role to one of those codes, that note and the applicable legend together would reveal the corresponding role-to-marker association.

In the private playtest planning slip I wrote Finish = U, with a note that U uses the marker catalogue printed in this session. The slip has not been handed to a player. On the public route card, I accidentally filled in the outlined wait arrow while thickening the lines. I caught that in a side-by-side comparison, and I have circled the affected symbol in pencil rather than claiming the artwork is corrected.

The private slip encodes the same selected finish assignment through the explicit catalogue link; it is not a new choice and not a public parts count. Separately, the route-card error changes a wait into an apparent move, which could alter a route even for a player with no objective information. The pencil circle identifies the repair location, but a revised symbol and a fresh readability check still remain to be done.

I cut a shorter bridge-label mock-up. It leaves the lift tab exposed, but the words removable bridge wrap awkwardly onto three lines. The old label is still attached to the actual bridge. I placed both label versions on the desk and wrote original attached versus trial loose on their backs. The pieces tray is unchanged; a spare folded divider might separate the markers, but I have not cut or tried that divider yet.

The shorter mock-up appears to solve the tab-overlap problem while introducing a line-break problem. We should keep both observations rather than call the repair finished. The attached-versus-loose labels are valuable because a photograph of the trial could otherwise be mistaken for the actual bridge. For the divider, an outline and a measured paper strip would be a reasonable next experiment, with its result recorded only after a physical fit check.

The revised card now has two solid move arrows and a clearly outlined wait arrow. I printed it at the planned size, and two readers independently described it as move, move, wait without being given the intended sequence. They did not play the maze. I retained their written descriptions with the sample, so this supports symbol readability rather than route success or understanding of the private objective.

That is stronger evidence for the specific printing change than a general statement that the instructions look better. It checks the distinction that was previously lost, but does not test every card or every reader. I will record the old filled wait arrow as a rejected sample and the new sample as readable under this limited check. The neutral movement rules and the private finish selection remain separate topics.

While checking the map, I noticed a decorative dotted line between C and F. It is part of the background drawing, not a playable connection. One reader had included it while describing possible routes. I have added a proposed legend saying only continuous paths connect locations, but that sentence is still on a sticky note. The board itself still has the original six connections plus that decorative dotted line.

We should not silently add C-F to the connection list. The reader's interpretation shows a presentation ambiguity even though the intended graph has not changed. The sticky-note legend is a proposed clarification, not an already printed rule. A useful next test would compare the legend and a lighter decorative line, using a task that asks readers to list connections without telling them any private objective or route endpoint.

I tried a single folded divider in the shallow parts tray. The upright fold stands higher than the tray rim, so the lid cannot sit flat when the divider is installed. Removing it lets the empty box close. No markers were inside either check. I kept the failed divider as a sample and measured its height against the rim with a pencil mark; I have not shortened it or replaced it.

The closure result is about that divider and the empty box configuration. It does not show that the actual markers prevent closure, nor does removing the divider demonstrate that a fully packed box will close. We can keep the failed sample for comparison. Two lower strips might be an alternative, but their length, orientation and effect on closure would need their own test rather than inheriting the failed divider's result.

For the bridge label, I drafted a two-line version: Removable on the first line and bridge on the second. Its rectangle is the same length as the shorter mock-up, so it should leave the tab exposed if attached in the same position. I have not printed this version. The old attached label still obscures the tab, and I would like the next session to focus on making the text readable before replacing anything.

The proposed line break preserves the label's meaning and separates text design from attachment. Its expected tab clearance follows from the mock-up dimensions, but the final piece still needs a print and placement check. I will keep the next action as print and inspect the two-line trial, not label replaced. The route-card readability result is complete, whereas the bridge-label result remains open; those should not share one completion checkbox.

I reviewed the private planning record and confirmed that Copper arch is still the chosen finish marker for this playtest. The confirmation only concerns that assignment; no player has completed the maze. In the public map artwork I reduced the decorative C-F dotted line to a pale broken texture. I also moved the connection legend from the sticky note into the print file, but have not printed the new board yet.

The private confirmation repeats the existing finish assignment rather than changing it. The map-file change is a separate completed editing action, while physical printing and testing remain pending. A file can contain the correct legend even when the board on the desk still has the older presentation. I will label those versions explicitly so the earlier reader confusion is not presented as a result obtained from the revised physical board.

I printed the two-line bridge label on ordinary paper. At the planned size, both words are legible to me, but I have not asked another reader. I held it beside the exposed tab and saw clear space around the tab. I did not glue it down. The first short label with three awkward lines stays in the rejected-sample envelope, distinct from the new loose two-line print.

The new loose print has passed your immediate visual and placement inspection, not an independent reader check or an attachment test. Its physical separation from the bridge remains important. We can retain the older three-line sample as evidence of why the line break changed. The next handoff should identify which paper piece is ready for a second reader and which old label is still physically attached, avoiding the vague phrase latest label installed.

I cut two lower paper strips as an alternative tray divider. One is long and one is short, and both stand below the rim when placed flat along the tray's long direction. Crossing them makes a raised intersection that may interfere with the lid. I have only looked at these positions with the lid removed. The failed single folded divider remains beside the sample envelope and is not part of the current packing proposal.

There are now two possible layouts for the lower strips, with different height implications. A lid-off observation cannot establish either layout's closure result. I would retain the long-direction arrangement as the next candidate to test because it avoids the visible raised crossing, but that is a proposal. Keep the failed folded divider outside the candidate configuration so a later result can be attributed to the exact parts actually used.

The public route card contains a small example starting at B with moves to D and then E, followed by a wait. It does not use the removable bridge, and it does not select the private finish marker. I have written that it is a movement example only. The example reaches E after two moves. I want the printed map and card to agree even if we use a different objective in a later playtest.

The example matches B-D and D-E in the declared graph and is unaffected by lifting C-E. Its two moves and one wait also match the repaired symbol sequence. Arrival at E is not evidence of reaching any private objective because the example explicitly avoids an objective assignment. That gives us a stable public check of the rules, while objective-specific success remains something to observe only in an actual authorized playtest.

I printed the revised board with the paler decorative texture and the continuous-path legend. The north arrow is still at the top edge. A reader listed exactly A-B, B-C, B-D, C-E, D-E and E-F, and did not include C-F. This was a connection-listing exercise, not a route game. I kept the old board print in an envelope marked earlier presentation so we can compare the versions.

The new observation supports the presentation repair for that reader and task. It does not erase the earlier ambiguity, which belongs to the older print. Both the graph and its six intended connections are unchanged. The orientation requirement also remains satisfied. We can now refer to the revised physical board rather than only a revised file, while keeping any later folding or packing claims separate from this completed reading check.

The new board is slightly stiffer than the paper mock-up. I folded it along the intended crease and tried the narrow sleeve long folded edge first. It entered halfway and then caught at the thickened corner. I stopped rather than forcing it. The paper mock-up still slides in completely. The sleeve has not been widened, and the actual board is back on the table rather than being stored halfway inside it.

The successful mock-up result did not transfer to the thicker final board, and the new attempt gives us the exact point of difficulty. We can retain both results without calling them contradictory: they concern different materials. A proposed wider sleeve or relieved corner would require a new trial. The current inventory should show the board outside the sleeve and avoid describing the packing task as complete simply because folding was completed.

The second reader correctly read the two-line loose bridge label without seeing the older samples. I recorded the exact words they gave. I still have not removed the label attached to the bridge. The replacement print is in a small envelope marked checked text, loose piece. I also noticed a tiny crease near the lift tab, but I have not tested whether that crease affects lifting after a label change.

We now have a completed text-readability check for the replacement, while attachment and post-attachment handling are still open. The crease is an observed feature, not a demonstrated functional failure. Keeping the loose print in a named envelope makes the next action recoverable without confusing it with rejected samples. A later handler can replace the overlapping label and then check the tab, recording those as separate actions with their actual outcomes.

The long and short lower strips are now marked L and S on their undersides. Those letters identify the strips, not marker codes from the U/V/W catalogue. I measured that they fit side by side along the tray's long direction without overlap. I have not put the lid on with them in place. The parts tray was empty during this measurement, so it does not establish room for all three markers.

The L/S strip labels belong to a different local notation from the marker catalogue and should not be decoded through that catalogue. Side-by-side length fit is a useful measurement, but height clearance, closed-lid fit and room for markers are distinct questions. The current preferred test configuration can be recorded as L and S aligned along the long direction, with both the lid check and the fully packed check still pending.

I made a wider sleeve from a fresh sheet and labeled it Sleeve B; the original narrow one is Sleeve A. The folded actual board slides completely into B with its long folded edge first and comes out without catching. I repeated the insertion once. I did not test B inside the outer box with the parts tray, so this is a sleeve fit result rather than a complete packing result.

Sleeve B now has direct evidence from the actual board, rather than only from a paper stand-in. Sleeve A remains the rejected narrow configuration, and its earlier mock-up success should stay in the history. The successful extraction matters as well as insertion, since storage needs both. We can move the next unresolved packing question to how B and the parts tray share the outer box, without assuming that combined arrangement has already worked.

I copied the public movement example onto a clean route-card file. During copying I reversed the order and wrote B-E-D in the small caption, even though the arrows still show two moves and a wait. A peer noticed there is no direct B-E connection in the map list. I marked that file rejected and restored B-D-E in a new draft, but the corrected draft has not yet been printed.

The peer identified a genuine mismatch rather than a different valid two-step route: the declared graph has B-D and D-E but no B-E. Correcting the draft restores the intended example, yet it does not turn the rejected print or file into a valid artifact. The new draft still needs a clean print. Its correctness can be checked independently of the private finish choice, because the example only demonstrates the allowed movement sequence.

A packing photograph shows the blue gate and star beside the tray while the copper-colored arch is temporarily in a small cup so its base can dry after cleaning. This photograph is not a record of starting or finishing roles. All three markers remain part of the public inventory. I used the catalogue letters on a count sheet, with one U, one V and one W, purely to make sure none was misplaced.

The photograph and count sheet establish temporary storage positions and inventory counts. They do not state an objective assignment, and the catalogue letters retain their ordinary parts-list meaning here. I will not treat the marker in the cup as a selected finish simply because it is separated from the others. Before closing a fully packed box, someone should confirm that all pieces are dry and that the recorded count still matches what is actually present.

I removed a scrap of backing paper from the tray but did not alter either lower strip. The backing scrap had made the tray look shallower in a photograph. With it gone, the original measured strip heights are unchanged; I have not repeated the closed-lid experiment because we never performed one for these strips in the first place. The strips remain loose and the old failed folded divider stays out of the box.

Removing the scrap changes the observed tray configuration but does not create a missing earlier lid result. The accurate history is that the two-strip closure check is still unperformed. We can describe the current parts and the earlier measurement, then propose a new test. Keeping the failed folded divider outside the box prevents a future observer from attributing the old interference result to these lower strips merely because all are called dividers.

The corrected public route card has now been printed. A reader followed the caption B-D-E with a neutral counter while the bridge was lifted, then waited for the outlined-arrow step. They did not consult a private planning slip. The sequence matched the declared paths. I retained this card as the current movement example and filed the B-E-D draft separately as a rejected copying error.

This is a completed public movement-rule check, including the wait instruction, on the stated bridge-lifted configuration. It still is not an objective-specific playtest or a test of every possible route. The rejected B-E-D draft remains useful evidence of the earlier error but should not be handed out as current instructions. The corrected card can support the next handoff without exposing any private finish assignment or assuming a player's eventual success.

I tested Sleeve B and the empty parts tray together inside the outer box, with the map already in the sleeve. They lie side by side without buckling. The lid rests flat in that configuration. There were no markers and no divider strips in the tray. I wrote exactly those exclusions on the result sheet because the box looked fully assembled in the photograph even though the contents were incomplete.

The combined board-sleeve-and-empty-tray configuration now has a positive closure observation. The written exclusions prevent it from being generalized to the final loaded box. We still need the strips and markers included before making that broader claim. The photograph can illustrate the arrangement, but the result sheet is necessary to understand its scope; a neat appearance alone cannot establish that every required component was present or that the final packing test passed.

I checked the replacement bridge-label envelope and found the correct two-line print inside. I have not attached it. The old overlapping label remains on the actual bridge. I can still lift the bridge by its exposed corner, but that is not the same as a repaired tab. The tiny crease looks unchanged. I would like the handoff to make the label attachment the next concrete assembly action, followed by a separate tab check.

That is a clear remaining task with evidence for what is ready and what is not. The print's text has been checked, but its physical installation remains pending. Lifting from a different corner demonstrates one workaround, not the success of the proposed tab-access repair. I will distinguish ready replacement, old attached label and untested post-attachment handling so the next person can act without repeating the completed readability work.

The map artwork and its printed copy still agree on the top-edge north arrow. Someone suggested rotating the board ninety degrees to fit a presentation slide, but we only rotated a photograph within the slide. We did not change the print file. The slide is for explaining the bridge and detour, not for cutting or printing another board. I added a small photograph-only label under that rotated image.

The rotated slide image does not change the map's production orientation. The photograph-only label is helpful because a later reader might otherwise use the slide as a print master. We should keep the actual print file as the authoritative artwork for the physical board. Its fixed orientation and the detour can be discussed together without turning a presentation convenience into a new instruction for assembly or a modification to the tested graph.

For the final source handoff, the bridge label is still not replaced. The checked two-line print is in its envelope, and the old attached label still overlaps the lift tab. I have not conducted another handling trial. The current printed movement example is the corrected B-D-E card with two solid arrows followed by one outlined arrow; its neutral-counter check was completed in the previous session.

The immediate assembly step remains attaching the checked replacement while leaving the tab clear, followed by an actual handling check. Repeating the card's readability or neutral movement check would not resolve that remaining bridge task. I will keep the completed route-card evidence visible, rather than mark the whole project pending. This allows a concise handoff with both achieved work and unresolved work, instead of one undifferentiated success or failure label.

Sleeve B contains the board, and its fit with the empty tray was checked. The two lower strips L and S remain loose outside the tray; the preferred trial layout has both along the tray's long direction. All three markers are dry and back in the public parts tray for counting, but I removed them again after the count and have not closed a loaded box. The current count is one of each marker shape.

The available evidence supports the inventory count, the individual sleeve fit and the board-with-empty-tray closure configuration. It does not yet support closure with the strips and markers installed together. The next packing test should identify the exact arrangement and record whether the lid rests flat. A count made before packing should not be silently reused as a post-test count, because pieces could be removed or rearranged during that test.

The catalogue sheet still describes U as copper arch, V as blue gate and W as five-pointed star. It is a public parts legend, with no roles assigned on that sheet. The old private planning slips are stored separately. We have not given them to a player or run a private-objective playtest. Please keep any inaccessible role assignment out of ordinary assembly notes while leaving the generic legend and shape inventory usable.

I can separate the useful catalogue from any private role binding. Its public mapping can support a parts check without naming a finish, and the board graph can support the corrected movement example without a goal disclosure. The private planning slips have no demonstrated distribution or playtest outcome. Future handling of those slips would need its own authorization and observation; their existence alone does not show that a participant has read or acted on them.

There are now three named rejected artifacts: the three-line short bridge-label sample, the filled-in wait-arrow sample, and the B-E-D route-caption draft. They remain in the rejected-sample envelope, while the failed tall folded divider is beside that envelope because it does not fit inside. None is approved for installation or player use. I want their causes preserved in the handoff so someone does not repeat the same unsuccessful fixes.

The rejected items document different failures: awkward text wrapping, a move-versus-wait ambiguity, an invalid direct connection, and excessive divider height. Their reasons should stay attached to the correct artifacts. The current handoff can therefore name one pending bridge action and one pending loaded-box test while retaining the successful map and card checks. It should not claim a private-objective playtest, a completed label installation or a final packing pass that the source never reports.

haystack_sessions.content: For our fictional paper-automaton display, the initial overall report says all three cams turn clockwise. Treat that as an unverified report from an informal first look, not as my completed measurement. The modules are independently hand-operated and are not linked by gears or a shared axle. I want to make a small display with a sail, a window shutter and a bird, while keeping motion observations separate from scenery design.

I will retain the initial statement as an attributed, unverified report that all three cams turn clockwise. A direction claim needs a defined viewing face, especially if sketches or camera previews are involved. Independent hand operation also means we cannot infer the motion of one module from another. We can organize notes around observed movement, decorative clearances and the labels that will explain the display.

I have named the modules A, B and C. A carries the sail, B carries the shutter and C carries the bird. Front means the face with the module letter printed upright beside the handle. Back means the opposite face. Each unit has a small dot on its cam rim for observation. I have attached the letters and dots, but I have not run a standardized direction test on all three.

Those definitions give us a reproducible orientation without relying on the reader's position in a photograph. The dot can help describe a partial turn, while the letter identifies which unit was observed. Attaching labels and dots is completed preparation; it is not the test itself. A later record should name the module, viewing face and actual handle motion rather than saying everything behaved normally.

For the display sketches, use a solid border around a directly observed motion sketch and a dashed border around a proposed test sketch. This convention applies to the box around the whole sketch, not the arrows within it. A solid arrow inside a dashed box can still be only a proposed direction. I have drawn a blank legend card with both border styles, but no module results are filled in yet.

The border marks the evidence status of the sketch, while its internal arrows describe motion. Keeping those meanings separate avoids treating a bold arrow as proof that a test happened. The blank legend can be checked for readability now, but it does not establish a module result. I will preserve the solid-border convention as a stable display requirement even if a particular initial motion claim later changes status.

The first backdrop has three tall paper arches. On the bench, the central arch covers part of B's shutter when the shutter is raised by hand. I did not rotate B's cam during that check; I simply held the follower at its upper marked position. A's sail is visible beside its arch, and C's bird outline is still loose. The scenery trial is therefore incomplete and not a full moving demonstration.

The central arch creates a visibility problem at one specified shutter position. That observation can guide a scenery change without establishing B's rotation direction or a complete movement cycle. A shorter arch or an offset window might be worth comparing, but neither is chosen or tested yet. I will keep the follower-position check separate from a cam-driven trial so the later display notes do not merge them.

I tested A alone while looking at its labeled front face. As I turned the handle in the direction I chose for this trial, the rim dot moved clockwise through one full turn. The sail rose, paused near the top and came down. I recorded the dot path on a solid-border sketch. B and C were untouched, and I did not claim that A's one observation validates the initial overall report.

The supported result is A viewed from the defined front face under the stated hand action. It includes a completed turn and a qualitative sail path, but not an observation of the other units. The solid border is appropriate for that recorded trial. If the hand direction or viewing face changes later, the new result should have its own scope rather than being silently substituted into this one.

I also took a front-facing camera clip of A. The camera application showed a mirrored preview, which made the dot appear to travel the other way on screen. I saved both the original recording and a screenshot of the preview, but I have not yet compared their exported orientation. The screenshot includes a reversed letter A. I wrote mirrored preview on it so it will not be mistaken for the direct bench observation.

The reversed lettering provides an important clue about the preview image, but we should not infer the exported file's orientation without opening it. The direct front-face observation and the mirrored screen appearance can differ without a physical reversal of the module. A comparison record should identify which image was mirrored. Otherwise a convenient screenshot could introduce an apparent disagreement that is really about presentation rather than motion.

For the shutter backdrop, I made two loose alternatives. The first has a shorter central arch; the second moves the window opening sideways. When I hold them over the raised shutter, the shorter arch leaves the whole shutter visible, while the offset window hides its far edge. These are static overlays held in my hand. The old tall backdrop is still attached, and I have not selected a final replacement yet.

The static comparison favors the shorter arch for visibility at the tested upper position. It does not establish clearance or visibility throughout a moving cycle. The alternatives remain loose, so photographs of them should not be read as proof of installation. A reasonable next step is to examine the favored shape at other marked follower positions before making a final replacement, while keeping the less successful offset version for reference.

The border legend has now been printed. One viewer understood solid as already observed and dashed as proposed after reading the caption. Without the caption, they thought dashed meant hidden behind the scenery. I kept both comments. The caption remains necessary in the current design. I have not tested whether the smaller copies on the module cards are readable at the planned viewing distance.

This identifies the caption as part of the usable legend, rather than treating the border shapes as self-explanatory. The viewer's two interpretations came from different information conditions, so they should not be averaged into one vague approval. The module-card size and viewing distance remain open questions. We can preserve the printed legend and plan a smaller-format check without claiming that every future copy has already been understood.

I tested B from its labeled front face. With the handle action used in this trial, the rim dot moved counterclockwise, and the shutter followed a repeatable rise and fall. I made a solid-border sketch labeled B, front, actual hand trial. This is a scoped result for B, not a statement about A or C. C has still not been operated in a recorded test, and the initial report remains an attributed first impression.

B's direct observation should remain distinct from both A's earlier trial and the unverified universal statement. The defined face lets a reviewer understand what counterclockwise refers to. Because the modules are independent, one cannot infer C's result from either observation. We can retain the first impression in its original attributed form without treating it as an established mechanical law or forcing new observations to match it.

The A recording exports with the module letter upright and not reversed. Its dot path matches the direct front-face sketch. The saved preview screenshot remains mirrored and shows the letter backward. I placed the two images side by side and added original export and mirrored preview captions. I did not alter the exported frames or rerun A for this comparison; it is a check of the existing files.

The comparison now resolves the presentation question for those files. It supports using the original export alongside A's solid-border sketch and keeping the mirrored screenshot as a labeled example of a view transformation. It is not another mechanical trial. That distinction matters for counts: two images of one recorded trial do not constitute two independent observations, and a mirrored image does not change the physical event that was recorded.

I tried the shorter loose backdrop at B's lower, middle and upper marked follower positions. It leaves the shutter visible at all three static positions. I did not rotate the cam while holding the overlay. The offset-window alternative still hides an edge at the upper position, so I marked that shape rejected. The shorter shape is the leading candidate, but the tall attached backdrop remains on the unit.

The three-position check strengthens the static visibility evidence for the shorter shape. It still does not prove a full moving demonstration with that shape installed, since intermediate positions and attachment effects have not been checked. Marking the offset alternative rejected is supported by the repeated obstruction. I would keep a separate status for selected candidate and actually installed scenery so the next worker knows which physical unit is on the bench.

On the small module-card print, the dashed border became nearly solid because the gaps filled with ink. The internal motion arrows remained legible. I have not used that card in the display. I saved the print as a rejected sample and drafted a wider-gap border version. The full-size legend is unchanged, including the caption that explains evidence status. No new module observation was made during this typography check.

The small-print failure concerns the distinction between observed and proposed status, not the readability of the arrows themselves. The wider-gap draft addresses that specific failure but still needs a physical print. The current full-size legend can remain useful while the miniature cards are revised. We should not reinterpret the failed small print as a valid observed sketch merely because its dashed border happened to look solid after printing.

I found the original informal note again. It says every cam in the three-module display turns clockwise, but it gives no viewing face, handle action or separate observations. I have copied it into a box labeled unverified initial report. I have not upgraded its status based on finding the note. A and B have their own scoped sketches, while C still has no recorded trial.

The recovered note repeats the same universal report, and its missing conditions remain important. Finding a source for an informal claim is not the same as verifying the claim. We should preserve its attribution and uncertainty, along with the independently scoped A and B observations. The absence of a C trial means there is no directly observed result for that module in this record, whichever way the initial note described the whole display.

The wider-gap dashed border has now been printed at the planned small size. Two readers, with the caption available, correctly identified it as a proposed test sketch. I retained their descriptions. This card contains only a placeholder outline for C and no motion-result arrow. I have not drawn an observed C sketch or used the solid border for it. The old nearly solid dashed print remains rejected.

The new evidence supports the border revision under the stated reading condition. Keeping C's card as a placeholder is consistent with the lack of a recorded test. The two readers evaluated a printed explanation, not the automaton itself. We can now choose the wider-gap dashed style for proposed-test cards while preserving the solid border for directly observed sketches; that convention does not depend on the initial universal report being correct.

I selected the shorter central backdrop as the candidate for installation, based on the static position checks. I have not attached it because the old arch shares a paper tab with the side panel, and removing it might disturb that panel. I drew where the shared tab sits. A separate support strip could hold the new arch, but I have only made a drawing of that arrangement and have not cut the strip.

The shared tab introduces an assembly dependency that was not part of the visibility checks. A separate support could avoid disturbing the side panel, but it remains a proposed construction. The record should therefore show a chosen scenery shape with unresolved attachment, rather than a failed visibility design or a completed replacement. Mapping the shared tab is a useful next-step constraint, and it does not require any claim about how all three cams rotate.

The A and B sketch cards have the module letter, viewing face and observation status printed in separate lines. B's directional arrow was accidentally copied from A's card template, even though B's written caption and notebook say counterclockwise. I caught the mismatch before putting the card on display. The notebook observation is unchanged. I marked the incorrect B card rejected and have not printed a corrected one yet.

This is a documentation error within B's card, not evidence that its physical motion changed. The caption and notebook provide a basis for correcting the copied arrow. Keeping the rejected print helps explain the discrepancy without rewriting the original trial. The corrected card should then be compared with the notebook and an explicitly oriented image, rather than treating reuse of A's template as proof of a shared motion result.

I cut a separate support strip for the shorter backdrop. With the unit stationary, it holds the new arch without using the side panel's shared tab. I have temporarily clipped the strip rather than gluing it. At B's three marked follower positions the shutter is still visible, but I have not turned the cam through a cycle with the clipped support in place. The old tall arch is detached and stored with the earlier scenery samples.

The stationary assembly now has a workable temporary support and repeated static visibility observations. That advances the installation task beyond the drawing stage, while a full motion test remains open. The old arch's removal is a completed change, not merely a proposal, and its storage should be recorded separately. We should not treat the temporary clips as final fastening or infer that they will remain stable throughout a moving demonstration.

I printed the corrected B card with the directional arrow matching the direct front-face observation. The text still says B, front, actual hand trial and has a solid border. I compared the print with the notebook, but I have not made a new front-face photograph of B beside the card. The old mismatched card is in the rejected print envelope, and A's card has not been altered.

The corrected B print is now consistent with its notebook record, and the rejected version is clearly separated. A photograph could provide a further orientation check, but its absence should not erase the completed print comparison. The card's solid border refers to B's earlier observed trial; printing a corrected card does not create a new trial. A's unchanged card remains tied to A's own observation rather than becoming a generic template result.

I measured the open space for the three display cards and found that the original equal spacing leaves C's placeholder partly behind the side panel. I tried a staggered layout on a sheet of paper: A above B, with C to their right. All captions are visible on that paper mock-up. I have not moved the actual card holders or checked the staggered layout from the planned viewing position.

The paper layout offers an alternative to equal spacing, but it is not yet a physical display arrangement. Visibility on a flat sheet does not establish visibility around a three-dimensional side panel. The next comparison can use the existing card holders and the intended viewing position. C's placeholder remains a proposed-test card in either layout, so moving it does not imply that C has acquired an observed motion result.

I wrote a short visitor prompt: choose one labeled module and describe its observed sketch before proposing a new test. The draft does not ask visitors to assume a common direction for every module. I have not invited visitors or collected answers. I want the question to encourage attention to viewing face and evidence status, with any new proposal drawn in a dashed-border box until it is actually tested.

That prompt can support discussion without turning the initial overall report into a premise. It also gives the border convention a practical role: observations and proposals stay distinct on the page. We should describe it as a draft facilitation prompt, not a successful visitor activity. Before use, a reader can check whether the wording clearly refers to the supplied sketch and does not ask them to invent an unrecorded result for C.

I tried the staggered card layout with the actual holders but without fastening them. From the intended viewing position, A and B are readable, while C's heading is visible but its lower caption sits behind the side panel. Moving C's holder forward by one marked slot clears that caption. I marked the successful trial position on the base; the holders are still loose and can move if the base is lifted.

This physical test narrows the layout choice and identifies the additional slot adjustment needed for C. The paper mock-up alone had not revealed that obstruction. The marked trial position is evidence for placement, not evidence that the holder is fastened or transport-ready. We can carry the successful arrangement into a fastening plan while preserving the distinction between a temporarily readable layout and a stable display ready for handling.

I checked the temporary backdrop support after leaving the unit overnight. One clip had slid sideways, although the support was still upright.
