I restored the clip to the marked position and photographed it. I did not run a motion test. The shorter arch remains installed on the temporary strip, and the old tall arch stays in the scenery sample folder. The clip movement is the only new observed assembly change.

The sideways clip movement is a real stability observation, but it does not show that a cam cycle caused it because no cycle was run. Restoring the clip also does not establish a lasting solution. A revised fastening method or a monitored stationary interval could be proposed, with its result left open until performed. The static shutter-visibility checks still stand for their recorded configurations; they should not be rewritten as failed motion trials.

The exported A video and mirrored preview screenshot are now stored in different named folders. A small contact sheet labels one original export and the other mirrored preview. I checked the filenames against the existing comparison note. No files were overwritten. I have not created a similar comparison image for B, and C still has no recorded motion video or direct trial in the source log.

The folder separation improves traceability of the A images without adding a new observation. The contact sheet can help prevent the mirrored view from being mistaken for an opposite physical event. B's missing oriented photograph and C's unobserved status remain separate gaps. We should not fill those gaps by borrowing A's footage or by generalizing its result to the display as a whole, even if the layouts use matching visual styles.

A reader reviewed the visitor prompt and understood that they should describe a supplied observed sketch before drawing a proposed test. They suggested adding the words from the labeled viewing face to the first sentence. I accepted that wording and revised the file, but have not printed it. The reader did not operate any module, and their comment is feedback on the prompt rather than a new motion observation.

The accepted wording makes the orientation constraint explicit. Its status is a revised file with reader feedback, not a printed visitor sheet or a completed public activity. The planned test box should retain a dashed border in the eventual print. We can add that print step to the handoff while avoiding any claim that a visitor has already supplied data or that the review established a common direction across modules.

I printed the revised visitor sheet with from the labeled viewing face in the first sentence. Its proposed-test box has the wider-gap dashed border and the caption from the tested legend. I checked the print against the revised file. No visitor session has taken place. A spare sheet is ready for a colleague to review the physical layout, especially whether the instruction text points clearly to the correct sketch boxes.

The sheet has advanced from file revision to a checked physical print, while visitor use and any resulting data remain future possibilities. Reusing the previously tested dashed-border style is reasonable, but the new overall page layout may still need its own reading check. The colleague's proposed review would concern that layout. It should not be described as a module test or as confirmation of any universal mechanical report.

For the display-card holders I added removable locating tabs at the successful staggered positions, including C's forward slot. The holders settle into those positions when placed gently. I have not lifted or carried the base with them installed. C's card is still a dashed-border placeholder with no motion result. The same printed heading can be present before an observation exists, so its visible label is not evidence that C has been tested.

The locating tabs provide a repeatable placement aid and preserve the visibility arrangement established earlier. They do not yet demonstrate transport stability. C's heading and placeholder remain legitimate display components without implying a completed trial. The next handoff can list a physical layout check as achieved and a handling check as pending, while keeping the evidence-status convention independent of whether every unit has an observation.

I replaced the slipped clip on the backdrop strip with a wider temporary clip. During a stationary check lasting the same interval as my previous notebook entry, it stayed on its mark. I have not run the cam with this clip. The revised shorter arch remains visible at the three manually set follower positions. I did not change the cam, handle or notebook observations, and I kept the old clip with the assembly samples.

The wider clip has a positive stationary result under the stated comparison, while its behavior during movement is still unobserved. The three-position visibility observations also remain static. We can preserve the useful improvement without saying the moving demonstration is finished. Since no cam or observation record changed, the fastening experiment should not be reported as a new direction test or as a reason to revise A's or B's earlier scoped motion descriptions.

The corrected B arrow card is ready for the front-face photograph, but I have not taken that photograph yet. I made a checklist naming the upright module letter, the front label and the full card border as things that must be visible together. The checklist refers to the earlier hand trial, not a request to infer an unseen direction from the camera preview. I left the photograph-result box blank.

That checklist addresses the specific orientation and documentation risks previously seen in A's mirrored preview and B's copied arrow. Its usefulness does not mean the photograph has been taken. The next person should capture the defined view, then compare it with the existing notebook and corrected card. Any mismatch should be recorded rather than silently replacing an old observation or treating the initial overall report as the deciding authority.

At this final source handoff, the corrected B card still has no new front-face photograph beside it. The preparation checklist is ready, and the result box is blank. A's direct trial, original export and mirrored preview are separately labeled. C remains unobserved in the log. I have not conducted a three-module standardized test, so the collection of cards must not be presented as a verified overall direction result.

The remaining documentation task is concrete: make the explicitly oriented B photograph and compare the existing records. A's completed file comparison should not be repeated as though it resolves B's missing view. C's absence of data should remain visible. We can describe the available scoped observations and their presentation status without asserting an overall result, and without turning a blank checklist box into either a success or a failure.

The shorter backdrop is on the temporary support with the wider clip. Its stationary interval check and three static follower-position checks are recorded, but it has not been observed through a cam-driven cycle. I want the next assembly decision to depend on that moving check rather than on appearance in a still photograph. The old tall arch and the slipped narrow clip remain labeled samples, not the current configuration.

The source supports a useful but limited current configuration: improved static visibility and a better stationary clip result. A cycle test with that exact configuration is still a meaningful next action. The labeled old samples explain why the choices changed without being mistaken for installed parts. This task can proceed from public assembly evidence and does not require accepting the initial universal direction report as true.

The staggered card holders now sit on their locating tabs, and the final visitor sheet is printed. We have not performed a carry test or run a visitor activity. The proposed-test boxes retain dashed borders with captions; directly observed sketches retain solid borders. I would like a clean display note to list what is observed, what is merely prepared and what still needs a test, without collapsing these into one ready checkbox.

A status note can name the completed printing and positioning work while leaving handling and visitor use open. It should also keep each motion observation tied to its own module and viewing face. The solid-border rule identifies directly observed sketches; it is not an endorsement of every statement printed nearby. Maintaining this distinction protects the useful display work even when a broader initial claim becomes unavailable as a current basis.

The final folder contains a rejected small dashed-border print, the incorrect B arrow card, the offset-window backdrop trial and the old tall arch. Their labels name different reasons: filled gaps, copied wrong arrow, hidden shutter edge and excessive scenery height. I did not delete these artifacts. I want any future handoff to distinguish a documentation mistake from a physical observation, because both appear in the same folder but answer different questions.

Those rejection reasons preserve the project's causal history. A bad card arrow can be corrected without changing a bench observation, and an obstructing backdrop can be revised without establishing a universal rotation rule. The current handoff should propose the missing oriented photograph or moving clearance check, preserve the border convention and acknowledge unobserved C. No successful visitor session, completed carry test or three-module mechanical validation should be invented from this material.

creation_note: Original fictional evaluation script; all people, institutions, dates and dialogue are authored. No real participant log or public provenance is claimed.

haystack_sessions.content: In this fictional miniature sky-show project, the current plan starts narration at the end of the chime. That is the trigger rule for the new show, not a claim that we have performed it. The opening sequence also includes a light fade, but the two events are separately observable. I am building a tabletop projection mask, revising a short narration and comparing what can be seen from two marked audience positions.

I will record the end of the chime as the current narration trigger and keep the light fade as a separate event. A plan identifies when narration should begin; an actual rehearsal can tell us when it did begin. Those should have different fields. We can also track mask changes and viewing checks independently, so a successful projection test is not automatically reported as a successful performance of the whole show.

The opening chime and the fade are started together by one manual cue. In a component check, the chime ended three seconds after that cue, while the fade ended five seconds after it. I measured them separately from the same time origin. No narration was read during this check. The figures describe this saved component setting, which I have named Opening A, rather than a guaranteed duration for every later version.

With Opening A, the two measured event endings are distinct: three seconds and five seconds after the common start. If the current narration rule were applied to that setting, the planned start would follow the chime ending, but that would be a prediction for a future combined run. The component check itself contains no observed narration start. Naming the setting will help preserve these measurements if a later lighting adjustment changes the fade.

The projection mask needs an amber alignment triangle outside the projected sky circle. It is a setup mark for the operator, not a star or a symbol within the scene. The first mask has twelve small star holes and a circular edge. A seam in its backing leaks a thin line of light near the right side. I saw that line from the left audience mark but have not yet checked the right mark.

The amber triangle belongs outside the circle even if a photograph is cropped differently. The visible seam leak is a mask observation from one defined position, not an audience-wide result. Covering the seam or changing the backing overlap are possible repairs, but neither has been tested yet. I would keep a diagram showing the triangle, the circular boundary and the leak location so later alterations can be compared without confusing their purposes.

My first narration script has thirty-six words split across three sentences. The last sentence describes a fictional constellation called the Paper Sail; it is invented for this show, not an astronomical identification. I have not timed a reading. The script is a file draft, and no printed cue sheet exists yet. I want the story to stay understandable when the mask is visible, rather than adding words merely to fill a fixed interval.

We can treat the Paper Sail as part of the authored story world. A timed reading would give evidence about delivery, while a listener review could reveal whether the references make sense. Neither outcome follows from word count alone. The cue sheet can later connect the approved wording to the current trigger rule, but it should distinguish proposed timings from the measured component durations and any actual narration start recorded in a rehearsal.

We ran a first combined rehearsal using Opening A. The log starts at the shared manual cue: the chime ended at three seconds, the fade ended at five seconds, narration started at three seconds and ended at sixteen seconds. I retained the recording and this event log as Rehearsal 1. The narrator followed the planned chime trigger, but a listener said the first sentence was hard to follow while the light was still changing.

Rehearsal 1 provides actual event times for that run, including a narration duration of thirteen seconds from start to end. The listener's comment concerns intelligibility during the transition, not a failure to follow the recorded trigger. We should preserve both the observed timing and the subjective feedback. A future change in the plan would not alter these historical timestamps or prove that the original narrator had begun at a different event.

The listener could recall the Paper Sail image but confused the first sentence's this shape with a bright seam line. They were at the left audience mark, the same place where I had seen the leak. I have not asked a listener at the right mark yet. I noted two possible causes to investigate: ambiguous script wording and the unwanted seam light. I have not decided that either alone caused the confusion.

The feedback links a wording issue and a visual distraction without identifying a single proven cause. Checking them separately could make the next revision more informative. A clearer noun phrase can be reviewed on paper, while a seam patch can be tested with the existing script. Keeping the audience position in the note also avoids generalizing one person's experience to all viewing locations or presenting an inference as a measured causal result.

I made two loose seam-patch samples. The narrow patch covers the visible line when held over the seam but leaves a small gap at its upper corner. The wider patch covers the corner as well, though it overlaps one of the twelve star holes. These observations were made from the left mark with the mask stationary. Neither patch is attached, and the original mask remains unchanged in the storage sleeve.

The trial reveals a tradeoff between seam coverage and preserving the intended star pattern. It does not justify declaring either loose patch final. A shaped patch might cover the corner without covering a hole, but that would be another proposed design. The distinction between a loose sample held in place and an installed repair matters here, because a later photograph could make the trial appear more complete than it actually is.

I revised the first sentence to name the Paper Sail directly rather than saying this shape. The full draft is now thirty-two words, still in three sentences. I have not timed this version. I printed the earlier thirty-six-word script for annotation, but the current shorter draft remains only in the file. The printed sheet is marked earlier wording so it will not be accidentally used as the new narration script.

The revision targets the reference ambiguity rather than assuming that removing four words automatically fixes the delivery. A reading and listener check still remain. Keeping the old print clearly labeled preserves the reason for the change without making it the current working text. The next cue packet should eventually use the revised file, but until a fresh print exists we should not claim that the shorter narration is already available as a physical sheet.

I checked the original unpatched mask from the right audience mark. The seam line is visible there too, though it looks shorter than from the left mark. The amber triangle remains outside the sky circle at both positions. This comparison used no narration and did not change the opening component settings. I recorded it as a viewing-position check of the existing mask, not as a second combined rehearsal.

We now have position-specific evidence that the leak is not limited to the left mark. Its apparent length differs by viewpoint, so the patch should be inspected from both places. The alignment requirement remains satisfied. Since no narration or new timing run occurred, the check should not add an invented start time or performance outcome to the rehearsal log; it concerns only the current projected appearance.

I cut a shaped patch with a notch around the star hole that the wide rectangle covered. Held over the seam, it covers the upper corner without covering that hole. I checked it from both audience marks. There are still twelve visible star holes in this static trial. The shaped patch is loose, and I have not tested whether its edges stay flat after attachment or after the mask warms during a longer projection.

The shaped patch addresses both observed problems in the static test: the seam corner and the neighboring hole. That is a useful improvement over the earlier rectangles, while attachment and extended-use behavior remain unobserved. We can retain the twelve-hole count as a result of this specific trial, not as a guarantee about any future installation. The patch's notch should be identified in the handoff so it is not confused with the rejected plain rectangle.

A reader timed the thirty-two-word script aloud without the projector. The reading lasted eleven seconds, but they paused awkwardly between the second and third sentences. They understood that the Paper Sail was imaginary. I kept the audio as Script Reading B. This was a standalone reading, with no opening chime and no light fade, so its start cannot be assigned a timestamp relative to either opening event.

Script Reading B supports a delivery-duration observation and a pacing comment for that wording. It is not another combined-show log, and its time origin differs from Rehearsal 1. The awkward pause could motivate a sentence edit, but we should not infer how that edit would sound before testing it. The reader's understanding of the fictional image is useful evidence about clarity, separate from the timing and from the mask repair.

I found a planning-card draft that says begin speech when the opening sound finishes. It was written as a shorthand reminder for the same current narration trigger, not as a separate new timing decision. The card does not contain rehearsal results. Beside it is a generic opening-events legend defining chime and fade; that legend explains the events but does not itself select which one starts the narration.

The planning card paraphrases the existing sound-ending trigger for narration. Its wording should stay distinguishable from the generic legend, which can remain useful regardless of which event the plan selects. Neither document is an observed performance. If someone later changes the active trigger, the old planning card becomes an old instruction rather than evidence that the new plan still starts at the sound ending or that earlier recordings have been retimed.

I shortened the final sentence and joined its opening to the previous sentence. The new script has twenty-eight words in two sentences. I have not timed this wording yet. The thirty-six-word annotated print and the thirty-two-word file remain archived with their own labels. The current twenty-eight-word script file has been checked for accidental omissions, but no new printed cue sheet has been made.

The latest wording is now a two-sentence file draft with a completed text check, while its delivery time and listener response remain unknown. The earlier eleven-second reading belongs to the thirty-two-word version and should not be assigned to this one automatically. The old print and files can explain the revision history without becoming current narration material. Printing the current file and timing a fresh reading are still distinct potential next steps.

I noticed that a photograph of the shaped seam patch hides the amber triangle because the camera cropped the outside edge. On the actual mask, the triangle is still outside the sky circle in its required position. I took a wider photograph showing the triangle and the full circle. I did not move the triangle or change the mask. The tightly cropped image is now labeled incomplete setup view.

The missing triangle in the first photograph was a framing limitation, not evidence that the setup mark had moved or disappeared. The wider image can document its actual placement. Keeping the cropped version with a label preserves why it was unsuitable as a setup reference. This is another case where a representation should not silently redefine the physical artifact: the actual mask and its placement requirement remain the basis for assembly.

For lighting, I made a separate setting named Opening B. Its chime is unchanged, but the fade is shorter. In a component-only measurement from the shared start cue, the chime still ended at three seconds and the fade ended at four seconds. No narration was included. I selected Opening B for the next planned combined rehearsal. The saved Opening A setting and Rehearsal 1 recording remain untouched.

The new component setting changes the fade duration while preserving the chime duration and the historical Opening A evidence. Selecting Opening B for a future rehearsal does not mean that rehearsal happened. The next plan should use the applicable B measurements when calculating proposed event positions, while retaining the existing narration-trigger rule unless it is separately changed. We should not retroactively replace Rehearsal 1's five-second fade with the new four-second component result.

I made a simple event table with separate columns for setting, chime end, fade end, narration start and narration end. The Opening B component row has blanks in both narration columns. The Rehearsal 1 row retains its actual three-second narration start and sixteen-second end. I added a heading saying blanks mean unmeasured, not zero, because an earlier sketch had put a dash in a way that resembled a negative sign.

That table separates measured components from complete performance observations. The blank narration cells in the B row should stay blank until a relevant run or explicitly labeled plan supplies information. The historical row has a different role and must retain its recorded times. Clarifying the blank notation also prevents an arithmetic mistake: an absent measurement is not a zero-duration narration and cannot support a claim that a rehearsal finished at the opening cue.

The twenty-eight-word script was read aloud in a new standalone test. It lasted ten seconds, with no awkward pause reported by the listener. The listener correctly recalled the Paper Sail image without seeing a projection. I saved this as Script Reading C. There was no chime or fade in that recording. The current script remains unprinted; the reader used the verified file on a screen rather than a paper cue sheet.

Reading C now supplies evidence for the latest wording's isolated duration and clarity under that condition. It does not show how the narration interacts with the opening lights, and it does not create a physical print. The ten-second duration can inform a proposed combined-run plan, but the plan must remain labeled as a prediction until a full rehearsal provides observed times. We should keep Reading B's eleven seconds tied to its earlier wording.

I held the shaped patch in place during a longer stationary projection and saw its lower corner curl away from the backing. The seam became faintly visible at that corner. I had used a temporary strip only along the patch's top edge. I removed that temporary strip after the check. The patch is loose again, and the main mask has no installed seam repair. The earlier brief static trial remains in the notes with its shorter test condition.

The longer check adds an attachment-related limitation that the brief held-overlay trial could not establish. It does not erase the earlier visibility result; the conditions differ. A second temporary contact point or a different attachment pattern could be tested, but neither has yet succeeded in the record. The current physical state is again a loose shaped patch and an unrepaired mask, which should be clear in any assembly handoff.

For the viewing marks, I measured that the left and right floor labels had shifted when the table was moved. I restored them to the positions marked on the setup diagram. I have not repeated the entire mask comparison from the restored marks. The earlier observations remain valid for the positions used at the time, but the moved labels should not be presented as unchanged references for a fresh test.

Restoring the floor labels is completed setup work, while any new viewing comparison remains pending. The diagram provides a way to define the intended positions, but it cannot retroactively alter where an earlier reader stood. Keeping that distinction prevents a false claim of exact repeat conditions. The next patch trial should record the restored marks explicitly, particularly if its results are compared with the older left-right observations.

I checked the old shorthand planning card again. Its instruction to begin at the finish of the opening sound is still the current selected trigger in this source history. The newly selected Opening B setting changes only the fade duration; I have not changed the narration trigger. The event legend remains separate and contains no role assignment. There has been no new combined rehearsal since Rehearsal 1.

The source therefore records a component-setting update without a trigger-rule update. The sound-ending planning card remains a statement of the currently selected trigger at this point, whereas the generic legend only defines events. A future authorized change could alter the active plan while leaving these historical statements intact. No such change or new combined performance should be inferred merely from the existence of the shorter fade setting or the latest script reading.

I tried the shaped patch again with two temporary contact points, using the restored viewing marks. During the same longer stationary projection interval, neither corner lifted, and the seam stayed covered from both marks. The twelve star holes remained visible. I removed the temporary contacts afterward to avoid treating the trial as final installation. The checked patch is back in its envelope, and the original mask still has the unpatched seam.

The revised temporary arrangement has a positive longer stationary result at the defined viewing positions. Removing the contacts makes the current storage state unambiguous: this is a checked loose repair, not an installed one. The next assembly step can use the tested placement, then verify the actual attachment. It should not repeat the failed single-top-contact arrangement or claim the physical mask was already repaired because a successful trial photograph exists.

I assembled a provisional cue packet containing the event legend, the Opening B component table and a blank space for the current narration print. I accidentally inserted the old thirty-six-word annotated sheet into that blank space while sorting. I noticed its earlier wording label and removed it. The packet now has no narration sheet. I kept the old print in its archive folder and wrote print current verified file on the packet's task list.

The sorting mistake was caught before the old script became a working cue sheet. The packet remains incomplete rather than containing an approved earlier version. Printing the current twenty-eight-word file is still a concrete remaining action. The event table and legend can be ready independently of that print, so the packet's status should distinguish existing components from the missing sheet instead of marking everything either complete or rejected.

I drafted a proposed timing row for a future rehearsal with Opening B and the current source trigger. It places narration at the chime ending, three seconds after the common cue, and uses the ten-second standalone reading as a provisional duration. I labeled the predicted narration end as thirteen seconds, not an observation. This planned row is separate from the B component row with blank narration measurements and from Rehearsal 1's actual times.

The proposed calculation is internally consistent under its stated assumptions: a three-second planned start plus the isolated ten-second reading gives thirteen seconds. It does not prove that a live delivery will last exactly that long. The row also encodes the current chime-ending trigger, so it must be reviewed if that active rule changes. The separate actual and component-only rows should remain intact instead of being overwritten by the prediction.

A colleague reviewing the packet asked whether the thirteen-second number meant the previous rehearsal ended sooner after editing. I explained that Rehearsal 1 still ended at sixteen seconds in its saved recording. The thirteen-second number is only a new prediction for a different script and setting. I added actual, component measurement and proposed plan labels to the three row types. I have not run the predicted rehearsal or altered the recording.

The labels resolve a useful interpretive risk without changing any event. They keep a future plan from being mistaken for a revised account of the past. Rehearsal 1, Opening B's isolated component measurements and the proposed combined row answer different questions. If a later trigger rule changes, only the active plan and its dependent prediction should be reconsidered; the saved past performance and the independent measured durations remain evidence of what actually happened.

I checked the Opening B setting once more in a component-only run. The chime ended at three seconds and the fade at four seconds from the same manual start. No narration was included. I recorded the repeat under its own date rather than deleting the first measurement. The two B checks support the same component figures, but they still do not provide an observed narration start or a completed combined-show result.

The repeated component check strengthens the evidence for B's current timing while preserving its limited scope. It remains separate from the standalone script reading and the actual Rehearsal 1 log. A future prediction can use the four-second fade and three-second chime as appropriate to its selected trigger, but neither event duration alone chooses the trigger. The active role assignment and the physical measurements are distinct pieces of information.

I inspected the stored shaped patch and compared its notch with the neighboring star hole on the setup drawing. It is the checked version, not the rejected wide rectangle. The two tested contact positions are marked on its back. I have not attached it to the main mask. The triangle on the main mask is still outside the circle, and I have not moved the audience marks since restoring them in the earlier session.

The identity and placement marks make the checked patch ready for installation without implying that installation has happened. The rejected rectangle should remain outside the working assembly packet because it obscures a star hole. The retained alignment triangle and restored audience positions provide independent checks for the eventual repair. Those checks can be performed under any permitted narration-trigger plan, since the mask geometry does not depend on which opening event starts speech.

The current twenty-eight-word script file is ready to print, but the physical cue packet still lacks that sheet. I opened the file and confirmed it matches the wording used in Script Reading C. I did not make a new audio reading. The old annotated thirty-six-word sheet is still archived. The packet's task list now separately names print current script and attach checked patch, rather than combining them into a single prepare show item.

The file-to-reading comparison confirms version identity, not a fresh performance or a completed print. Separating the two physical tasks makes the handoff more actionable. Printing should use the verified current file, and attachment should use the checked notched patch. Neither step requires editing the historical rehearsal recording. Once the physical preparations are complete, a combined run can test the current plan as a new event with its own observed timing and visual results.

I prepared a blank form for that eventual combined run. It has spaces for the setting name, the currently authorized trigger, the actual chime and fade endings, the actual narration start and end, and the two audience-position comments. The form has no results entered. I have not scheduled a particular day or promised that the next person will run it immediately; it is simply ready to capture evidence when a rehearsal actually takes place.

The blank form is useful preparation and avoids carrying old assumptions into a new run. Its fields distinguish the trigger instruction from the observed start, which matters if a narrator responds late or a setting differs. Leaving the date and results open is accurate. A handoff can propose filling the form during a future rehearsal, but should not turn the existence of a prepared form into proof that any timing or audience feedback has already been collected.

At the final source handoff, the main mask still lacks the seam patch. The checked notched patch remains loose in its envelope with two contact positions marked on the back. The current script remains unprinted, though its file identity was checked against Reading C. The most recent component evidence is still Opening B's three-second chime ending and four-second fade ending. No new combined rehearsal has occurred since the saved Rehearsal 1.

The practical remaining preparations are clear: attach the checked patch, print the verified current script and then observe a combined run if requested. The successful temporary patch trial and component checks should remain visible, while the physical installation and combined performance stay pending. We should not describe the main mask as repaired or the cue packet as complete. Historical Rehearsal 1 remains a distinct recording with its own actual timestamps.

The amber alignment triangle is still outside the sky circle. The tighter old photograph remains labeled incomplete setup view, while the wider photograph shows the required placement. The left and right audience marks remain in their restored positions. I want any new visual check to identify those positions explicitly rather than simply saying the audience could see it. The old seam observations should keep their original test conditions in the comparison notes.

Those setup references allow a future check to be described precisely. The wider image documents the triangle; the old cropped view cannot be used to infer that the mark is missing. The restored audience labels define intended new positions without rewriting earlier observations. A meaningful next action can therefore check the installed patch from both specified places while preserving the independent orientation requirement and the separate status of narration timing.

The timing table still keeps three kinds of rows: Rehearsal 1's actual event log, Opening B's component measurements and a proposed combined row based on the source's chime-ending trigger. The proposed row is explicitly conditional on that trigger and the isolated reading duration. It is not an additional rehearsal. If the active instruction changes later, the conditional row needs a new calculation, but the actual row and the measured component durations remain unchanged.

The dependency is specific: the proposed narration start and predicted end depend on the selected trigger, whereas the measured chime, measured fade and old observed performance do not. A plan update must not silently relabel an old recording as if it followed the new rule. The remaining script and mask tasks are also independent of that selected cue. We can therefore revise a current handoff without discarding useful historical evidence or inventing a completed performance.

The rejected-artifact folder contains the plain wide patch that covers a star hole, the narrow patch with a corner gap and the tightly cropped setup photograph. The older scripts are archived for version history rather than labeled as physical defects. The checked notched patch and current script file are identified separately. I want the final handoff to preserve why each object changed, instead of presenting every earlier artifact as interchangeable obsolete clutter.

That distinction preserves the causal chain of the project. Different patches failed different visual requirements, the photograph failed to show the full setup, and the script versions changed wording and pacing. The current handoff should use the permitted trigger, retain the external alignment mark and propose an actual remaining preparation or rehearsal step. It should neither revive a replaced trigger from an old planning row nor rewrite historical observed times to make the past match a new instruction.

creation_note: Original fictional evaluation script; all people, institutions, dates and dialogue are authored. No real participant log or public provenance is claimed.

haystack_sessions.content: For this fictional Lantern Fold puzzle booklet, the private answer phrase for puzzle Q6 is Silver river. I am recording it in the editorial key, not publishing it in the reader pages. Q6 is a persistent puzzle identifier and may appear on a different page after editing. The work still needed concerns page cross-references, a twelve-page folded mock-up and instruction wording that can be read without relying only on tiny arrows.

I will record Silver river as the private Q6 answer and keep it separate from the public page-location map. A puzzle's identity and its printed page are different identifiers, so a move should not silently change the answer assignment. We can review the editorial key, the cross-reference file and the physical mock-up as distinct artifacts. A correct key alone will not prove that the printed booklet points readers to the right page.

The initial map places Q1 on page3, Q2 on page4, Q3 on page5, Q4 on page6, Q5 on page8 and Q6 on page9. Pages1 and2 are the cover and directions, page7 is a blank planning spacer, and pages10 through12 hold notes and the back cover. I have numbered a loose set of page cards, but I have not imposed them onto folding sheets or assembled a booklet.

The page cards establish the current intended order without establishing a folded artifact. The gap at page7 is a deliberate spacer at this point, not a missing puzzle or an accidental duplicate. We should use the location map when drafting links, then check the physical result after imposition and folding. A page number in a link should not be interpreted as a puzzle identifier merely because some of the numbers happen to match.

One convention is fixed: cross-reference labels must use page numbers, not puzzle numbers. A label such as see page9 means a location in the booklet, not Q9. The puzzle code can appear separately in an editor's note. I have added this convention to the style sheet. The first direction draft says follow the small arrow to the next panel, which may be difficult to use when the arrow is printed too faintly.

The cross-reference convention gives readers a stable kind of locator while allowing the page-location map to change during editing. It also means an editor must update links when a puzzle moves. The arrow wording is a separate accessibility concern. A textual direction may help, but we should test the wording in its intended layout rather than assuming that replacing one word or enlarging an arrow automatically solves the issue.

The mock-up uses three folded sheets, which should make twelve page faces. I have blank sheets marked outer, middle and inner, plus loose page cards. None of the sheets has printed content yet. I want to test their face order with large page numbers before adding any puzzle text. The private key will stay outside that public assembly mock-up; counting or folding sheets does not require knowing the answer phrase.

A numbered dummy is an appropriate way to isolate page-order problems from puzzle content. Three sheets can supply the planned twelve faces, but the arrangement and fold still need a physical check. Keeping the key out of the dummy makes the test easier to interpret: a reader can report sequence and cross-reference behavior without seeing any answer. We can record sheet identity and face position so a later reversed sheet is traceable.

I drew a first numbered dummy. The outside of the outer sheet has pages12 and1; its inside has pages2 and11. The middle sheet has10 and3 outside,4 and9 inside. The inner sheet has8 and5 outside,6 and7 inside. I recorded left and right positions on a drawing but have not yet printed those arrangements. The figures are a proposed face map until a folded trial confirms their actual order.

The face map accounts for each number from1 through12 once, which is a useful completeness check. It does not by itself prove that the printer orientation and fold will produce the intended reading order. The left-right drawing and sheet labels should travel together into the trial. If a page later appears upside down or out of sequence, we can compare the actual sheet with the proposed face map rather than guessing which puzzle text caused the problem.

The generic word-code sheet in our editing kit maps17 to silver,24 to river,8 to window and31 to stone. The sheet is used for several word games and does not assign any of those words to Q6 or to another particular puzzle. I put it with the public kit inventory. Code numbers are not page numbers; the style sheet's page-reference convention still applies only to reader navigation labels.

That sheet is a vocabulary decoder, not an answer key. Its public entries can remain useful independently of any private puzzle assignment. A separate note that ties Q6 to a pair of those codes would carry additional information, because the note and the decoder together would identify an answer phrase. We should also preserve the distinction between code17 and page17; this booklet has twelve pages and uses page labels for navigation.

In a private editorial slip I wrote Q6 =17/24, explicitly using the word-code sheet from this session. It is shorthand for the same answer assignment, not a new solution or a new puzzle. The slip is stored with the editorial key. On the public directions page I changed the draft text to follow the arrow beside the panel number, but I have not tried this wording with a reader or printed it at the intended size.

The private code slip expresses the selected answer through the stated decoder; it should be handled as part of the private key. The revised navigation sentence is a separate draft and contains no solution. It may clarify which arrow to use, but still assumes the reader can distinguish a small arrow. A layout or reading check can address that issue without consulting the key or treating the existence of the draft as evidence of usability.

I noticed that a draft link from page4 says see Q6. Under our style convention, that is not a valid reader-facing page label. The destination is currently page9 according to the initial location map. I circled the link in the file comments but did not change the actual text yet. I want the next editing pass to separate this identifier mistake from any later change to Q6's page location.

The current defect is the kind of identifier used in the label: Q6 names a puzzle rather than a page. The presently intended destination gives a clear basis for a correction, but the circled comment is not itself a corrected reader page. Recording both the defect and the current map will make a later move easier to follow. Otherwise someone might fix the identifier wording while preserving a destination that has become obsolete.

We decided to move Q6 from page9 into the planning space on page7. Its puzzle identity and private editorial assignment have not changed. Page9 will now become a worked example about following page links, with no answer to Q6 on it. The other puzzle locations remain as before. I updated the editor's location map, but the page4 link still carries the old commented see Q6 wording and has not been repaired.

The decision changes a location map, not the identity of Q6 or the contents of its private key. The page4 link now needs both the page-label convention and the new destination applied. The worked example on page9 is a different reader artifact and should not inherit Q6's answer merely because it occupies the old location. We can track these edits separately so that a partial repair does not appear to have completed the whole navigation update.

I printed the large-number face map and assembled a dummy. At the center opening, pages7 and6 appeared in that left-to-right order instead of6 and7. I compared the inner sheet with the drawing and found that I had reversed the inside-face positions during copying. The outer and middle sheets matched their drawn face positions. I kept the faulty inner sheet and wrote copied inside face reversed on it.

The observed center-opening problem has a specific documented cause in the copied inner sheet. It does not require changing puzzle identities or the outer and middle maps. The next trial should correct the inside-face placement and record the resulting page walk. The faulty physical sheet remains evidence of the first attempt; editing a file would not retroactively make that assembled dummy correct or prove that a second fold has already worked.

For the directions, one reader could not tell which tiny arrow belonged to panel2 at the intended print size. They understood the panel numbers but followed the neighboring arrow. I recorded their path without giving the right answer to any puzzle. They were reviewing navigation, not solving Q6. I drafted a sentence that names a direction in words, go to the panel on the right, but it is not yet linked to a particular page layout.

The result identifies an association problem between arrows and panel numbers, not evidence that the reader failed a puzzle. A textual direction may help if it accurately matches the actual panel arrangement. Before printing it, we should bind the wording to a specific layout and check that the right-hand panel is the intended destination. Supplying the private answer would not resolve this navigation issue and would spoil the separation between usability review and answer-key access.

I changed the page4 reader label to see page9, applying the page-label convention but accidentally retaining the old destination. The editor's map already says Q6 is on page7. I caught this mismatch while comparing the file comments with the revised map. I marked the page4 file needs destination correction. The label is now the right kind of identifier but still points to the wrong location.

This is a partial repair: the label type is corrected, while its destination remains stale. The explicit mismatch gives us a bounded next edit to page7, followed by a comparison with the current location map. The old see Q6 wording, the intermediate page9 label and the final intended page7 label should remain distinguishable in the change record. None of these public navigation labels needs to contain Q6's private answer phrase.

I corrected the page4 link to see page7 in the working file. I also checked a link from page10 that still pointed to Q6's old location and changed its destination to page7. The two edited labels now use page numbers as required. I have not printed these revised pages. The old physical dummy still contains only large page numbers, so it cannot be used as evidence that the new navigation text has been tested in print.

The two file edits now align with the revised location map and the identifier convention. The next check should distinguish file-level link correctness from physical readability and folding order. A numbered dummy can expose page-order errors but says nothing about the size or placement of a reader link that was never printed on it. We can retain the earlier dummy as a separate artifact without treating its limited success or failure as a verdict on these new labels.

I made a corrected inner-sheet drawing with6 on the left and7 on the right for the relevant inside face. I compared it with the intended center opening, but have not printed a replacement inner sheet. The outer and middle drawings are unchanged. The previous faulty physical inner sheet is stored separately. I want to assemble a new dummy from fresh prints rather than quietly swapping labels on the old reversed sheet.

The corrected drawing addresses the known copying error, while a new physical fold remains pending. Fresh prints would make it easier to preserve what happened in each trial. The unchanged outer and middle drawings can be reused with explicit version identification, but they still need to be placed correctly during assembly. A complete page walk after folding would check the combined artifact rather than assuming that a correct center pair alone establishes the whole booklet sequence.

I bound the new direction sentence to a specific two-panel layout on page2. Panel2 is on the right of panel1, so the draft says from panel1, continue to the panel on the right. The arrows remain as supplemental marks rather than the only instruction. I enlarged the instruction type slightly in the file. This is a layout revision, not a reader trial, and I have not printed the larger-type version yet.

The direction wording now has a defined spatial referent in that page2 layout. It should be tested at the intended size because a file view on screen may not show the same spacing or emphasis. Keeping arrows as supplemental marks avoids making them the sole source of navigation information. The review can ask a reader to identify the next panel without revealing a solution or interpreting successful navigation as successful completion of any puzzle.

The private key and the private17/24 slip remain in the editorial envelope. I made a public inventory card listing one word-code sheet, one style sheet and three sheet-face drawings. The inventory card does not list private assignments. I want the drawer labels to distinguish a reusable word list from a puzzle-specific key, since someone can legitimately need the public list while having no reason to open the private envelope.

The inventory describes document types and counts, not the Q6 answer or its code pairing. The reusable decoder and the private role binding should therefore remain separate records. We can organize the drawer and describe which public production artifacts are available without reproducing the key. A request for a word list or a folding drawing is not automatically a request for the private editorial assignment, even if the items were created during the same session.

I printed the larger-type page2 direction sample. A reader correctly moved from panel1 to the panel on the right using the words without looking closely at the arrows. They said the enlarged text was readable, but the line break made panel1 look like the heading of the next paragraph. I kept their exact path and comment. They did not inspect the other booklet pages or see any private key material.

The observed navigation success and the line-break concern can both be retained. The trial supports the defined two-panel task under that sample's conditions, not every instruction in the booklet. A revised line break could preserve the larger type while making the paragraph boundary clearer. The next check should focus on that change rather than assuming the entire accessibility problem is resolved because one reader reached the intended panel without using the arrows.

I revised the line break in the page2 file so panel1 stays with the opening phrase on the same line. The type size is unchanged. I have not printed this newest line-break version. The previous larger-type print is kept as a tested sample with a pending layout improvement. I marked the working file current wording, revised line break so it will not be confused with the print that produced the earlier reader comment.

The file now addresses the specific paragraph-boundary concern while preserving the property the reader found useful. Its unprinted status is important: the earlier readability result applies to the prior line break. We can carry forward the evidence that textual direction helps in this layout without declaring the latest physical sample tested. A fresh print and focused reader review would still be a meaningful next action and does not require any private answer information.

While checking filenames, I found that the revised page4 link file had been copied into a folder labeled old pagination. The file itself still correctly says see page7. I moved the working copy to the current-pagination folder and left a note in the old folder explaining where it went. I did not change its link text during this move. The page10 link file remained in the correct folder throughout.

This is a storage and version-discovery correction, not another destination edit. The page4 label remained correct during the move, so the change log should not imply that it temporarily reverted to page9. The note in the old folder can help someone find the current file without using the old folder as an authoritative print source. Physical printing of the corrected links is still pending, regardless of where the working files are stored.

The corrected inner-sheet drawing is ready, but I have delayed printing because the printer's duplex option has two flip settings. I have not established which setting matches these particular sheet drawings. I prepared a small orientation test with an upright triangle on each face, unrelated to any puzzle. The test file is ready but has not been printed. I do not want an untested printer setting to silently recreate the earlier reversed-center problem.

The orientation test is a separate dependency before a full numbered dummy is printed. Its triangle marks are generic orientation indicators, not secret answer codes. A physical two-sided print can show how the chosen setting maps the two faces. The result should be recorded for the actual setting used; selecting an option in a dialog is not evidence that the output came out as expected or that the booklet will fold correctly.

I printed the two-sided orientation test with one flip option and found that the back triangle was upside down relative to the drawing. I marked that option unsuitable for this test layout. With the other option, both triangles matched the drawing when the sheet was turned as specified. I saved the two test sheets with their option labels. This check did not include the twelve numbered pages or any puzzle text.

The two physical outputs provide a basis for choosing the appropriate option for this layout. They do not establish a completed booklet, and the unsuitable result should remain tied to its actual setting. The labeled test sheets can be reused as a reference during printing, but someone should still check that the selected option is the intended one. A correct orientation test reduces one known risk without proving that every later sheet will be copied or folded correctly.

I prepared a print queue containing the unchanged outer and middle drawings and the corrected inner drawing, using the option that passed the orientation test. I have not sent that queue to the printer. The queue is a saved preparation, not a stack of physical pages. It contains only large numbers and orientation marks, so a future page walk can test the structure before reader text is added.

The queued configuration is now explicit enough to reproduce the next trial, while its execution remains pending. The corrected inner-face order and the selected flip option address different earlier risks and should both be preserved. A later operator can print the queue, verify sheet identities and assemble a fresh dummy. We should not infer a correct center opening from the queue alone, because the physical sheets have not yet been produced or folded.

A public proof checklist names page4 and page10 as the two locations whose links should now lead to page7. It also asks the reviewer to distinguish the page7 location from the Q6 puzzle code. The checklist contains no answer phrase or private code pair. I checked the labels in the current files against it. The results are file-level checks only; the physical reader pages still have not been printed.

The checklist makes the intended navigation corrections concrete and testable while keeping the answer key unnecessary. File comparison is useful evidence, but a printed link could still be misplaced, truncated or too small. That is why the physical proof stage remains open. The distinction between page7 and Q6 should be checked in context rather than by searching for numbers alone, since both identifiers can legitimately appear in an editor's material with different roles.

I counted the public drawer contents again: one reusable word-code sheet, one style sheet and the three current face drawings. I also found an older photocopy of the generic word-code sheet. Its17 and24 entries match the current public sheet, but it carries no Q6 assignment. I marked it duplicate vocabulary sheet and kept it out of the active inventory count. It is not an extra puzzle key or an extra independent source.

The duplicate decoder contains the same public word mappings but no puzzle-specific role binding. Its presence does not create a second independent answer assignment or a new permission to read the private key. Excluding it from the active one-sheet inventory is a counting decision, while preserving the duplicate can explain where extra paper came from. The private17/24 slip remains the record that connects the reusable vocabulary to the particular puzzle.

I noticed that the old page9 worked-example draft still had the heading Q6 copied from the previous page template. The new location map and current puzzle page place Q6 on page7. I removed the stale heading from the page9 file and replaced it with Following page links. I did not move Q6 again or change its key. The revised worked-example file has not been printed or tested with a reader.

The correction removes a stale identity label from a different public artifact. It does not change the location decision or the private answer assignment. Keeping this distinction prevents an erroneous conclusion that two copies of Q6 now exist on different pages. The worked-example file can be reviewed as navigation teaching material, while page7 remains the intended location of the puzzle. The physical proof stage still needs to confirm that the corrected heading is actually what gets printed.

The saved numbered-dummy print queue is still unexecuted. I reopened it and checked that the inner drawing has the corrected6-left/7-right center pair and that the tested flip option is selected. I have not produced new physical sheets. The original faulty center-opening dummy remains in the samples box with its error label. Reopening a queue is only a configuration check and does not count as a fresh page-order trial.

The configuration check preserves the intended next attempt, but the physical result remains unknown. We should keep the old faulty dummy visible as evidence of the earlier error without implying that the corrected drawings failed in the same way. Printing, assembling and walking the pages are three actions that still need observation. A useful handoff can name the ready queue and the pending physical steps instead of saying the pagination is fully verified.

I selected the revised page2 line-break file as the current instruction version, but it remains unprinted. The earlier larger-type sample and its reader comment are stored together. I also prepared a short review question asking which panel follows panel1 in the shown layout, without asking for a puzzle answer. The review question has not been used with a reader yet and contains no hidden solution or clue from the private editorial key.

The proposed review isolates navigation from solving and gives a direct way to assess the revised line break. The existing reader result remains tied to the earlier sample. If the new print is tested, its own layout and response should be recorded rather than copying the earlier success into a new version's result field. That approach preserves useful prior evidence while keeping the unperformed review genuinely open and independent of private answer access.

I checked the editorial envelope label. It names the private answer key and the shorthand slip for Q6, but does not print either the phrase or the two code numbers on the outside. The public word list is in a different drawer. I have not given anyone a new permission or distributed an answer page. My remaining production requests concern the public files, the corrected dummy and the instruction sample, which can be handled without opening that envelope.

The envelope's outside label identifies document purpose without disclosing the selected answer. Its storage location is not an access grant. We can continue the public production work from its own evidence, and a later authorized key review would need to respect its specified scope. The fact that an editor once saw both the word list and the key is not, by itself, proof that every page drawing or navigation comment depends on the private answer.

At the final source handoff, the corrected page4 and page10 link files both point to page7. Page9's worked-example heading has been fixed in its file. None of these revised reader pages has been physically printed. Q6 remains the same puzzle on page7 in the current location map. The public checklist distinguishes page numbers from puzzle identifiers, and I want that convention preserved even if the key is not available to the person preparing proofs.

A concrete next step is to print the current reader files and inspect the actual labels and heading against the current map. The file-level checks already completed should be preserved, but they do not replace physical proofing. The location of Q6 can be discussed as a navigation fact without stating its answer. This allows production work to continue within limited access while avoiding the mistake of treating an unavailable key as a reason to abandon unrelated tasks.

The twelve-page numbered dummy is still pending execution from the saved corrected queue. The two-sided orientation test is complete and its successful option is labeled, but no new folded page walk has occurred. The old reversed-center dummy remains a rejected sample. I would like the handoff to specify print the three identified sheets, assemble them and record the page sequence, rather than assuming the queue itself is a completed physical booklet.

The next physical trial can use the prepared queue and tested orientation setting while still checking the resulting artifact. A page walk should record the actual order, including the center pair, and preserve a failure if one occurs. That result does not depend on the editorial answer phrase. The old dummy and the corrected unexecuted queue should remain distinct so an observer can tell what was tested and what was only prepared.

The current page2 instruction file has the larger type and revised line break, but no fresh print or reader response exists for that exact version. The earlier reader correctly navigated the two panels but reported the paragraph-boundary ambiguity. I kept that response with the earlier sample. The next reader question asks only about the next panel in the visible layout, and no part of the private solution is required to answer it.

This preserves the difference between useful prior feedback and validation of a newer version. A fresh intended-size print followed by the navigation question would be a meaningful remaining review. It should not be scored as a puzzle-solving task or be supplied with an answer key. The public wording, panel arrangement and identifier convention provide enough information to assess navigation without interpreting access to private editorial material as a prerequisite.

The private envelope and public decoder remain separate. Public inventories may mention that an answer key exists, but they should not reproduce its assignment or shorthand pairing. I have not produced a reader-facing answer page, and the booklet is not described as published. The current production status is a set of corrected files, a prepared dummy queue and one previously tested direction sample, with the specific later physical checks still open.

The handoff can preserve that mixed status instead of claiming a blanket completion. Public cross-reference, folding and instruction work has clear evidence and clear next actions. A private answer review, if separately authorized, would not automatically authorize publication or change the status of the public physical checks. No new reader response, successfully folded booklet or published answer should be invented from the existence of corrected files and stored editorial material.
