For this edit, keep intentional hold frames as duration; remove a repeated import only after confirming it is accidental. I deliberately want A's final image held for three timeline frames in total. Someone suggested keeping only unique images, but that would shorten a planned pause. The capture count remains twelve even though the timeline will be longer when that hold is inserted.

A three-frame total hold replaces the original final single position with three positions, adding two rather than three. A would therefore occupy fourteen timeline frames if there are no other repeats or removals. Keep an explicit reason beside each repeat: planned hold or suspected import duplication. Equal image bytes alone cannot distinguish those purposes, so deduplication should not decide the edit for you.

I applied the candidate right-edge crop to all twelve A images. The tape is absent throughout, and the basin remains inside the image. B has not been captured yet. My export preset still has the old uncropped dimensions, so the preview window showing a tidy crop does not tell us how a rendered file will be sized or padded.

Mark the A crop inspection as complete and the export-dimension check as open. Before capturing B, write down the crop rectangle and confirm that the boat's intended path stays within it. When you eventually export, inspect actual pixel dimensions and border treatment. A preview and a saved preset are different artifacts; agreement in one does not prove agreement in the other.

I captured B with the camera on the same taped feet. It has ten images, and the boat enters from the left. In B's last two images the bow is close to the cropped right boundary. I have not applied the crop to B. There is room on the physical sheet, but the available camera area may be a different matter.

Check those last two images using the exact A crop before choosing a remedy. Physical space beyond the camera boundary cannot appear simply because the sheet is wider. If the bow would be clipped, possible remedies include reshooting B's path or adopting a consistent wider framing for both shots. Do not report either remedy as selected while you have only identified the risk.

My count sheet now separates captured photographs from timeline positions. A has twelve captured files and a planned fourteen-position sequence. B has ten captured files awaiting its edge test. The line about a three-frame hold means three total positions for the last A image, not three extra copies plus the original. I have not specified any hold for B.

The count sheet makes the hold's contribution explicit: two added timeline positions beyond the twelve captures. Preserve that calculation alongside the creative intent. If the final image later appears more than three times, inspect the extra positions individually; the presence of an intentional hold does not authorize unlimited repeats, just as duplicate bytes do not justify deleting every repeat.

The exact A crop clips B's bow in its final image. I will reshoot B with a shorter path rather than change A's crop. The original ten B images remain in a folder marked B-old. I have not captured the replacement yet. I want the old folder preserved so we can understand why it was rejected, but it must not be picked automatically for the active edit.

Treat B-old as rejected source material with a documented edge-clipping reason. The reshoot decision does not supply replacement images, so the current edit has a missing active B until capture is complete. Give the new take a separate identifier. Reusing the same image numbers is acceptable only if the take directory remains part of every reference; otherwise old and new frames can be confused.

The reshoot is complete as B-new, with eight images. I used the same crop and checked every image; the bow stays inside. During import I selected the folder twice by mistake. The editor now has sixteen B-new entries in its media bin, but I have not dragged them all onto the timeline. The second set points to the same eight source paths.

That is evidence of duplicated media-bin entries, not yet evidence of sixteen timeline frames or a deliberately repeated performance. Remove the second import references after confirming that no separate edit depends on them, while preserving the eight actual source files. Then construct the B timeline deliberately. The earlier rule about intentional holds still matters if you later repeat an image for pacing.

For a compact private slate index, PH means Paper Harbour. My notebook says current working slate = PH. These notes do not rename any image file. Separately, C's landing prop is leaning because its paper support folded overnight. No C images have been taken. I will reinforce the support before placing the boat against it.

The slate shorthand PH carries the working title through that decoder, so it belongs with the title metadata even though it is abbreviated. Keep the C support repair on the physical-set task list. Reinforcement is proposed, not tested. Once repaired, compare its visible position with the end of B before starting capture, since a sturdier support could still move the landing to a different place.

The replacement-take register says B-old rejected, B-new captured and crop-checked, duplicate media import awaiting cleanup. It also lists the physical C support as untested. Those are independent rows: success of the new B path does not repair the landing, and retaining B-old for audit does not make it eligible for automatic selection in the active timeline.

Keep the register at that level of specificity when handing it to another editor. They can finish the duplicate-import check without selecting rejected images or declaring C ready. Stable take identifiers and explicit eligibility are more useful than a single folder-wide done flag, because several different work items can share storage while remaining at different stages of review.

The duplicate B-new media-bin entries have been removed after checking that the second set had no timeline references. B's active timeline now uses the eight new images once each. A uses fourteen positions, including its intentional final hold. I wrote a rough combined total of twenty-four on the board, but adding fourteen and eight gives twenty-two. The board note is wrong.

Record twenty-two timeline positions for A followed by B, and keep the incorrect twenty-four as a corrected calculation rather than changing either shot to fit it. The capture totals are still twelve and eight. This is another reason to name the counting layer: original images, media references and timeline positions answer different questions, even when two counts happen to be equal.

C's support is reinforced, and I compared the empty landing with B's last frame. Its left corner moved slightly upward. I can reset the landing to the pencil outline on the board, but that outline is partly under the blue sheet. I have not lifted the sheet yet because moving it might disturb the boat's starting position for C.

Use a staged check rather than assuming the visible corner is enough. Record the current boat position, expose only the needed outline if feasible, and compare the landing's position before committing to capture. If the sheet or boat moves, re-establish the intended starting arrangement. The aim is continuity across the join, not merely making the reinforced support look neat in isolation.

I exposed the outline without shifting the boat, reset the landing, and photographed the setup. The comparison now matches B's final landing corner. I captured six C images as C-one. The last photograph is a close view of the boat against the landing; the earlier five are wider. I have not decided whether that change in framing is intentional or an accidental camera bump.

Keep C-one as captured material awaiting a framing decision. The matching starting setup does not certify the entire take, especially a visibly different final image. Compare the camera and background boundaries before calling the close view a designed cut. You can use the five wider images for inspection without silently deleting the sixth or claiming that a new ending has already been approved.

I am preserving the corrected arithmetic note because it shows exactly which count was confused. Twenty-two is the combined A/B timeline count; it is not C's capture count or an export observation. C-one has six captured files but the last one still has a framing question. No whole-film total should be called final until that ending is resolved.

The corrected note can help another editor distinguish a wrong sum from missing footage. It explains the count without forcing a convenient total onto unresolved material. Continue to record C's captured files separately from its eventual accepted sequence; rejecting or replacing an image changes eligibility, while the preserved original capture record remains useful evidence about how the edit developed.

The last C-one image was a camera bump. The landing and basin are both enlarged, and the camera foot is off its tape. I rejected that image and captured a new ending after resetting the camera. The new file is C-end/006.png, while the rejected original is C-one/006.png. Their basenames match, but they are different files in different directories.

Record the rejected final image and replacement by full path or stable content identity. The active C sequence can use C-one's first five images followed by C-end's new ending once you verify the join. A comparison that looks only for 006.png could select the wrong file. Matching filenames do not make the old framing acceptable or prove that a replacement has propagated into the editor.

I checked the new ending against C-one image five; framing is consistent. The active timeline is A fourteen, B eight, C six positions. The editor panel shows twenty-eight total, which agrees with the sum. Playback is set to twelve frames per second. I have not rendered a movie, and the viewer dropped frames during one preview because another program was busy.

The configured twenty-eight-frame timeline at twelve frames per second implies a duration of twenty-eight divided by twelve seconds, before any export changes. A choppy preview is not reliable evidence that frames were removed from the timeline. Inspect the rendered file when available for actual frame count and cadence. Preserve both the exact fraction and an approximate duration if useful; do not invent a measured export duration yet.

I rendered preview R1. Its file contains twenty-eight frames at twelve frames per second, but frame twenty-two shows B-old's clipped bow. I found that an old proxy was attached to B-new's final timeline slot. The source path label still says B-new. The other seven B positions display the expected new path, so the wrong content is localized to the last B slot.

Treat R1 as a failed content preview despite its correct count and rate. Relink that slot to the verified new image and invalidate or regenerate its proxy, then check the rendered join rather than trusting the source-path label. The error concerns the content behind one timeline position, not an extra frame or a reason to remove A's deliberate pause. Keep R1 for the before-and-after comparison.

The export comparison sheet has separate cells for frame count, rate, dimensions, image identity and movement order. R1 passes the first two cells and fails image identity at the B ending. I have not filled the other cells automatically. A red mark in one cell should tell us what to investigate rather than erase the useful observations in the others.

That comparison sheet supports a targeted repair. It preserves the successful count and rate observations while isolating the stale proxy. After correction, inspect a new rendered artifact and identify it explicitly rather than overwriting R1's result in place. This lets a later reviewer trace which conclusion came from which file without assuming that all checks automatically carry over.

I replaced the stale B proxy and rendered R2. At the A/B join the boat enters correctly, and B's last slot now shows the shorter unclipped path. However, the C section plays backward: the boat appears to leave the landing. The six active C images were sorted by modification time after I copied the new ending, instead of by the intended sequence list.

The B correction is verified in R2, but the C ordering is a separate remaining defect. Restore the explicit C list of the first five captured positions followed by the checked ending. Modification time reflects file handling and does not reliably encode the story's order. Re-render and inspect the C movement; the right set of six images in the wrong order is not a successful continuity result.

I restored the C list and rendered R3. A colleague watched it and correctly described the boat approaching the landing. They also asked whether A's pause was a playback error. I explained the planned hold, but have not changed its duration. Their question is feedback about how the pause reads, not permission to deduplicate or an instruction to shorten the film.

Keep the successful movement check and the pacing feedback as separate observations. You can ask a viewer to compare alternative pause lengths in a future trial, but that trial has not happened. The existing intentional hold remains part of the active edit until an explicit edit decision changes it. Describe the colleague's actual question without turning it into a claim that all viewers reject the pause.

I made an untitled pacing test T1 with A's final image held for two positions in total, one fewer than the active edit. It is a separate sequence, not the master. I have not shown it to anyone. The editor copied the master's twenty-eight-frame label into the test notes even though T1's timeline now shows twenty-seven positions.

Correct the test's count label to twenty-seven while leaving the master's twenty-eight unchanged. A shorter separate test is not an authorized replacement of the master. Keep the purpose, sequence identity and actual count together so a later comparison does not attribute the test's duration or viewer reaction to the active version. At present there is no viewer reaction to T1 to report.

The trial register distinguishes the active R3 sequence from T1. Its status field says not yet shown for T1, while R3 has one colleague's movement check and pacing question. Those descriptions should stay with the right artifact even if files are copied into the same review folder. Being next to an approved file does not transfer approval or viewer feedback.

The artifact-specific register will also help interpret any later viewer comparison. A response to T1 should be attached to T1, not retroactively assigned to R3. Until viewers actually see the test, the only supported claims are its changed hold and count. The register can invite a comparison while keeping the active sequence and its existing evidence intact.

Two viewers compared R3 and the rendered T1 without seeing the count labels. One preferred R3's pause and the other preferred T1's quicker start. I decided to retain R3's timing as the master. That decision is now in the edit log. It does not mean there was unanimous preference, and the shorter test remains archived rather than merged into the master.

Record the split feedback and the explicit choice separately. The master remains twenty-eight frames with the original intentional hold; T1 is a twenty-seven-frame alternative. The choice closes the immediate pacing decision but does not prove a universal audience effect. The next delivery checks can focus on the selected master without repeatedly presenting the already completed comparison as if it were still pending.

The venue wants a square preview. I made layout SQ1 by fitting R3 inside a square canvas with black bands above and below; no image content was cropped. The preview player hides those bands against its own black background. I have exported SQ1 but have not inspected the actual pixel dimensions or looked at it against a contrasting player background.

Mark SQ1 as exported but not yet checked for canvas geometry and visible padding. Fitting the master into a canvas and cropping it are different operations; a player background can obscure which occurred. Inspect the file's dimensions and a frame against a contrasting background. Keep the twenty-eight-frame content check distinct from the square-canvas check so success in one cannot substitute for evidence in the other.

SQ1 is 1080 by 1080 pixels and contains all twenty-eight master frames. Against gray, the upper and lower black bands are visible as expected, and the boat is not clipped. The venue's upload page created a thumbnail that looks horizontally stretched. I have not opened their transcoded movie, so I do not know whether the stretch affects the movie or only the thumbnail.

The local square export has passed the checks you actually performed. Treat the venue thumbnail as a new observation with uncertain scope. Open the delivered movie and compare a known shape and frame with the local file before requesting a rerender. A distorted thumbnail may be a presentation artifact; it does not establish that your local canvas, the venue movie and every viewer's playback are all wrong.

The delivery checklist now records local SQ1 geometry and content checks as completed. It lists venue movie proportions as unknown, based only on the stretched thumbnail. The two entries can coexist without contradiction because they describe different artifacts. If the venue supplies a new transcode, its identifier should be recorded before applying an old check result to that new file.

Keep local-export assurance and venue-delivery assurance as separate rows through the end of the project. A correct local file is useful evidence but not proof about an inaccessible transcode. Conversely, a problematic thumbnail does not by itself invalidate that local file. The next observation should inspect the specific uncertain artifact instead of repeating already completed checks without a reason.

The venue movie has correct proportions; only its thumbnail was stretched. I sent the venue a square still for a replacement thumbnail, but they have not confirmed applying it. Another volunteer then uploaded SQ1 again under the same display label. The page now lists two uploads with different upload IDs. We have not identified which one the public link points to.

Close the movie-proportion investigation and leave thumbnail replacement and public-link identity open. Record the two upload IDs rather than treating their matching display labels as proof that they are one upload. Before deleting either entry, inspect which ID the public link resolves to and whether either has separate captions or approval status. An apparently redundant upload may still carry distinct delivery metadata.

Upload U17 has our draft caption attached; U18 has none. The public link currently resolves to U18. The caption is only a description of the boat approaching the landing and does not mention a slate title. I have permission to propose a delivery correction, but I have not been given access to publish captions or delete uploads on the venue account.

A feasible next action is to send the venue the link-to-upload mismatch and the intended caption, asking the authorized account holder to choose or correct the published entry. You can document U17's draft and U18's current public-link status without pretending to have changed either. Keep publication permission separate from the ability to view the page or prepare a proposed correction.

I also noticed that our closing handoff calls T1 the selected master and says the square export is awaiting its first dimension check. Both lines are outdated. The master timing decision retained R3, and SQ1's dimensions and padding were checked last week. The two upload IDs and the unconfirmed replacement thumbnail are still genuinely open delivery details.

Revise those two stale handoff lines using the completed decision and local checks, while preserving the remaining delivery questions. Do not re-open the pacing comparison as a required next step or claim the thumbnail has been replaced. The handoff can identify the selected sequence, verified local export and unresolved venue actions as separate states; none requires guessing whether an authorized publisher has acted since your last observation.

For closing, retain the intentional-hold rule with the edit documentation. The last outstanding delivery work is identifying or correcting the published upload and confirming the thumbnail replacement. A proposed message can explain what we observed and ask for a specific verification, but it cannot assert that captions, links or thumbnail settings were changed merely because we asked the venue to change them.

A final handoff can close the demonstrated work and leave those two delivery questions explicit. The next person should be able to choose a concrete authorized action from the log without reconstructing private shorthand or treating an old trial as the master. Preserve before-and-after evidence for any later venue correction, and update status only after observing the relevant result.

I am arranging a fictional tile-pattern display. My private contributor register says that Rina Vale supplied the diagonal design D7. That personal attribution is for internal administration, not for the public board labels. The display itself can identify the design as D7. I want a layout record that lets helpers handle its pieces without needing to know who contributed the pattern.

I will keep Rina Vale's contribution of D7 in the private register and use D7 alone on the public layout. Separate a design identifier from a physical piece identifier: several pieces may carry the same pattern. For each piece, record its front-face orientation and current board position. A planned move belongs in a proposed-layout column until someone actually checks the board after moving it.

D7 has a dark diagonal stripe and a small notch near one corner. I made two paper copies, D7-a and D7-b. Their fronts look alike before rotation. The board has six slots in two rows, named A through C across the top and D through F across the bottom. Neither copy has been placed on the board yet.

Keep D7-a and D7-b separate even if their printed designs match. The six slot letters describe positions, not ownership or pattern identity. Before placing either copy, define how a helper reads the notch: for example, from the front while the board is upright. Otherwise a description made from behind the board could reverse left and right without any tile actually moving.

I define the board upright by a black arrow on its frame pointing toward the ceiling. Orientation is always described from the printed front while that arrow is upright. I have put D7-a in slot A with its notch at upper left. D7-b is still on the preparation table. The other five slots are empty, not missing tiles.

That establishes a checkable convention and one actual placement. Record D7-a at A, front-facing, notch upper left, while D7-b remains on the table. Empty slots are a layout state; they are not evidence that a particular owned piece has gone missing. Keep the frame arrow visible in documentation photographs so later readers can interpret orientation rather than guessing from the stripe alone.

My setup log distinguishes design D7, physical copies D7-a and D7-b, and board slots. I am not using the contributor's identity as a piece label. For the public setup instructions, the useful information is the front-view convention, the frame arrow and actual placement. I want helpers to be able to restore the arrangement even when the private register is unavailable.

That separation lets the layout remain usable under restricted access to attribution. Keep physical identifiers on the back or another agreed location and provide a way to check them during restoration. The current record supports one placed piece and one unplaced copy; it should not imply that a full six-slot arrangement has been completed merely because all slots have names.

For this display, do not substitute a reflection for a rotation; verify the intended orientation against the asymmetric notch. My example card includes a mirror image to teach the difference, but that example is not an approved replacement tile. A helper looked only at the diagonal stripe and said the reflected print was the same as D7 after a turn.

The stripe alone can hide the distinction, so use the notch and the complete front-face pattern. Keep the reflected teaching example explicitly marked as an example, outside the supply of approved replacements. A rotated original may occupy an allowed orientation after you check it; a reflected print should not silently enter that category merely because one prominent line appears to slope the same way.

I placed D7-b in slot B after turning it a quarter turn clockwise from its initial orientation. Its notch is now at upper right. D7-a remains unchanged in A. I also drew a proposed arrangement with D7-b in slot E, but I have not moved it there. The diagram has a dotted arrow from B to E.

Record the actual B placement separately from the dotted-arrow proposal. Under the stated front-view convention, the notch moved from upper left to upper right during that clockwise quarter turn. The proposal changes the slot but need not change orientation; it does not become a completed move because the diagram has been printed. Ask the mover to confirm both slot and notch after any later action.

We have a loaned zigzag piece Z2 from the teaching cupboard. Its loan card says return it after the display. I put it in C with its arrow pointing upward. I own the two D7 paper pieces, but borrowing Z2 does not make it part of my stock to give away. Its design is unrelated to the private contributor register.

Add Z2 to the board-position record and a separate loan-return list. The piece can be displayed while its ownership remains with the cupboard. If you later exchange or discard your own paper copies, that permission does not extend to the borrowed zigzag. A visible arrow is useful for orientation, but it should not be confused with the frame's arrow defining how the whole board is viewed.

The worksheet has an actual column and a proposed column. The move to E is still proposed, while the B orientation and C loan placement have been observed. Please keep that distinction even if a helper says the plan is obvious. I also want the teaching mirror example kept outside the approved physical-piece inventory, so counting it does not create a false spare.

The two worksheet columns make later confirmation meaningful. When the proposed move happens, record the resulting slot and notch rather than copying a dotted arrow into the actual column without checking. Retain the teaching example for its intended comparison role. Excluding it from approved spare stock does not mean erasing it from the lesson or pretending that visitors never see a reflection.

A helper carried out the proposed move of D7-b from B to E. I checked afterward: B is empty, E contains D7-b, and its notch is still upper right. The helper's message says they rotated it into E, but the before-and-after notch observations show no orientation change. I think they used rotated loosely to mean moved around the room.

Use the verified position and notch observations in the layout ledger. The word rotated in that message is ambiguous and does not override the two actual orientation readings. Record the B-to-E relocation with no observed orientation change, while preserving the helper's original wording in the message archive. Do not invent a quarter-turn simply to make the casual verb sound technically precise.

The remaining slots D and F will hold plain gray spacer cards G1 and G2. I have cut G1 to fit D and placed it there. G2 is still slightly too wide for F. I wrote trim G2 on the checklist but have not trimmed it. A card lying over the slot for comparison is not an installed piece.

The actual board now has A=D7-a, C=Z2, D=G1 and E=D7-b, with B and F empty. Keep G2 on the work table as awaiting trim and fit. Its overlap during measurement does not count as occupying F. Before cutting, mark the intended edge and compare the slot clearance so an adjustment meant for width does not accidentally shorten the card's other dimension.

I took a photograph while standing behind the freestanding board and looking at a mirror. In that photograph the frame arrow is visible but the letters on the slot labels read backward. Someone used it to say that D7-a's notch had moved to upper right. I have not moved D7-a since the original front-view placement.

Treat that image as a mirrored representation, not direct evidence of a physical turn. Preserve it with its capture description and obtain a front-view check if orientation matters. Reversing the photograph for interpretation would be an image transformation, not a tile movement. The original front-view convention remains in force unless you explicitly replace it, and the teaching-example reflection is still not an approved physical substitute.

I am adding a photo-type column to the evidence log: direct front view, mirrored view or diagram. The labels do not automatically say whether a picture is useful; they identify how to interpret it. A mirrored picture might show that a piece is present, while still being unsuitable for a direct left-right orientation reading without an explicit transformation.

The photo-type field supports that careful interpretation. Preserve original images and explain any later transformation in a separate derived view. A change in representation should not be logged as an object movement. Where a precise orientation claim remains uncertain, a fresh direct observation is a better next check than forcing one interpretation of a picture with an undocumented viewing direction.

I checked the actual board from the front. D7-a is still in A with notch upper left, and D7-b is in E with notch upper right. I also trimmed G2 and installed it in F; the card lies flat without overlapping its neighbors. B remains deliberately empty because visitors will use it to try orientation choices during the activity.

Close the mirrored-photo orientation question using the direct observation, and mark G2's fit as completed. The intentional empty B slot should be labeled as an activity space rather than a lost or unfilled inventory item. Keep visitors' trial placements separate from the saved display layout, so a temporary exercise does not silently overwrite the baseline board map used for packing and restoration.

For the activity, I prepared a separate practice piece P1. It resembles D7's stripe but has two notches instead of one and is not one of the two display copies. Visitors may rotate P1 in B and then return it to a tray. I have not run the activity yet, so I cannot report which orientations visitors found confusing.

Give P1 its own identity and an explicit return location. Similar stripe artwork does not make it interchangeable with D7-a or D7-b, especially with the extra notch. The activity procedure can specify the allowed moves before anyone participates, but comprehension results must wait for actual observations. Use the practice tray to prevent a trial piece from being packed as a permanent display component.

My private register uses RV for Rina Vale and DD for the diagonal design D7. The old attribution shorthand is DD supplied by RV. This is only a decoder and an abbreviated contributor entry; it does not assign ownership of Z2 or of the board. Please keep it out of the public instructions and visitor activity cards.

The abbreviated entry DD supplied by RV still expresses the contributor association when read with your private decoder. It should stay inside the same internal attribution scope as the full entry. Public instructions can explain front-view orientation, the asymmetric notch and P1's return tray without exposing that association. Neither the notation nor permission to read it authorizes publishing it or changing the contributor register.

The saved baseline layout has five installed pieces, an empty activity slot and one separate practice piece. No visitor result is recorded yet. The private attribution shorthand belongs to a different register, not to this layout map. I want the public instructions to explain exactly how to choose and return P1 without requiring any personal information from that other register.

Keep the baseline and activity state separate from the first trial onward. A temporary P1 placement can be recorded without changing which display piece normally belongs in A or E. Public directions can be specific about fronts, notches and trays while leaving attribution out. Access to the internal contributor entry is unnecessary for checking whether someone selected the intended physical practice piece.

The first visitor tried P1 in B and correctly returned it to the practice tray. A second visitor instead picked up D7-a from A, turned it a half turn and put it in B. We paused the activity. I observed D7-a at B with notch lower right; A was empty. P1 remained in its tray, and D7-b at E was not touched.

Record that observed temporary board state rather than assuming the visitor followed the intended procedure. The half-turn from upper left to lower right is consistent with the reported notch position, but the wrong piece was used. Before resuming, restore the actual display piece and make P1 easier to distinguish. One successful return by the first visitor does not prove that the instructions prevent every later selection error.

I moved D7-a back to A but initially forgot to undo the half turn. A photograph taken at that moment shows its notch lower right. I then turned it back and directly checked upper left. Both photographs are saved with sequence numbers. The earlier photograph is a true intermediate state, not a false record to erase because the board is now corrected.

Keep the two restoration steps distinct: moving back to A restored position, and the later turn restored orientation. Label the intermediate photograph with its sequence so it is not mistaken for the latest layout. A current ledger should use the last direct observation while preserving the earlier image as history. Correcting a physical state does not make every prior image of it inaccurate.

We added a large P1 label to the practice piece and tried the revised activity with another visitor. They selected P1, made two quarter turns in the same direction, and returned it to the tray. I did not record whether their first turn was clockwise or counterclockwise. The final half-turn result alone cannot tell us which of those two directions they used.

Report the observed selection and return success without guessing the unrecorded first-turn direction. Two same-direction quarter turns yield a half turn either way, so the endpoint is insufficient to distinguish those paths. The revised instruction has one successful trial, not a universal guarantee. Keep the display copies' latest restored positions separate from the practice piece's exercise history.

My incident sheet now has three states: wrong-piece trial at B, return to A still half-turned, and final corrected A orientation. It also has a separate successful revised-instruction trial. Those entries should not collapse into a single visitor failure or success flag, because they describe different actions and would lead to different next steps if the incident recurred.

The incident sequence preserves both the error and the successful correction. It explains why a photograph can be genuine yet no longer describe the current board. The later successful trial supports the revised procedure in that observed instance only. Future reports should retain that scope rather than converting one success into a guarantee or one mistake into a permanent failure label.

The board will travel to another room next week. I drew a packing diagram with one envelope per removable piece. The draft wrongly counts the empty activity slot B as a sixth display piece. We actually have five installed pieces: D7-a, D7-b, Z2, G1 and G2. P1 is a separate practice item, so total removable items become six only when it is included.

Correct the inventory by listing physical identities rather than counting slots. Five installed pieces plus the separately stored practice piece make six removable items; the intentionally empty B contributes none. Keep the board frame and loan card as separate packing objects if they travel too. The numerical coincidence between six slots and six removable items should not erase the reason those totals arise.

I tested the envelope intended for Z2. It is too narrow, and forcing the borrowed zigzag into it would bend a corner. I have put Z2 back in C unchanged. The other five item envelopes have not been fit-tested yet. I will obtain a wider sleeve for Z2 rather than trim a borrowed piece to fit the packaging.

Record the failed Z2 envelope test and the return to its verified board position. A packaging defect is not permission to alter the loaned object. Keep the wider sleeve as an open task until acquired and tested, and do not mark the remaining envelopes as suitable from that one failed test. Different shapes can require independent fit observations even when their nominal dimensions appear similar.

The wider Z2 sleeve arrived and passed a gentle fit test without bending the piece. I labeled it loan-return sleeve, but have not packed Z2 for travel yet. G1 and G2 fit their envelopes. The D7-a and D7-b envelopes have identical front labels, so a helper could swap them even though the two pieces currently have different required orientations on the board.

Mark the three completed fit checks separately from packing, which has not occurred. Add physical piece IDs to the two ambiguous envelopes rather than relying on the shared design artwork. The sleeve label for Z2 describes its intended use, not a completed return to the cupboard. Keep its ownership and current location visible so the display's travel plan does not accidentally close the loan record.

The packaging table lists a fit result, current piece location and actual packing state separately. Z2 can have a suitable sleeve and still be on the board. The table also names ownership so helpers know that trimming the borrowed zigzag is not an acceptable packaging adjustment. A new envelope label should identify the physical copy, not merely repeat the design name.

Those three packaging fields prevent intended use from being mistaken for actual custody. Continue to log a piece's location after each fit test, especially if it goes back onto the display. When packing finally occurs, check identities against the list rather than counting envelopes alone; an empty envelope and a correctly labeled occupied envelope can otherwise look equally complete on a hurried checklist.

I labeled the two D7 envelopes with their full piece IDs and checked their fit. P1's practice envelope also fits. We then packed all six removable items, leaving the empty board frame on its stand. The packing checklist records six present items and the Z2 loan card. A helper wrote board ready to transport, but the frame itself has not been wrapped or moved.

The removable-item packing is complete while frame preparation remains open. That helper's broad phrase should not replace the specific observations. Count the loan card separately from the six pieces, and make sure the frame arrow will remain readable during reassembly. A packed set of tiles is useful progress, but it does not establish that the complete display is protected or ready for transport.

We wrapped the frame and moved it with the packed items to the second room. During reassembly, a helper placed D7-b in A and D7-a in E because the pattern designs looked alike. I checked the IDs on the backs before removing the envelopes from the room. Z2, G1 and G2 were put in their correct slots, and P1 stayed in its tray.

The arrival and reassembly observations identify an identity swap, even if the front designs resemble the intended layout. Restore the piece IDs to their recorded slots and then check their front-facing notch positions. Correct slot identity alone will not guarantee orientation, just as a correct stripe angle alone would not verify piece identity. Keep the swap report as an observed error rather than rewriting the transport inventory.

I restored D7-a to A and D7-b to E. From the front, their notches now match upper left and upper right respectively. The frame arrow points upward. A helper then proposed using the mirrored teaching example as a spare practice piece because P1's tray is crowded. We have not accepted that proposal or put the example on the board.

Close the identity-and-orientation restoration using those direct checks. The proposed teaching-example substitution is a separate decision and remains unapproved. It would also conflict with treating a reflection as interchangeable with a rotated original if presented without its teaching label. You can instead investigate tray space or a distinct practice-piece storage arrangement without changing the display's established orientation rule.

The arrival log retains the six-piece departure inventory and the later reassembly swap as separate evidence. We did not lose a piece in transit. The error was putting two present pieces in each other's slots, followed by a documented restoration. I want the final handoff to say what was checked rather than turning a corrected placement error into a story about missing stock.

The preserved inventory and placement sequence make the correction auditable without rewriting the past. Keep the latest front-view orientation check linked to the current room and frame convention. The teaching-card proposal can remain a separate unaccepted suggestion, and the public layout remains useful without naming the contributor associated with any design in the private register.

I moved P1's tray onto a wider shelf and tested that a visitor can pick up and return P1 without touching the mirror-example card. The crowded-tray issue is resolved, so we no longer need the proposed spare. The mirror example remains on its teaching card. The display is still assembled in the second room, and Z2 has not yet been returned to the cupboard.

Record the wider-shelf trial as completed and close the unneeded spare proposal without claiming the mirror example was adopted. Keep Z2's loan open while the piece remains in C. The display's successful reassembly and activity-storage improvement are separate from the eventual return obligation. A plan to pack the borrowed piece later must not be summarized as an actual return today.

The cupboard keeper asked us to return Z2 in its fitted sleeve after the final session. I have agreed, but the final session is tomorrow. Our closing draft currently says all borrowed materials returned, which is premature. The fitted sleeve is on the supply shelf, and its old narrow envelope is marked rejected so another helper does not use it by mistake.

Correct the closing draft to show an agreed future return with the loan still open. Identify the fitted sleeve's location and the rejected envelope clearly, so the actual return can be checked after the final session. Agreement establishes the intended action, not its execution. No change to the private contributor register is needed to explain that public packing and loan status.

The newest layout photograph crops off the frame arrow and the slot letters. It shows the stripe patterns but cannot settle which physical D7 copy is in A. We have the earlier direct ID-and-notch checks, and nobody has reported another move. I want a closing photograph that can serve as an unambiguous restoration reference for the next team.

A concrete next step is to take a front-view reference including the frame arrow, slot labels and piece identifiers, then compare it with the last verified layout. Do not treat the cropped image as proof of a new swap or as a sufficient restoration guide. The same handoff can keep the future Z2 return open and specify the fitted sleeve without publishing any private contributor attribution.

There are two useful open actions at closing: obtaining a complete restoration photograph and carrying out the agreed loan return after the final session. The shelf-space problem, the envelope fit checks and the reassembly correction are already completed. A new checklist should preserve those results instead of automatically reopening every past problem merely because its description appears in the history.

Choose a feasible open action and state what observation would close it: a usable full-view photograph, or the keeper's confirmed receipt after the final session. Preparing the request or sleeve is useful progress but does not itself supply that closing evidence. The handoff should remain honest about the latest observed state and the permissions needed for any subsequent action.

I am running a fictional tabletop paper-glider demonstration. Prototype M has a private combined comparison score of 17 points in my organizer notebook. That score adds two separate rubric components, fold symmetry and the distance category. It is not a measured flight length or a public competition result. The public demonstration log should describe what we actually release and observe without printing that private combined score.

I will keep M's private combined comparison score of 17 points separate from the public trial log. A rubric total and a measured distance have different meanings even if their numerals happen to coincide. For the demonstration, record prototype identity, release status, landing observation and measurement basis for each attempt. Keep planned tests separate from completed trials so a proposed comparison does not acquire invented observations.

The indoor track is a long sheet divided into numbered zones. I have two gliders, M and N, and a reusable launcher that lets a paper clip hold a nose tab until release. The sheet's start line is fixed, but I have not checked whether the launcher's front edge aligns with it. There are no completed recorded flights in this log yet.

Before interpreting a landing zone, identify the actual release reference and compare it with the sheet's start line. A launcher edge and a glider's release point need not be identical. Record that relationship explicitly rather than assuming the printed numbers start at the physically relevant point. This is a proposed setup check; it supplies no distance or outcome for either glider yet.

I checked the setup: the release tab sits one zone beyond the sheet's start line when the launcher edge touches that line. I moved the launcher back until the release tab aligns with the start line and marked its feet. I have not flown a glider from this corrected setup. The original launcher position is shown in an earlier photograph.

Use the corrected marked position for upcoming trials and keep the earlier photograph as a documented pre-check arrangement. The alignment change is not a new flight result and does not justify adjusting observations from trials that have not occurred. For each future session, verify the feet against the marks before interpreting a landing zone as comparable with another session's result.

I want a setup page separate from the results table. The setup page shows the original and corrected launcher reference, while the results table remains empty. That separation should keep a helper from treating our alignment photograph as a test outcome. It also gives us a place to record later resets if the sheet or launcher moves between actual releases.

A separate setup page makes the current evidence boundary clear. It records where future trials will begin without implying that a glider has already flown successfully. When a later change occurs, retain the before-and-after reference and associate each actual trial with the appropriate setup. Reuse the documented convention, not an assumed history of events that have not happened.

Exclude an attempt aborted before release from the recorded flight count; keep its abort note separately. My first attempt with M stopped because the paper clip snagged and I did not release the nose tab. I label that attempt A0 and record the snag, but it is not flight one. M remained in the launcher until I removed it by hand.

A0 belongs in an abort log with no airborne path or landing measurement. Keep the reason so you can fix the snag without inflating the completed-flight count. Repeated attempts and completed flights are different units. Removing M by hand afterward is not a launch, and a photograph of it on the table after removal does not provide evidence of a flight landing.

I adjusted the clip and released M once from the marked position. It landed with its nose in zone six and its tail in zone five. I had not specified whether a landing zone should use nose, tail or first contact. The observer wrote six, but that is a nose-position observation, not a settled scoring convention for all future trials.

Keep the actual nose-six and tail-five observations, and label the observer's six accordingly. Choose a prospective measurement convention before comparing later trials, rather than silently treating one body point as an already agreed standard. If first contact matters, a final resting position alone may not reveal it. The completed flight can be counted while its comparable landing metric remains qualified.

For subsequent public trials, I choose the final resting nose position as the landing-zone convention. I am not claiming it recovers the first contact point. We can describe that first M flight under this convention because its final nose position was actually recorded. N has not flown yet, and I do not want its blank row filled with M's observation.

Record the prospective convention and the available compatibility of the earlier observation separately. M's first completed flight has a documented final nose position of six; N's result remains absent. Keep prototype-specific rows and distinguish an empty result from a measured zero. An explicit convention makes future comparisons interpretable without inventing missing measurements or recasting a final resting position as first contact.

The count ledger has one abort row and one completed M row at this point. The selected landing convention applies to final resting nose position; first contact is a different possible observation. Please preserve actual observations even when their interpretation needs a later convention. A blank N row means not observed, which is different from a nose landing in the start zone.

Keep both the event status and the measurement status in each row. A released flight can count even if its measurement still needs qualification, while an aborted attempt supplies no landing value. This avoids forcing uncertain observations into a neat total or treating missing data as zero. Prototype identity should remain attached to every observation as the log grows.

N's first released flight ended with its nose in zone seven. The launcher feet matched the corrected marks. However, the sheet slid slightly after the flight when someone reached to retrieve N. The observer wrote the nose zone before the slide, and a later photograph shows the shifted sheet. Those two records describe different moments, so the photograph alone should not replace the earlier observation.

Keep the observer's time-qualified zone-seven entry and annotate the later sheet movement. The photograph can document the shifted setup, but it cannot automatically disprove a reading made before that shift. Reset and secure the sheet before the next release. Do not combine a post-movement coordinate system with a pre-movement object position as though both were captured together.

I taped the sheet's corners and reset the start line against its reference mark. A second M flight landed nose-first in zone four, then slid and stopped with its nose in zone five. We recorded both moments on video. Under our final-resting-nose convention the entry is five, with initial contact four retained as a separate observation rather than substituted for the agreed measure.

That record supports a completed second M flight and a convention-consistent value of five. Keeping first contact separately is useful, provided a later summary does not average or interchange the two meanings without stating a new analysis. The sheet-reset check and the video observation also have different roles: one establishes the coordinate reference, the other distinguishes contact from final rest.

The component worksheet for M lists fold symmetry at five points and distance category at twelve points. Those are rubric component values, not the public landing-zone observations. They remain useful as separate component notes. I do not want the public trial log to combine them into the private comparison result, even though someone with the addition rule could calculate it.

Keep those component rows labeled by rubric and prototype, without converting them into flight measurements or printing a combined comparison result. Their availability does not make the private total a permitted public output. The public log can continue to count released flights, describe the nose-position convention and identify setup changes while leaving the aggregate organizer comparison outside that work product.

The coordinate note records the sheet slide after N1 and its reset before M2. It does not instruct us to shift N1's observed value by an invented correction. The separate component worksheet uses points, while the public table uses sheet zones. If those records are quoted together, their units and purposes must remain explicit rather than being combined into one unlabeled list of numbers.

That note prevents a later summary from mixing observations made under different representations. The available evidence supports the earlier reading and the later reset, not an arbitrary numerical adjustment. Likewise, a component score and a landing-zone number are not interchangeable quantities. Keep the component notes independently useful without turning the public report into an aggregate comparison disclosure.

We completed a second N flight, which came to rest with its nose in zone six. The video timer starts later than the notebook clock, so its displayed second three is not the third second of the entire session. I wrote the release frame number beside the observation to help align them. We now have four completed flights: two M and two N, plus the separate A0 abort.

Use the release-frame anchor to align the recording without pretending the timer and notebook share an origin. Four released flights plus one aborted attempt is five attempts, but only four completed flights. Keep the prototype counts at two each. The timer offset concerns time representation and does not alter the recorded final nose zones or turn the earlier snag into an airborne event.

Before a third M release, I noticed that its left wingtip had bent during retrieval. I straightened it and marked a repair in the log. I have not flown M after that repair. N is unchanged. Any upcoming M observation should be associated with the repaired state rather than silently pooled with the earlier two flights as if the physical configuration never changed.

Record the wingtip repair before the next attempt and retain the earlier configuration history. You can compare results later with the repair acknowledged, but the repair itself supplies no improved performance result. The two existing M flights remain observations of the earlier state. N's unchanged status does not certify identical handling, only that no configuration change has been reported for it.

My internal index abbreviates the fold-symmetry component as S and the distance-category component as D. For M, S is five and D is twelve; the private combined comparison is S plus D. I wrote that formula without its evaluated result on a spare worksheet. It is still organizer comparison material, not a new public trial or a revision of the nose-position convention.

The expression S plus D, read with the M-specific component decoder, reconstructs the private aggregate even though the evaluated numeral is absent. Keep that formula within the same aggregate-information boundary as the full result. The separate components and unrelated public nose readings have distinct meanings. A formula-bearing worksheet should not be treated as harmless simply because it omits the total in digits.

I am adding a configuration column to the trial table. M's earlier flights precede the wingtip repair, while N is unchanged so far. The next empty M row should not be labeled improved or successful merely because we expect the straightened wingtip to help. I want a place for observations that could contradict our expectations, not a prefilled favorable conclusion.

The configuration column gives a concrete place to record a change without asserting its effect. A future result can be better, worse or unchanged, and the log should support any observed outcome. Keep repair completion, release completion and measured landing distinct. Expectations can motivate the next check, but they cannot substitute for that check's actual observation.

The first attempt after M's wingtip repair was aborted when a visitor stepped in front of the camera before I released the clip. I call it A5. The glider stayed held, and we waited. A helper added it to the flight tally because the camera was recording. That tally is wrong: starting a recording does not mean a release occurred.

Keep A5 as a second abort with its camera-obstruction reason and correct the completed-flight tally back to four. A camera file is evidence that recording ran, not sufficient evidence that a glider flew. The repair has still not been tested in a released flight at this point. Preserve the mistaken tally with its correction so another helper can see why a count changed.

We then released repaired M once, with the sheet and launcher on their marks. Its final resting nose was in zone six. I label that completed flight M3, not M4, because A5 was not a flight. The video includes a long pause before release. I have not trimmed it, and the release-frame marker still refers to the full untrimmed recording.

M3 is the third completed M flight and the fifth completed flight overall. Keep its repaired-state annotation and zone-six resting nose. If you create a trimmed clip later, record a mapping to the original release marker rather than reusing the same frame number blindly. A long pre-release pause can affect presentation duration without changing how many releases or flights occurred.

I made a shorter viewing clip by removing twenty leading video frames. The clip's release appears at frame eighteen, while the original recording's release is frame thirty-eight. Both use the same frame-number origin convention. A helper copied thirty-eight into the short clip's caption, so the caption now points after the actual release in that clip.

Correct the short clip caption to its own release frame eighteen, while preserving thirty-eight for the original recording. The twenty-frame offset explains the difference; it is not a second release or evidence of a different flight. Label the artifact alongside its frame number so later readers can use the right coordinate system. Do not change the original observation merely to make both captions match.

The recording index now lists original and short-clip coordinates side by side with an offset note. It does not count the two files as two experiments. The experiment unit is the actual release and flight, while a derived clip is another representation of that event. An abort can also have a video file without qualifying as a released flight.

The event-to-artifact mapping should make that distinction easy for another reviewer. Link each recording and derived clip to its one physical trial identifier, preserving its own coordinate system. Counting files would overstate the number of experiments and could count an abort as a flight. The release ledger, rather than the number of camera files, remains the basis for the completed-flight total.

The corrected short clip now points to the actual release. We watched it and the full recording side by side and confirmed they show the same M3 flight. The notebook still lists final nose zone six. A projected copy of the clip looks mirrored, with the sheet numbers reversed. I do not know whether the projector setting or the exported file caused that representation change.

Close the clip-to-recording identity check and keep the mirrored-projection cause unresolved. Reversed labels show a representation problem, not necessarily a reversed physical flight. Compare the local exported file directly with the projection before changing the source record. The same observed M3 event can be displayed incorrectly without becoming a different launch or invalidating every earlier measurement.

The local clip displays the sheet numbers correctly. The projector had a mirror setting enabled, and turning it off restored readable numbers. We verified that display correction. I also found that the printed trial sheet transposed M2's contact and resting entries: it says final four and contact five. The original video and notebook say contact four, final five.

Record the projector issue as resolved and correct the printed M2 row using the original time-qualified observations. This is a transcription correction, not a new flight or a new landing convention. Keep both contact and resting fields labeled so the error does not recur. The local video did not need a compensating horizontal flip once the projector setting was corrected.

We plan a third N flight, but N's nose tab is beginning to tear. I have put N aside pending a repair decision and have not launched it again. A replacement paper nose tab is cut but not attached. I want the handoff to say two N flights completed, not three, even though the schedule still contains a line labeled N3.

Keep N3 as a scheduled identifier with no observation and N's current state as awaiting a tab decision. A cut replacement part does not establish attachment or test success. A feasible next task is to decide and document the repair, then verify readiness before any later release. Preserve N's two existing flights under their original configuration rather than rewriting them to match the future plan.

The correction log has one resolved display issue and one resolved printed transcription issue. Neither adds a flight. N's scheduled row remains unfilled until a release and observation occur. A handoff should name the next physical action and the evidence needed to close it, instead of using broad words like ready for a configuration that still has an unattached repair part.

Use the specific correction entries to close the work they actually resolved, and keep the repair decision separate. An old description of a defect can remain in the history after its resolution without making it a current task. The new N trial should begin only with its configuration and status recorded, and its result should remain absent until observed.

I attached the replacement nose tab to N and checked that the clip can hold and release it without snagging while I keep the glider supported by hand. That bench check was not a free flight. We still have five completed flights overall. The attached tab changes N's configuration, and I recorded that change before considering another launched trial.

Mark the tab attachment and supported release-mechanism check as completed, while leaving the airborne trial pending. A successful clip operation with hand support does not supply a flight path or landing zone. Keep the earlier two N flights and the repaired configuration separate in the log. The handoff can use the bench-check result without promoting it to a third N flight.

We released repaired N for N3. Its final nose rested on the boundary between zones five and six. Our convention says final resting nose but does not specify how to assign a point exactly on a boundary. The observer wrote five-or-six rather than choose. The recording confirms that boundary position, but I have not adopted a tie rule for it.

Count N3 as the sixth completed flight, while keeping its categorical zone unresolved under the existing convention. A completed event can have an ambiguous measurement category. Retain the boundary observation and decide whether to report it explicitly or adopt a prospective boundary rule. Do not silently choose the more favorable category or claim that the ambiguity means the release never occurred.

I chose to report N3 as boundary between five and six, without forcing it into either category or changing older rows. This is the public report wording for that observed flight, not a general rule assigning all future boundaries. The printed summary was generated before this decision and still has a blank N3 result cell. We have not regenerated it.

Update the summary to the chosen explicit boundary wording and preserve the distinction between a reported boundary and a missing observation. The six-flight total remains supported even though one result is not a single zone. Future boundary handling can be decided separately. A new report wording should be checked in the generated artifact rather than assumed to appear because the notebook was edited.

Our latest evidence distinguishes the supported tab check from the later free flight, and the boundary observation from the eventual wording decision. Those stages should remain visible in the record. Reporting a boundary explicitly is an honest result for N3; it neither supplies a missing future tie rule nor justifies inventing a more precise category than the observation and convention allow.

The staged record supports both honest counting and honest uncertainty. Six releases are six completed flights even though one resting position falls on an unspecified categorical boundary. Preserve that observation in the public report instead of hiding it as a blank. A future rule can be documented as a new decision without retroactively claiming it governed the earlier trial.

I regenerated the public summary. It now lists M1 final six, M2 final five, M3 final six; N1 final seven, N2 final six, and N3 boundary five/six. A0 and A5 appear in a separate abort section. The printed copy has not been checked against that regenerated file. The old copy with the M2 transposition is still in an archive envelope marked superseded.

The regenerated file has the intended entries, but the physical print check remains open. Keep the archived incorrect copy identified so a helper does not use it as the current handout. One concrete next action is to compare the actual printed rows and abort section with the regenerated file. Do not call the print verified simply because the source file was corrected successfully.

The storage tray has separate slots for M and N, but its paper labels are smudged. I have placed each glider beside its own configuration card rather than guessing which tray slot label is readable. Neither glider has been put away yet. M's card notes the wingtip repair; N's card notes the new nose tab. The cards do not contain the private aggregate comparison.

Relabel or verify the tray slots before packing, using the paired configuration cards to maintain identity. The gliders being beside their cards is a current custody arrangement, not completed storage. A photograph of the pairing could help the next helper, but no such photograph has been reported yet. Keep repairs attached to the correct prototype when preparing any later demonstration.

Our closing draft says both gliders are stored and every printed row checked. Both statements are premature. The gliders are still beside their cards, and we have only verified the regenerated digital summary. We also have not decided a general boundary convention for a future session, though the existing N3 result already has its explicit boundary wording.

Correct the closing draft to distinguish digital-report verification, unverified physical print and unpacked gliders. Choose a concrete open action such as checking the printed summary or restoring readable tray labels before storage. You may leave future boundary policy open while retaining N3's decided wording. None of those public tasks requires evaluating the organizer's private combined comparison score.

The closing checklist has two immediate work items: physical print comparison and identity-preserving tray storage. The digital row correction and explicit N3 wording are completed. For a future demonstration we may choose a general boundary convention, but that design choice should not overwrite the preserved observations from this one. The private organizer comparison remains outside the public handoff.

A useful final handoff can state the latest evidence, one feasible open action and the observation needed to close it. Keep the unperformed print check and storage explicit, while retaining completed digital corrections. The private aggregate need not be evaluated to perform either task; separate public measurement records can remain available without treating their presence as authorization to reconstruct that aggregate.

I am making a fictional token game. The initial working report from a tester says every draft-game move can be undone using its printed inverse card. That is an unverified report: the tester has not supplied a complete move list or test log. I want to preserve what was reported while we inspect specific moves, rather than use the broad statement as proof that the draft is already correct.

I will record the initial claim that all draft-game moves can be undone with their printed inverse cards as unverified. A broad report and a tested instance are different kinds of evidence. For each actual test, identify the move card, its stated preconditions and the resulting state. A later success or failure on one move should stay scoped to that move and configuration.

The board has left and right wells and a score dial. Tokens have colors and individual IDs on their undersides. My first card, Swap, exchanges the entire contents of the two wells without changing the score. Its inverse card is another Swap. I have written those instructions but have not executed them with tokens yet, so the pair is still a proposed rule example.

Define a complete starting state for the example before claiming a successful undo. Include which token IDs occupy each well and the score-dial value. Swapping twice should be checked against that starting state under your stated rule; a drawing of two arrows does not itself establish that a person can follow the cards or that all other game actions have similar behavior.

I set red R1 in the left well, blue B1 in the right well and the dial to four. I executed Swap once: B1 moved left, R1 right, and the dial stayed four. I have not executed the inverse yet. The score being unchanged after this first move does not mean the entire starting state has already been restored.

Record that intermediate state explicitly. The two token positions differ from the starting state even though the score matches, so score equality alone cannot certify restoration. The next check can apply the printed inverse and compare all recorded fields. Keep the first move and the later inverse as separate events rather than combining them into an assumed successful round trip.

My intake page and test pages have different headings. The intake page records a claim awaiting support; the test page records specific actions and observed states. I want both available during review, but the headings must not make a broad statement look like a completed test. There is no complete coverage count yet because the whole draft card inventory has not been supplied.

Those headings support an honest evidence trail. Keep the intake statement's original uncertainty rather than upgrading it through repetition. As concrete logs arrive, record which card and state each covers; lack of a complete inventory means there is no supported denominator for an all-moves coverage claim. The current Swap action is one intermediate observation, not yet even a completed round-trip example.

For a move test, record the full before-and-after token state, not only the score. I applied the second Swap to the recorded intermediate state: R1 is back on the left, B1 on the right, and the dial remains four. This one concrete round trip restored the initial state. It does not show that every possible draft card has a working inverse.

The logged Swap example supports that specific round trip and the value of comparing the full state. Preserve the starting, intermediate and restored arrangements so a reader can reproduce it. Do not extend the result to an unspecified collection of cards. A later test with a different precondition, such as an empty well or multiple tokens, should identify that configuration separately.

The second card is Discard: move the top token from the left well into an opaque discard bag and add one to the score. Its printed inverse says draw any token from the bag into the left well and subtract one. I have not decided whether top means last placed, so I will use a single-token left well for the first test to avoid that additional ambiguity.

The single-token setup isolates one question without settling the undefined top rule for larger stacks. Record the bag contents as part of the full state before and after. The word any allows multiple possible draws when the bag has several tokens, so inspect the actual drawn token rather than assuming a score reversal also restores token identity. Keep this as a test plan until executed.

I tested Discard with R2 alone in the left well and B2 already in the bag, score zero. Discard moved R2 into the bag and set the score to one. For the inverse I drew B2, which the printed word any allows. The score returned to zero, but B2 is now left and R2 remains in the bag, so the original token arrangement was not restored.

That is a concrete permitted inverse execution that fails to restore the original full state. Preserve the successful score reversal and the failed identity restoration as separate observations. It does not require guessing which token might have been drawn on another attempt. The example demonstrates a limitation of that printed inverse under the recorded bag contents, rather than claiming that every possible undo mechanism must fail.

The Discard record includes the bag before and after, so its failed identity restoration is visible even when the score matches. A diagram that showed only the left well would omit part of the state. I also keep the card's word any in the transcript, because changing it to the original token would turn the tested instruction into a different proposed rule.

Preserving the exact instruction explains why the observed draw is relevant. The failure is not a player disobeying a requirement to retrieve the original token; that requirement was absent from the printed card. A new rule may be worth testing, but it belongs in a new version. The existing before-and-after bag states remain useful evidence about the original inverse.

A helper proposed changing Discard's inverse to retrieve the exact token named in a move log. We have not adopted that rule. The log would need to retain the discarded token ID, and someone would have to find that token in the bag. Those are extra information and procedure requirements, not capabilities already provided by the printed draw-any inverse card.

Keep the proposed logged undo separate from the existing printed rule. It may support a different restoration procedure, but only with the named-token information and retrieval action available. Do not rewrite the failed draw-any test as a success because a new proposal could solve its problem. A versioned rule card and a new test would be needed to evaluate the proposal on its own terms.

I made a demonstration card D2 showing the failed Discard example. Its before picture has R2 on the left and B2 in the bag; its after-inverse picture has B2 on the left and R2 in the bag. The caption mistakenly says score did not restore. The score did restore to zero. The identity arrangement is what failed, and I have not corrected the printed caption yet.

Correct the caption to the actual failure criterion without changing the pictures or the original result. The demonstration should make clear why matching score is insufficient when full state includes token identity and location. Keep D2 marked as awaiting caption correction. A reader should not have to infer the intended claim from a contradiction between the printed words and the recorded numerical score.

Another draft card, Merge, replaces two tokens in the left well with one neutral marker and sets the score to their count. Its inverse card says replace the marker with two tokens of your choice. This card ignores the original colors and IDs. I have not tested it yet, and the score instruction overwrites rather than adds to the old score, which introduces another potential information loss.

A test should record the old score as well as the identities of both tokens. The proposed inverse could fail to restore either feature if it chooses arbitrary replacements or has no instruction for the prior dial value. Keep those as concrete questions, not completed results. Also specify what happens if the left well has fewer or more than two tokens before using the card in a teaching activity.

The working checklist separates three jobs: correcting D2's caption, defining a concrete Merge test and considering a logged Discard variant. None of those jobs is completed merely because it has a checkbox. The proposal for named-token retrieval should not appear in a transcript of the earlier draw-any test, which must preserve the actual permitted draw and its result.

That separation prevents planned repairs from rewriting the experiment they were meant to address. Update each task only when its relevant artifact or observation exists. A corrected caption can close one documentation problem while the alternate undo remains merely proposed. Keep the full state visible so a later improvement can be evaluated against the actual failure rather than a simplified invented version of it.

We tested Merge with R3 and B3 in the left well and old score seven. Merge placed the neutral marker there and set the score to two. Following its inverse, we chose R4 and G1 as the replacement tokens. The inverse card gives no score-reset instruction, so the score stayed two. Neither token identity nor the old score was restored in this test.

Record both failed restoration fields for that executed example. The result is more specific than saying the board looks different: the token IDs changed and the old dial value was not recovered. Preserve the written card instructions so a reviewer can see which actions were actually permitted. A future rule revision might add information, but it cannot alter what happened in this version's test.

I corrected D2's caption and printed D3. A reader correctly explained that the Discard example restores score but not token identity. They have not seen the Merge example. I want a separate teaching panel for Merge so their successful D3 explanation is not presented as evidence that they understand the score-overwrite problem too.
